one_line: Synthetic data for segmentation saturates at the generator's effective mode count, and the plateau is predictable from generator recall metrics before any downstream training
problem: Teams generate ever-larger synthetic segmentation sets without knowing when adding images stops helping, wasting generation compute and training time.
core_hypothesis: Downstream mIoU as a function of synthetic set size plateaus when the set exhausts the generator's distinct-mode capacity, so a generator-side diversity/recall measurement predicts the plateau location without training any segmenter.
falsifiable_prediction: For several generators of differing diversity, the synthetic-set size at which downstream mIoU gains fall below a threshold will correlate strongly (rank correlation) with a pre-computed generator recall/coverage score, and generating past that point yields near-zero gain.
why_important: A pre-training stopping rule for synthetic data generation would save large amounts of compute and settle how much synthetic data is worth making for a given generator.
why_possibly_novel: Scaling analyses of synthetic training data typically report curves post hoc; tying the plateau to an a priori generator-intrinsic coverage measurement, for dense prediction specifically, appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take 3 generators (e.g., differently-sized mask-conditioned diffusion models), compute a recall/coverage proxy on samples, generate nested synthetic sets (10k to 500k), train identical segmenters, locate plateaus, and test rank agreement between predicted and observed plateau ordering.
main_risk: Downstream plateaus may be driven by segmenter capacity or optimization budget rather than generator coverage, confounding the correlation.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: More synthetic data monotonically helps until it roughly matches real-data scale, and the safe strategy is to generate as much as budget allows.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Deduplication-adjusted effective sample size may matter more than mode coverage; a low-diversity generator could still help indefinitely if its samples act as a regularizer.
fastest_falsification: Two generators, three nested set sizes each, small segmenter, check whether plateau order matches coverage order; roughly one GPU-week.

one_line: The optimal synthetic-to-real mixing ratio follows a power law in the real-data count, so the right ratio for any dataset size is predictable from two pilot runs
problem: Every synthetic-data paper picks a mixing ratio by grid search at one dataset scale, and practitioners have no guidance for their own data regime.
core_hypothesis: The mIoU-optimal synthetic fraction decays as a power law in the number of real labeled images, with an exponent that is stable across datasets within a sensor family, because synthetic data substitutes for missing real coverage whose marginal value itself follows a power law.
falsifiable_prediction: Fitting the optimal-ratio curve at two small real-data scales will extrapolate the optimal ratio at a 10x larger scale to within a small factor, and this will hold across at least two segmentation datasets.
why_important: Turns an expensive per-project grid search into a two-point measurement, and gives synthetic-data economics a quantitative footing.
why_possibly_novel: Scaling laws exist for model and data size, but a transferable law for the mixing ratio between synthetic and real dense-label data has not, to my knowledge, been articulated as a testable power law.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one driving and one aerial dataset, sweep synthetic fraction at real-set sizes {250, 1k, 10k}, fit the law on the two small scales, predict and verify the optimum at 10k.
main_risk: The optimum may be flat and broad, making the 'optimal ratio' ill-defined and the law unfalsifiable in practice.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Mixing ratio is a dataset-specific hyperparameter with no expected regular structure across scales.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Ratio optima may be governed by class imbalance interactions that differ per dataset, destroying any cross-scale regularity.
fastest_falsification: Nine training runs on one dataset (3 ratios x 3 real sizes) to check whether the optimum moves monotonically with real size at all.

one_line: Synthetic data acts as a regularizer at low fractions and a distribution attractor at high fractions, producing a reproducible U-shaped real-domain error curve
problem: Reported effects of synthetic data range from strong gains to harm, and the field lacks a mechanism-level account that predicts which regime a given setup is in.
core_hypothesis: There are two competing mechanisms: small synthetic fractions add gradient noise and coverage (regularization; helps), while large fractions pull the learned distribution toward the generator's distribution (attraction; hurts on real data), yielding a U-shape in real-domain error versus synthetic fraction whose minimum shifts right as generator fidelity improves.
falsifiable_prediction: Real-domain error versus synthetic fraction will be non-monotonic with a single interior minimum, and the minimum's location will move toward higher fractions monotonically as the generator is made more faithful (e.g., by fine-tuning it on the target domain).
why_important: Explains contradictory literature results with one curve and tells practitioners which side of the U they are on before they scale up generation.
why_possibly_novel: The U-shape is often observed anecdotally; the claim that the minimum's location is a monotone function of generator fidelity is a sharper, mechanism-linked prediction that appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One dataset, one generator at three fidelity levels (base, lightly fine-tuned, heavily fine-tuned on target-domain images), sweep synthetic fraction in 6 steps, verify U-shape and monotone minimum shift.
main_risk: The two mechanisms may not be separable; fidelity fine-tuning also changes diversity, confounding the minimum shift.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Synthetic data helps up to some fraction and then merely stops helping; harm is attributed to low generator quality rather than a lawful attraction effect.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Harm at high fractions might be entirely explained by label noise in synthetic pairs rather than distribution attraction, which a label-noise-controlled variant would reveal.
fastest_falsification: Six-point fraction sweep with one generator on a small dataset; if error is monotone, the U-shape core claim dies immediately.

one_line: At matched compute, few-scenes-many-renders loses to many-scenes-few-renders by a margin that grows with target-domain layout diversity
problem: Synthetic pipelines choose between building many scene layouts (expensive) versus rendering many variations of few layouts (cheap), with no quantitative rule for the trade.
core_hypothesis: Scene-level diversity (layouts, object arrangements) is the binding constraint on transfer for segmentation, so image count per scene has sharply diminishing returns after a handful of renders, and the crossover point is a measurable function of target layout entropy.
falsifiable_prediction: Holding total rendered images fixed, sets with more distinct scenes will outperform sets with more renders-per-scene, and the performance gap will correlate with an independent measure of target-domain layout diversity across multiple target datasets.
why_important: Directly prices the most expensive part of synthetic pipelines (scene authoring) against the cheapest (re-rendering), guiding budget allocation.
why_possibly_novel: Ablations of renders-per-scene exist inside individual papers, but a cross-dataset law linking the optimal scenes-versus-renders trade to measured target layout entropy appears unformulated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Using a procedural scene generator, create matched-budget sets {100 scenes x 100 renders, 1k x 10, 10k x 1}, train identical segmenters, evaluate on two real targets with visibly different layout diversity (e.g., highway driving vs urban driving), test the predicted ordering and gap direction.
main_risk: Procedural scene quality may covary with scene count (authoring shortcuts), contaminating the comparison.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Total image count is the headline number that matters; appearance randomization over few scenes is considered an adequate substitute for scene diversity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For texture-bottlenecked targets (e.g., homogeneous industrial scenes), appearance diversity might dominate and reverse the ordering.
fastest_falsification: Two matched-budget sets (extreme ends), one segmenter, one target; a null or reversed gap at the extremes kills the strong version.

one_line: Near-duplicate synthetic images cause sharper memorization than near-duplicate real images because rendering noise is lower-entropy than capture noise
problem: Synthetic sets are full of near-duplicates (same scene, tiny parameter jitter), and their effect on dense-prediction training is assumed to mirror real-data duplication, which is likely wrong.
core_hypothesis: Because renderer/generator noise between near-duplicates is far lower-entropy than real capture noise, gradient updates from synthetic near-duplicates reinforce identical features, accelerating memorization and shrinking effective dataset size more than the same duplication rate in real data.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched duplication rates, training on duplicated synthetic data will show earlier train-test divergence and higher per-image memorization scores (e.g., ability to reconstruct masks of training images) than duplicated real data.
why_important: Deduplication thresholds tuned on real data are being silently reused for synthetic corpora; if synthetic duplication is more harmful, dedup policy must be stricter for synthetic data.
why_possibly_novel: Duplication studies focus on web-scraped real data and generative-model training; the asymmetry of duplication harm between synthetic and real data for a downstream segmenter appears unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct real and synthetic training sets with controlled duplication (1x, 5x, 20x copies with natural jitter), train segmenters, compare memorization metrics and val-gap trajectories between the real-dup and synth-dup arms.
main_risk: Defining 'matched duplication' across real and synthetic data is subtle; jitter magnitudes may not be commensurable.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Duplication is duplication; standard dedup practice transfers unchanged to synthetic corpora.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern augmentation pipelines may inject enough entropy at training time to erase the difference between duplicate sources.
fastest_falsification: Small-scale run with 20x duplication in both arms and a memorization probe; one GPU-day.

one_line: Synthetic data keeps improving boundary pixels long after it stops improving interior pixels, so scaling decisions should be made on boundary metrics
problem: Synthetic-data scaling decisions are made on mIoU, which is dominated by easy interior pixels and may hide where synthetic data actually keeps paying off.
core_hypothesis: Interior-pixel accuracy saturates quickly because it depends on coarse appearance cues that small synthetic sets already cover, while boundary accuracy depends on rare local configurations whose coverage grows slowly with set size, so the boundary-metric scaling exponent is systematically larger.
falsifiable_prediction: Across nested synthetic set sizes, boundary F-score will continue improving at set sizes where interior IoU has plateaued, with a scaling-exponent gap reproducible across at least two datasets and two architectures.
why_important: If true, teams under-generate synthetic data whenever downstream applications care about boundaries (robotics grasping, medical margins, mapping), and mIoU-based stopping rules are systematically premature.
why_possibly_novel: Scaling curves for dense prediction are rarely decomposed by distance-to-boundary; the claim of a strictly larger exponent for boundary pixels is a specific, checkable regularity.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train on nested synthetic sets (5 sizes), evaluate interior IoU (pixels >10px from boundary) and boundary F-score separately, fit power laws to both, compare exponents with confidence intervals.
main_risk: Boundary metrics are noisier; exponent differences may not reach significance without many seeds.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: A single scaling curve summarizes synthetic-data value; metric choice does not change the qualitative stopping point.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Synthetic boundary labels may be exactly the least trustworthy part of generated pairs, so boundary gains could plateau first rather than last.
fastest_falsification: Re-evaluate existing checkpoints from any prior scaling sweep with a boundary metric; zero new training needed if checkpoints exist.

one_line: Rare classes gain disproportionately from synthetic data, and the per-class gain is predictable from the class's real-data frequency alone
problem: Synthetic data value is reported as a single aggregate number, hiding that its economics may be entirely about the long tail.
core_hypothesis: Synthetic data primarily substitutes for missing real examples, so per-class IoU gain from adding synthetic data follows a decreasing function of real-class pixel frequency, tight enough to predict which classes will benefit before generating anything.
falsifiable_prediction: Across datasets, regressing per-class synthetic-data gain on log real-class frequency will yield a strong negative relationship, and classes above a frequency threshold will show gains statistically indistinguishable from zero.
why_important: Would let teams generate synthetic data only for tail classes, cutting generation cost while keeping most of the benefit, and reframes synthetic data as a class-balance instrument.
why_possibly_novel: Class-conditional analyses of synthetic-data benefit exist in scattered ablations, but a cross-dataset frequency-to-gain law usable as a pre-generation predictor has not been established.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On two long-tailed segmentation datasets, train with and without class-balanced synthetic data, plot per-class gain against real frequency, test the predicted relationship and threshold.
main_risk: Class difficulty (appearance ambiguity) confounds frequency; some rare classes may fail to benefit because the generator cannot render them faithfully.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Synthetic data lifts all classes roughly uniformly, with quality of generation determining the size of the lift.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Generators are themselves worst on rare classes, which could invert the relationship: the classes that need synthetic help most are the ones synthesized worst.
fastest_falsification: Single dataset pair of runs (with/without synthetic), per-class gain vs frequency scatter; two GPU-days.

one_line: A generator fine-tuned on the test domain's unlabeled images leaks benchmark performance without memorizing any test pixel, making 'no test images in training' an insufficient contamination standard
problem: Contamination auditing checks for image-level overlap, but generation pipelines can transmit test-set-specific distributional information through generator weights.
core_hypothesis: Fine-tuning a generator on unlabeled test-domain imagery (or even the test split itself) and training a segmenter on its outputs confers a benchmark advantage comparable to a meaningful fraction of true target supervision, with zero nearest-neighbor overlap between synthetic images and test images.
falsifiable_prediction: Segmenters trained on synthetic data from a test-split-fine-tuned generator will outperform those trained on data from an unrelated-split-fine-tuned generator by a margin exceeding seed noise, while pixel/near-duplicate audits detect nothing.
why_important: Benchmark integrity: as synthetic augmentation becomes standard, leaderboards need contamination standards that account for generator-mediated leakage, not just image overlap.
why_possibly_novel: Contamination via generative intermediaries is discussed for LLM text benchmarks; a quantified demonstration for dense-prediction benchmarks with overlap audits appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Split a benchmark's unlabeled test-domain pool in half; fine-tune two copies of a mask-conditioned generator on each half; train segmenters on each generator's output; evaluate on one half's labeled test set; the same-half generator arm should win if leakage exists.
main_risk: The effect may be small at realistic fine-tuning scales, making the demonstration underpowered rather than the claim false.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: If no test image (or near-duplicate) appears in training data, the evaluation is clean.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Generator fine-tuning on small unlabeled sets may transmit only generic style information already available from any same-city imagery, in which case the 'leak' is just legitimate domain knowledge.
fastest_falsification: The two-generator split experiment on one benchmark; if arms tie, generator-mediated leakage is negligible at that scale.

one_line: The plateau of synthetic-data scaling can be forecast mid-generation from gradient diversity of a probe model, before training any full segmenter
problem: There is no cheap online signal telling a generation pipeline 'stop, additional samples are redundant for the downstream task'.
core_hypothesis: The marginal downstream value of new synthetic batches is proportional to the fraction of their per-sample gradients (on a small frozen probe segmenter) that are not spanned by gradients of already-generated data, so a running gradient-novelty statistic predicts the scaling plateau.
falsifiable_prediction: The generation step at which gradient-novelty falls below a fixed threshold will predict, within a small factor, the set size at which downstream mIoU gains vanish, across at least two generators and two datasets.
why_important: Converts synthetic-data budgeting from post-hoc sweeps into an online stopping rule embedded in the generation loop.
why_possibly_novel: Gradient-based data valuation exists for sample selection; using it as an online stopping criterion for synthetic generation targeted at dense prediction appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate 500k images while logging gradient-novelty on a probe; train segmenters on nested prefixes; compare predicted vs observed plateau locations.
main_risk: Probe-model gradients may poorly represent the training dynamics of the full model, breaking the correspondence.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Synthetic data value can only be measured by training downstream models; generation is budgeted by cost, not by information content.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Downstream value may hinge on rare hard examples whose gradients look 'novel' forever, making the statistic never converge.
fastest_falsification: Log the statistic over one existing generation run and check whether it is even monotone and convergent; near-zero cost.

one_line: Past a real-data epoch threshold, repeating real images beats adding fresh synthetic images at equal step budget, and the crossover is predictable from domain distance
problem: Practitioners assume fresh synthetic samples always beat re-epoching a small real set, but the comparison at matched optimization budget is rarely made cleanly.
core_hypothesis: Synthetic samples carry domain bias whose harm accumulates linearly with steps while their novelty benefit decays, so beyond a crossover number of steps, an additional epoch over real data yields more target-domain improvement than the same steps on new synthetic data; the crossover step count shrinks as measured synthetic-real domain distance grows.
falsifiable_prediction: In matched-step experiments, the ranking of (repeat-real) vs (fresh-synthetic) will flip at a crossover point, and that crossover will occur earlier for generators with larger measured domain gap to the target.
why_important: Gives a concrete, budget-aware rule for when generation pipelines are worth running at all versus simply training longer on available real data.
why_possibly_novel: Fresh-vs-repeated data comparisons exist for language-model pretraining; the domain-distance-indexed crossover for dense prediction with synthetic data appears unformulated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix 1k real images; compare training schedules that extend by (a) more real epochs vs (b) fresh synthetic batches from two generators with different measured gaps; locate crossovers and test the predicted ordering.
main_risk: Learning-rate schedule interactions with epoch count could dominate the comparison and require careful matching.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Fresh data, even synthetic, is always at least as good as repeating old data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: With strong augmentation, repeated real epochs may behave like fresh samples, hiding any crossover within noise.
fastest_falsification: One generator, one real set, two matched schedules; check for any regime where repeat-real wins.

one_line: Decaying the synthetic fraction over training ('synthetic annealing') beats every fixed mixing ratio at equal budget, because synthetic data's role shifts from coverage to bias over training
problem: Mixing schedules are almost always constant; if the value of synthetic data is phase-dependent, all fixed-ratio results understate what synthetic data can do.
core_hypothesis: Early training needs coverage (synthetic-rich mixes help), late training needs unbiased boundary statistics (synthetic-poor mixes help), so a monotone decaying schedule dominates the entire fixed-ratio frontier at matched step budget.
falsifiable_prediction: A simple linear or cosine decay of synthetic fraction will match or beat the best fixed ratio found by grid search on at least two datasets, and the reverse schedule (increasing synthetic fraction) will be the worst arm tested.
why_important: A free-lunch training-schedule change that would immediately improve most synthetic-data pipelines and reframe mixing as a dynamic control problem.
why_possibly_novel: Curriculum work focuses on sample difficulty; treating the synthetic fraction itself as the scheduled quantity, with a phase-based mechanism, is a specific and under-tested claim.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One dataset, fixed budget: grid of 4 fixed ratios vs decay vs reverse-decay schedules, 3 seeds each; compare best-fixed against decay.
main_risk: Gains may be within seed noise on well-tuned baselines, making the claim true but practically irrelevant.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: A well-chosen constant mixing ratio captures essentially all the value; schedule shape is a third-order detail.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If synthetic label noise is the binding constraint, late-training synthetic exposure may not be harmful at all and the schedule direction would not matter.
fastest_falsification: Three runs (best-fixed, decay, reverse) on a small benchmark; a loss or tie for decay against best-fixed kills the strong claim.

one_line: Synthetic-only pretraining shifts the optimal architecture: wider decoders matter more than deeper encoders when labels are geometrically perfect
problem: Architecture choices are tuned on real-data benchmarks and copied unchanged into synthetic-pretraining pipelines, assuming data source does not interact with architecture.
core_hypothesis: Perfect synthetic labels remove annotation noise as a capacity sink and shift the bottleneck toward decoding fine geometry, so under synthetic pretraining the compute-optimal architecture allocates relatively more capacity to the decoder than under real-data training.
falsifiable_prediction: Sweeping encoder/decoder capacity splits at fixed total FLOPs, the argmax split will differ systematically between synthetic-pretrained and real-trained regimes, with synthetic favoring decoder-heavy splits, reproducibly across two datasets.
why_important: If data source changes compute-optimal architecture, all synthetic-pretraining comparisons using real-tuned architectures are biased against synthetic data.
why_possibly_novel: Data-architecture interaction studies focus on scale, not label-noise character; the label-perfection mechanism for decoder-shift appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: 3x3 grid of encoder/decoder capacity splits, trained on (a) synthetic-only and (b) real-only data at matched FLOPs, compare argmax locations.
main_risk: The optimum may be too flat to localize with affordable grids.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Architecture optima are a property of the task, not the data source; whatever wins on real benchmarks is used everywhere.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Synthetic appearance simplicity may reduce encoder needs and boundary perfection may reduce decoder needs simultaneously, leaving the split unchanged.
fastest_falsification: Two extreme splits (encoder-heavy, decoder-heavy) under both data regimes; an interaction sign check in four runs.

one_line: The sim-to-real gap for semantic segmentation is dominated by mid-frequency texture statistics, testable by frequency-band swapping between domains
problem: The sim-to-real gap is treated as an unstructured constant to be minimized, with no accepted decomposition of which image statistics carry it.
core_hypothesis: Low frequencies (layout, shading) and high frequencies (sensor noise) are either easy to match or easy to randomize away, so the residual transfer gap concentrates in mid-frequency bands that encode material texture, and swapping only those bands between synthetic and real images moves most of the gap.
falsifiable_prediction: Training on synthetic images whose mid-frequency band is replaced with real-image statistics will close a larger fraction of the sim-to-real gap than replacing low or high bands, consistently across two synthetic-real dataset pairs.
why_important: A verified frequency localization of the gap turns 'make it photorealistic' into a targeted, cheap spectral matching problem.
why_possibly_novel: Frequency-domain analyses exist for adversarial robustness and style transfer; a controlled band-swap decomposition of the sim-to-real segmentation gap specifically appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct band-swapped hybrids (low/mid/high) between a synthetic driving set and a real driving set, train identical segmenters on each hybrid, measure real-domain mIoU ordering.
main_risk: Band swapping introduces artifacts of its own; conclusions may reflect swap artifacts rather than the gap's true spectral location.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: The gap is spread across appearance holistically; global photorealism or global style transfer is the remedy.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For LiDAR-like or texture-poor domains the gap may sit in geometry/layout, making the spectral account domain-specific rather than general.
fastest_falsification: Three hybrid training runs on one dataset pair; ordering of gaps gives an immediate verdict on mid-band dominance.

one_line: Layout realism (object co-occurrence and spatial arrangement statistics) explains more sim-to-real gap than per-object appearance realism for scene segmentation
problem: Synthetic pipelines spend most of their budget on appearance (materials, lighting) while scene layout is procedurally crude, without evidence about which investment closes more gap.
core_hypothesis: Segmentation networks exploit contextual priors heavily, so mismatch in object co-occurrence and spatial arrangement statistics between synthetic and real scenes contributes more to transfer failure than mismatch in per-object appearance, especially for context-dependent classes.
falsifiable_prediction: A 2x2 experiment crossing {real-like layout, crude layout} x {high appearance realism, low appearance realism} will show larger main effect for layout than appearance on real-domain mIoU, with the effect concentrated in context-dependent classes (e.g., sidewalk vs road).
why_important: Would redirect synthetic-pipeline investment from renderer quality toward layout modeling, a cheaper and more automatable axis.
why_possibly_novel: Appearance-vs-content decompositions are common in style-transfer framing, but a controlled factorial isolating layout statistics against appearance realism for segmentation transfer is rare to absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: In a procedural scene generator, sample layouts either from fitted real-scene statistics or from uniform/random placement, render each at two realism tiers, train four segmenters, run the factorial ANOVA on real-domain performance.
main_risk: Layout and appearance interact (real layouts create realistic occlusion shading), so main effects may not cleanly separate.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Photorealism is the primary axis of synthetic data quality; layout crudeness is a secondary nuisance.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern high-capacity backbones may rely less on context than assumed, making appearance the true bottleneck after all.
fastest_falsification: The four-cell factorial at small scale (quarter-resolution, short schedules) gives effect-size signs in under a GPU-week.

one_line: Simulating the camera pipeline (demosaicing, noise model, tone curve) closes a larger share of the sim-to-real gap than improving content realism, for matched effort
problem: Sim-to-real work equates realism with content (geometry, materials), while the deterministic sensor pipeline separating scene radiance from stored pixels is usually ignored or handled by generic augmentation.
core_hypothesis: A substantial, separable fraction of the gap is caused by the absence of camera-ISP transformations in rendered images, so passing synthetic images through a measured or fitted ISP model (Bayer sampling, denoiser, tone mapping, JPEG) recovers that fraction regardless of content quality.
falsifiable_prediction: Adding an ISP simulation stage to a fixed synthetic set will improve real-domain segmentation more than an equal-effort content upgrade (higher-poly assets or better materials), on at least two camera-specific real targets.
why_important: ISP simulation is cheap, reusable across all content, and target-camera-specific, offering a high-leverage standard component for every sim-to-real pipeline.
why_possibly_novel: ISP modeling is studied in low-level vision (denoising, RAW processing); its quantified contribution to the semantic segmentation sim-to-real gap versus content realism appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix one synthetic dataset; create arms {vanilla, +fitted ISP, +content upgrade}, train identical segmenters, evaluate on a real target captured by a known camera; compare gap closure per unit of engineering effort.
main_risk: Modern real datasets are heavily post-processed and diverse in ISPs, so fitting a single ISP may cap the achievable gain.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Photometric augmentation (color jitter, blur, noise) already covers whatever the sensor pipeline contributes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Generic augmentation may indeed span the ISP family well enough that explicit simulation adds nothing measurable.
fastest_falsification: One synthetic set, one fitted ISP stage, two training runs; compare against a color-jitter-matched control.

one_line: Transfer is asymmetric: sim-to-real degrades more than real-to-sim at matched training scale because synthetic domains are lower-entropy, and the asymmetry measures generator entropy deficit
problem: The sim-to-real gap is reported as one number; nobody checks the reverse direction, which carries information about why the gap exists.
core_hypothesis: A model trained on the higher-entropy domain (real) generalizes to the lower-entropy one (sim) with less degradation than vice versa, so the signed asymmetry between the two transfer directions is a practical measure of the synthetic domain's entropy deficit, usable to compare generators without target labels being scarce.
falsifiable_prediction: Across multiple synthetic-real pairs, transfer degradation will be systematically larger in the sim-to-real direction, and the asymmetry magnitude will rank generators consistently with independent diversity measures of their outputs.
why_important: Provides a label-cheap, directionally meaningful diagnostic for synthetic dataset quality that separates 'wrong statistics' from 'too few statistics'.
why_possibly_novel: Bidirectional transfer measurement is trivial to run yet almost never reported; elevating the asymmetry to a generator-quality metric with a stated mechanism appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For three synthetic datasets and one real dataset, train both directions with identical recipes, compute signed asymmetries, and rank-correlate against sample-diversity metrics of the synthetic sets.
main_risk: Label-convention differences between domains contaminate both directions unequally, biasing the asymmetry.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: The gap is a property of the pair of domains; direction is an implementation detail nobody interprets.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Asymmetry could be dominated by label-quality differences (perfect synthetic labels vs noisy real labels) rather than entropy, reversing the interpretation.
fastest_falsification: Both directions on one pair with a shared label convention subset; if real-to-sim degrades as much or more, the entropy account fails.

one_line: Shadow fidelity is the single largest unmodeled appearance axis in outdoor sim-to-real segmentation, and shadow-only interventions move the gap more than full style transfer
problem: Synthetic outdoor scenes have simplistic shadow rendering (hard shadows, wrong penumbra, wrong ambient occlusion), but shadows are never isolated as a gap factor.
core_hypothesis: Real-world shadows create the dominant within-class appearance variation for ground-plane classes, so models trained on shadow-poor synthetic data fail disproportionately in shadowed real regions, and matching shadow statistics alone (without touching materials or textures) recovers a large share of the total gap.
falsifiable_prediction: Stratifying real-domain errors by a shadow mask will show error concentration in shadowed regions for synthetic-trained models; a synthetic-data variant with physically-based shadow rendering (soft shadows, measured sun/sky ratios) will preferentially fix those pixels and close more aggregate gap than a matched-cost global style-transfer arm.
why_important: Identifies a cheap renderer setting, not a learned adaptation, as a first-order lever for outdoor deployment domains such as driving, agriculture, and aerial mapping.
why_possibly_novel: Shadow robustness is studied for detection and remote sensing individually, but shadow fidelity as a quantified, isolated axis of the sim-to-real segmentation gap appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render one scene corpus twice (hard/simple shadows vs physically-based soft shadows), train two segmenters, evaluate real-domain error inside vs outside shadow masks obtained from an off-the-shelf shadow detector.
main_risk: Shadow detectors on real data are imperfect, adding noise to the stratified analysis.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Shadows are one of many photometric nuisances adequately covered by brightness augmentation and style randomization.
why_it_might_be_wrong: High-capacity models with strong augmentation may already be shadow-invariant, leaving little headroom for shadow-specific fixes.
fastest_falsification: Error stratification by shadow mask on any existing synthetic-trained model against a real-trained control; requires no new training.

one_line: Defocus and depth-of-field statistics are a first-order sim-to-real axis for close-range robotic segmentation, unlike for driving where they are negligible
problem: Sim-to-real conclusions from driving benchmarks are transplanted to manipulation and close-range robotics, where optical blur structure is completely different.
core_hypothesis: At close range, real cameras produce depth-correlated defocus that segmentation models exploit as an implicit depth cue; pinhole-rendered synthetic data lacks it, so the gap for close-range tasks has a large defocus component absent in far-field domains, and rendering with thin-lens depth-of-field closes it.
falsifiable_prediction: Adding physically parameterized depth-of-field to synthetic renders will improve real-domain segmentation for a tabletop/manipulation dataset by a margin several times larger than the same intervention applied to a driving dataset.
why_important: Warns against a benchmark monoculture (driving) shaping sim-to-real folklore, and gives close-range robotics a concrete renderer checklist item.
why_possibly_novel: Depth-of-field is used aesthetically in graphics and studied in autofocus literature; its role as a domain-shift axis interacting with task range appears unquantified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render matched tabletop and driving synthetic sets with and without thin-lens DoF, train four segmenters, compare real-domain deltas between the two task ranges.
main_risk: Real tabletop datasets vary widely in aperture settings, so the 'real' defocus statistics may be too heterogeneous to match with one parameterization.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Optical blur is minor noise handled by Gaussian-blur augmentation; range regime does not change the sim-to-real recipe.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Random blur augmentation may already span defocus variation well enough that structured DoF adds nothing.
fastest_falsification: Compare DoF-rendered vs blur-augmented arms on one tabletop dataset; if they tie, structured defocus is redundant.

one_line: Single-axis sim-to-real gap measurements do not add up: interaction terms between gap axes dominate the total, breaking the implicit linear decomposition used in ablation studies
problem: Papers ablate one realism axis at a time (texture, lighting, layout) and implicitly assume the measured contributions sum to the total gap, an assumption never tested.
core_hypothesis: Gap axes interact strongly (e.g., realistic lighting only helps when materials are realistic enough to respond to it), so the sum of single-axis gap reductions substantially misestimates the joint reduction, and a factorial design will reveal large interaction terms with a consistent sign pattern.
falsifiable_prediction: In a full 2^3 factorial over texture realism, lighting realism, and layout realism, interaction terms will account for a large share of explained variance in real-domain mIoU, and single-axis ablations will overpredict the joint effect of combining the two weakest axes.
why_important: If interactions dominate, the entire ablation-based literature on 'which realism matters' needs reinterpretation, and pipeline optimization must be joint rather than greedy.
why_possibly_novel: Factorial designs are standard in experimental science but essentially absent from sim-to-real studies, which are almost universally one-factor-at-a-time.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Procedural pipeline with three binary realism switches, render all 8 cells, train 8 segmenters at reduced scale, fit the ANOVA and report interaction shares.
main_risk: Reduced-scale training may compress differences between cells, understating both main effects and interactions.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Realism axes contribute roughly independently; one-factor ablations identify the important ones.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Deep networks' invariances may effectively orthogonalize the axes, making the linear model a good approximation after all.
fastest_falsification: Run just the 4 cells needed to estimate one two-way interaction (texture x lighting); a near-zero interaction is immediate evidence against dominance.

one_line: Material/BRDF realism matters for segmentation transfer only near boundaries between appearance-adjacent classes, so realism budgets should be spent per class-pair, not globally
problem: Renderer material realism is bought globally (better BRDFs everywhere), though its downstream value likely concentrates where classes are distinguishable only by material.
core_hypothesis: For class pairs separable by shape or context (car vs road), material realism is irrelevant; for appearance-adjacent pairs (dirt vs gravel, water vs wet pavement), it is decisive; therefore per-class-pair confusion deltas under material-realism upgrades will be highly non-uniform and predictable from a class-pair appearance-similarity score.
falsifiable_prediction: Upgrading BRDF realism in synthetic training data will reduce confusion mainly for class pairs with high appearance similarity, with near-zero effect on shape-separable pairs, and the effect size will correlate with a pre-computed pairwise texture-similarity metric.
why_important: Enables targeted realism spending: render expensive materials only for confusable class pairs, cutting rendering cost while keeping transfer benefits.
why_possibly_novel: Material realism studies report aggregate gains; a class-pair-resolved account tied to a predictive similarity score appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render one corpus at two BRDF fidelity tiers, train two segmenters, compare full confusion matrices on a real target, regress per-pair confusion change on pair appearance similarity.
main_risk: Confusion-matrix deltas are noisy for rare pairs; may need many seeds for significance on the tail.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Material realism is a global quality knob whose benefit spreads across all classes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Material realism may act indirectly through global feature statistics (normalization layers), producing diffuse rather than pair-localized effects.
fastest_falsification: Confusion-matrix comparison between existing low/high-realism trained checkpoints if any pair exists publicly; otherwise two reduced-scale runs.

one_line: Camera-pose distribution mismatch (height, pitch, lens) is a quietly dominant sim-to-real axis in driving segmentation, fixable by resampling viewpoints rather than adapting features
problem: Synthetic driving data is rendered from viewpoint distributions that only loosely match any target vehicle's camera rig, and viewpoint mismatch is confounded into 'the domain gap' instead of being measured.
core_hypothesis: Segmentation networks internalize strong priors on where classes appear in the frame (row-wise class statistics), which are functions of camera height/pitch/FoV; matching the viewpoint distribution to the target rig closes a larger fraction of the gap than photometric adaptation of the same data.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-rendering (or geometrically re-warping) a synthetic set to match a target rig's camera geometry will beat matched-effort photometric style adaptation on that target, and the gain will vanish when evaluated on a different rig, confirming the mechanism is viewpoint-specific.
why_important: Viewpoint is controllable at zero marginal cost in simulation; if it dominates, cheap geometry configuration outperforms elaborate appearance adaptation for every new vehicle program.
why_possibly_novel: Viewpoint priors are known in principle, but a quantified head-to-head of viewpoint-distribution matching versus photometric adaptation for sim-to-real segmentation appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One synthetic world, two render passes (source-default rig vs target-matched rig), plus a style-adapted arm of the default pass; train three segmenters and evaluate on a target with known rig geometry.
main_risk: Public real datasets mix rigs, diluting the single-rig matching effect.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: The sim-to-real gap is primarily photometric/textural; geometric rig mismatch is minor because augmentation crops cover it.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Random crop/scale augmentation may already span rig variation, leaving viewpoint matching with nothing to add.
fastest_falsification: Evaluate any synthetic-trained model on real subsets stratified by camera height/pitch metadata; strong stratified error differences support the axis, flat differences kill it.

one_line: After style transfer 'closes' the appearance gap, the residual sim-to-real gap is mostly boundary micro-geometry, measurable by boundary curvature spectra of the two domains
problem: Style-transferred synthetic data still underperforms real data, and the residual is attributed vaguely to 'content gap' without a concrete, measurable carrier.
core_hypothesis: Synthetic object boundaries are geometrically too clean (polygonal, low-curvature-entropy) compared to real boundaries (fractal-like, occlusion-fringed), and this micro-geometry mismatch survives any pixel-appearance transfer; the divergence between domain boundary-curvature spectra predicts the residual gap.
falsifiable_prediction: Across several synthetic sets style-transferred to one target, the residual gap after transfer will correlate with the distance between boundary-curvature spectra of synthetic labels and real labels, and artificially roughening synthetic boundaries (geometry-aware perturbation of masks and matched image edits) will shrink the residual.
why_important: Names and instruments the notorious 'content gap' remainder, converting it into a measurable, optimizable geometry statistic for asset and scene authoring.
why_possibly_novel: Boundary statistics are used to evaluate predictions, not to characterize domain gaps of training corpora; using label-geometry spectra as a domain-distance component appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute curvature spectra for three synthetic datasets and one real target; style-transfer all three to the target; train and measure residual gaps; test rank correlation between spectra distance and residual gap.
main_risk: With only a handful of synthetic datasets, the rank correlation is underpowered; needs several corpora to be convincing.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Residual gap after style transfer is 'content-level' in an unspecified sense, addressed by better generators rather than by measurable geometry.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The residual may instead be label-convention mismatch (what annotators call a boundary), which curvature spectra would only partially capture.
fastest_falsification: Compute the two spectra for one pair; if synthetic and real boundary spectra are already indistinguishable, the premise dies without any training.

one_line: Per-class sim-to-real transfer is predictable from the diversity of the 3D asset pool used for that class: asset count is a stronger predictor than rendered-instance count
problem: Synthetic datasets report image and instance counts but rarely asset counts per class, and nobody knows which number governs transfer.
core_hypothesis: Networks memorize per-asset shape signatures, so a class rendered from few unique 3D assets transfers poorly no matter how many instances are rendered; per-class transfer gap is therefore predicted by unique-asset count with instance count adding little after controlling for it.
falsifiable_prediction: Across classes within a synthetic dataset with known asset inventories, regressing per-class real-domain IoU on log unique-asset count and log instance count will show the asset term dominating, and subsampling assets (not instances) will reproduce the degradation causally.
why_important: Establishes asset-pool size as the budget-relevant unit for synthetic content acquisition and explains persistent per-class failures in asset-poor categories.
why_possibly_novel: Instance-level scaling is commonly discussed; isolating unique-asset cardinality as the causal variable with a controlled asset-subsampling design appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pick one class with a large asset pool; create training variants at {5, 50, 500} assets with matched instance counts; train and compare real-domain IoU for that class against variants matched on assets but varying instances.
main_risk: Asset pools differ in quality as well as count; quality confounds require random subsampling to mitigate.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Rendering more instances with randomization substitutes for having more assets.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Strong pose/material randomization may genuinely decorrelate renders of one asset enough to mimic asset diversity.
fastest_falsification: The asset-subsampling arm for a single class; three reduced-scale runs.

one_line: Synthetic scenes systematically under-occlude, and occlusion-statistics mismatch predicts sim-to-real transfer failure better than image-level realism metrics
problem: Procedural scene generators place objects to avoid interpenetration and heavy overlap, producing occlusion distributions unlike reality, and this bias is not measured or corrected.
core_hypothesis: Real scenes exhibit heavy-tailed occlusion (many objects mostly hidden), while synthetic placement logic truncates that tail; models trained on under-occluded data fail on heavily occluded real instances, and the divergence between occlusion-fraction histograms predicts per-dataset transfer gaps better than FID-style appearance metrics.
falsifiable_prediction: For several synthetic datasets against one real target, occlusion-histogram divergence will rank transfer gaps better than appearance-distribution metrics, and augmenting placement logic to match real occlusion tails will improve transfer specifically on high-occlusion instances.
why_important: Occlusion statistics are a controllable scene-generation parameter; identifying them as a dominant predictor gives a concrete dial that appearance-obsessed pipelines ignore.
why_possibly_novel: Occlusion handling is studied at the model level (amodal segmentation); occlusion statistics as a dataset-level domain-gap predictor appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate occlusion-fraction distributions (from synthetic ground truth and from amodal annotations or proxy estimates on real data) for 3 synthetic sets; correlate divergence with measured transfer gaps; then causally intervene on placement density in one generator.
main_risk: Estimating occlusion fractions on real data without amodal labels requires proxies that may be too noisy.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Transfer gaps are primarily appearance-driven; scene composition details like occlusion density are secondary.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Occlusion robustness may be conferred cheaply by copy-paste augmentation, making the dataset-level statistic irrelevant to final transfer.
fastest_falsification: Stratify real-domain errors of an existing synthetic-trained model by estimated instance occlusion level; no new training required.

one_line: Mask-conditioned diffusion training pairs carry a systematic boundary offset (objects rendered slightly inside/outside the conditioning mask), which downstream segmenters inherit as a measurable bias
problem: Generated image-mask pairs are treated as perfectly aligned supervision, but the generator only approximately obeys the conditioning mask, and any systematic disobedience becomes label bias at scale.
core_hypothesis: Mask-conditioned generators produce object extents with a consistent signed offset relative to the conditioning mask (direction depending on guidance scale and class), so segmenters trained on such pairs exhibit a matching signed boundary bias on real images, detectable as systematic over/under-segmentation.
falsifiable_prediction: Measuring signed boundary displacement between conditioning masks and re-segmented generated images will reveal a nonzero class-consistent offset, and downstream models trained on those pairs will show the same signed offset direction on real ground truth, unlike models trained on real pairs.
why_important: If generation-for-segmentation injects a directional boundary bias, every pipeline using generated pairs needs an offset calibration step, and reported boundary metrics on such models are systematically distorted.
why_possibly_novel: Pair-fidelity checks usually threshold on IoU agreement; the signed, directional character of generator disobedience and its inheritance by downstream models appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate 10k mask-conditioned images, re-segment with an independent strong model, compute signed boundary displacement distributions per class; train a segmenter on the pairs and measure its signed boundary error on a real labeled set against a real-trained control.
main_risk: The re-segmentation model has its own boundary bias; needs a real-pair control arm to difference it out.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Conditioning-mask disobedience is unbiased noise that averages out with enough generated data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Offsets may be zero-mean across classes and guidance scales, making the inherited bias negligible compared to real-label annotator bias.
fastest_falsification: Re-segment 1k generated pairs and compute the signed displacement histogram; a symmetric zero-centered histogram kills the premise in hours.

one_line: Text-prompted synthetic segmentation data imports language co-occurrence biases: classes appear in contexts dictated by prompt statistics, teaching context shortcuts that fail on real out-of-context instances
problem: Text-to-image pipelines generate scenes from prompt templates, so class-context pairings in the data reflect language statistics rather than visual-world statistics, and nobody audits the difference.
core_hypothesis: Prompt-derived synthetic data has narrower class-context distributions than real data (e.g., 'sheep' almost always on grass), so segmenters trained on it rely more on context and fail more sharply on out-of-context real instances, in proportion to the context-narrowness of the generating prompts.
falsifiable_prediction: Models trained on prompt-generated data will show a larger performance drop on out-of-context test instances (relative to in-context) than real-data-trained controls, and the per-class drop will correlate with a measured context-entropy deficit of the generated corpus for that class.
why_important: Reveals a shortcut-injection pathway unique to language-mediated data generation, with a concrete audit metric (context entropy) that pipelines can monitor and correct via prompt diversification.
why_possibly_novel: Context bias is studied for real datasets; tracing it quantitatively to prompt statistics in generated training corpora and to downstream out-of-context failure appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate a corpus from naturalistic prompts vs context-diversified prompts; train two segmenters; evaluate both on a curated out-of-context real test subset; compare drops and correlate with corpus context entropy.
main_risk: Out-of-context real test instances are scarce and may be too few for tight class-level statistics.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Generated data inherits the generator's visual diversity; prompt phrasing is a stylistic detail, not a bias vector.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern generators may inject enough compositional variety beyond the prompt that context distributions end up as broad as real data.
fastest_falsification: Measure class-context co-occurrence entropy of an existing generated corpus against a real dataset; if entropies match, the pathway is weak.

one_line: Mask-conditioned generators obey the mask in salient regions and improvise elsewhere, creating a spatial 'compliance map' that downstream models learn as a spatially varying label-trust prior
problem: Pair fidelity is scored with one global number per image, but generator obedience is spatially structured, and structured label error teaches structured model behavior.
core_hypothesis: Generator compliance with conditioning masks is systematically higher in high-saliency, high-texture-contrast regions and lower in peripheral or low-contrast regions; segmenters trained on such pairs learn to be accurate where the generator complied and biased where it improvised, producing a spatially non-uniform error signature on real data that mirrors the compliance map.
falsifiable_prediction: A compliance map estimated by re-segmenting generated images will be spatially non-uniform in a consistent way across images, and the downstream model's real-domain error map (in normalized image coordinates and per region-type) will correlate with the inverse compliance map, unlike a real-trained control.
why_important: Turns pair-fidelity auditing from a global filter into a spatial-weighting problem: training losses could be down-weighted exactly where generators are known to improvise.
why_possibly_novel: Per-image filtering of generated pairs is common; characterizing and exploiting the spatial structure of generator disobedience appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate compliance maps over 10k generated pairs; train a segmenter; test spatial correlation between downstream real-domain errors and compliance, with a real-trained control for baseline spatial error structure.
main_risk: Spatial error structure is also driven by class layout priors, requiring careful controls to isolate the compliance channel.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Generated-pair label noise is spatially unstructured, so global quality filtering per image is sufficient.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Compliance may vary more across images (by content difficulty) than within images spatially, making per-image filtering the right granularity after all.
fastest_falsification: Average pixelwise disagreement between conditioning masks and re-segmentations over 1k pairs in normalized coordinates; a flat map falsifies spatial structure immediately.

one_line: Self-consistency filtering of generated pairs (keep pairs a segmenter agrees with) preferentially removes hard boundary cases and can make filtered data worse than unfiltered data
problem: The standard hygiene step for generated training pairs is to re-segment and keep high-agreement pairs, assuming agreement measures label quality rather than example easiness.
core_hypothesis: Re-segmentation agreement conflates label fidelity with example easiness, so agreement-based filtering removes exactly the ambiguous-boundary and unusual-configuration examples that drive generalization, and beyond a filtering threshold the filtered dataset underperforms the unfiltered one despite higher average 'label quality'.
falsifiable_prediction: Sweeping the filter threshold will show non-monotonic downstream performance with an interior optimum, and the examples removed at strict thresholds will be enriched in high-boundary-complexity and rare-layout cases rather than in genuinely mislabeled pairs (verified by human audit of a sample).
why_important: A ubiquitous pipeline step may be silently deleting the most valuable training signal; establishing the easiness-fidelity confound would change filtering practice toward disagreement-aware retention.
why_possibly_novel: Filtering is standard, but the claim that its selection pressure is anti-correlated with example value at strict thresholds, with a human-audited decomposition of what gets removed, appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate a fixed corpus; filter at 4 thresholds; train segmenters on each; human-audit 200 removed pairs at the strictest threshold to classify removals into (mislabeled) vs (hard-but-correct); relate the ratio to the performance curve.
main_risk: Human auditing of 'correct' labels on generated images is itself ambiguous since there is no ground truth beyond the conditioning mask.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Stricter consistency filtering monotonically improves generated-data quality and downstream performance.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For weak generators the mislabeled fraction may be so large that filtering is monotonically beneficial across all practical thresholds.
fastest_falsification: Threshold sweep with 3 values on a small corpus; monotone improvement at all thresholds contradicts the interior-optimum claim.

one_line: FID is the wrong quality metric for generated segmentation pairs: a boundary-agreement metric between conditioning mask and generated image gradients predicts downstream value where FID fails
problem: Generated-data quality is reported in FID-like appearance metrics that ignore the label channel entirely, so pipelines optimize generator realism rather than pair usefulness.
core_hypothesis: Downstream segmentation value of a generated corpus is governed by mask-image alignment quality (whether image evidence actually supports the paired label), which is invisible to FID; a cheap alignment score (agreement between mask boundaries and image gradient structure) will predict downstream mIoU across corpora where FID does not.
falsifiable_prediction: Across corpora generated with varying guidance scales, conditioning types, and generator checkpoints, rank correlation between the alignment score and downstream mIoU will be high, while FID's rank correlation will be near zero or even negative in regimes where realism trades off against mask obedience.
why_important: Provides the missing intrinsic metric for generation-for-segmentation, letting teams select generator settings without training downstream models for every configuration.
why_possibly_novel: Alignment checks exist ad hoc; establishing a validated intrinsic metric that beats FID for predicting dense-prediction downstream value, across generator configurations, appears not to have been done systematically.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Produce 8 corpora varying guidance scale and conditioning; compute FID and the alignment score; train 8 downstream segmenters; compare rank correlations of the two metrics with downstream mIoU.
main_risk: Both metrics may fail if downstream value is dominated by corpus diversity rather than per-pair quality.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Lower FID (better realism) implies better synthetic training data; realism metrics are the accepted currency of generator quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: In high-obedience regimes alignment may saturate and FID may regain predictive power, restricting the claim to a specific operating region.
fastest_falsification: Two corpora at extreme guidance scales, two downstream runs, both metrics; a case where FID ranks correctly and alignment ranks wrongly is immediate counter-evidence.

one_line: The downstream value of generated scenes comes mostly from background diversity, not foreground objects: swapping generated foregrounds onto real backgrounds underperforms the reverse composition
problem: Generation effort is concentrated on rendering convincing foreground objects, but which part of the generated image actually drives segmentation transfer is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Foreground appearance is comparatively easy for models to learn from limited real data, while background/context diversity is the scarce resource; therefore hybrids of real foregrounds on generated backgrounds will train better segmenters than generated foregrounds on real backgrounds at matched scale.
falsifiable_prediction: In a compositional 2x2 (foreground source x background source), the background factor will show a larger main effect on real-domain mIoU than the foreground factor, consistently across two datasets.
why_important: Would redirect generation-for-segmentation toward background/context synthesis, which is also where mask fidelity constraints are weakest and generation is easiest.
why_possibly_novel: Copy-paste literature composes real foregrounds onto varied backgrounds for augmentation, but a controlled factorial isolating which generated component carries transfer value appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build the four compositional corpora with harmonization held constant, train four segmenters, run the factorial analysis on two real targets.
main_risk: Compositing artifacts (harmonization quality) may interact with the factors and blur the main-effect comparison.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Foreground object fidelity is the heart of useful synthetic data; backgrounds are filler.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For fine-grained or boundary-critical tasks, foreground fidelity may dominate, flipping the main effect.
fastest_falsification: Two diagonal cells of the factorial (real-fg/gen-bg vs gen-fg/real-bg) at small scale settle the direction quickly.

one_line: Latent-space mask conditioning destroys thin structures below the autoencoder's downsampling factor, so latent-diffusion synthetic data systematically hurts thin-structure classes
problem: Most mask-conditioned generation runs in a compressed latent space, and the interaction between latent downsampling and thin mask structures (poles, wires, vessels, cracks) is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: Structures thinner than the VAE compression factor cannot be faithfully represented in the latent conditioning pathway, so generated images either omit or thicken them relative to the paired mask; training on such pairs degrades downstream recall specifically for thin-structure classes, in proportion to structure width measured in latent pixels.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-class downstream deltas from adding latent-diffusion synthetic data will be negative or smallest for classes whose median structure width falls below the compression factor, and the same generation pipeline run in pixel space (or with higher-resolution latents) will remove the deficit.
why_important: Thin structures are safety-critical in driving (poles, riders' limbs), medical (vessels), and industrial (cracks) domains; a systematic generation-induced deficit there would be a serious hidden failure of a popular pipeline.
why_possibly_novel: VAE reconstruction limits are known for image quality; their propagation through mask conditioning into class-specific downstream segmentation deficits appears unquantified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate matched corpora with a latent-space and a pixel-space (or 2x-finer-latent) conditioned generator; train segmenters; compare per-class deltas stratified by median structure width in latent units.
main_risk: Pixel-space generators differ in overall quality, confounding the comparison; needs a same-family generator pair.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Latent compression artifacts are a rendering-quality nuance that averages out; class identity of affected structures is not considered.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Conditioning may be injected at multiple resolutions in modern architectures, partially preserving thin structures and shrinking the effect below detectability.
fastest_falsification: Measure thin-structure presence (re-segmentation recall of the conditioning mask's thin components) in 1k generated pairs; near-perfect recall kills the premise without downstream training.

one_line: Classifier-free-guidance scale maps monotonically to a memorization-generalization trade in the downstream segmenter, making guidance a dataset-design dial rather than an image-quality dial
problem: Guidance scale is tuned for visual appeal of generated data, though it controls the diversity-fidelity balance that should govern downstream training dynamics.
core_hypothesis: Higher guidance produces higher-fidelity, lower-diversity samples closer to the generator's modes; downstream segmenters trained on high-guidance corpora will show faster fitting, earlier overfitting, and worse out-of-distribution transfer, with the transition monotone in guidance scale.
falsifiable_prediction: Across corpora generated at 5 guidance scales (matched size), downstream in-domain accuracy will vary weakly while out-of-domain transfer and train-val gap will vary strongly and monotonically with scale.
why_important: Gives the generation-for-segmentation community a principled recipe for choosing guidance based on downstream robustness targets rather than sample aesthetics.
why_possibly_novel: Guidance effects on sample diversity are known within generative modeling; their systematic propagation into downstream dense-prediction generalization curves appears uncharacterized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One generator, five guidance scales, matched corpus sizes, five downstream segmenters, evaluated in-domain and on one shifted target; plot the three downstream quantities against scale.
main_risk: Guidance also changes mask obedience, entangling label fidelity with diversity; needs alignment-score monitoring as covariate.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Guidance is set once for 'good-looking' samples; its downstream effect is assumed second-order relative to corpus size.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Downstream training with strong augmentation may erase diversity differences between guidance settings entirely.
fastest_falsification: Two extreme guidance corpora, two downstream runs, one shifted-target evaluation; monotonicity in the middle can wait.

one_line: Sampling conditioning masks from real layout statistics beats jointly generating mask and image, at matched generator quality: layout is the component that must stay real
problem: Fully generative pipelines synthesize both the label map and the image, assuming generated layouts are as useful as real ones for training segmenters.
core_hypothesis: Generated label maps drift from real layout statistics (object counts, adjacencies, size distributions) in ways that matter more downstream than image appearance drift, so pipelines that keep real layouts (perturbed real masks or layout-model samples fitted to real statistics) and generate only images will dominate fully generative pipelines at equal budget.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched generator and corpus size, the real-layout arm will outperform the generated-layout arm on real-domain segmentation, and the gap will correlate with measured divergence between generated and real layout statistics.
why_important: Clarifies the division of labor in synthetic pipelines: spend generation capacity on appearance, anchor structure to reality, a design rule with immediate practical uptake.
why_possibly_novel: Layout-to-image generation is an established task, but the controlled comparison isolating layout provenance as the decisive factor for downstream dense prediction appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three arms with one image generator: (a) real masks as conditions, (b) perturbed real masks, (c) masks from a label-map generator; train three segmenters, evaluate on real target, measure layout-statistics divergence per arm.
main_risk: Real-mask conditioning may leak target-domain information beyond layout (annotation conventions), inflating arm (a).
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: End-to-end generation of pairs is the scalable future; layout realism will come along for free as generators improve.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern label-map generators may already match real layout statistics closely enough that provenance no longer matters.
fastest_falsification: Compare layout-statistics (class co-occurrence, size histograms, adjacency graphs) of generated vs real label maps; near-match falsifies the premise cheaply.

one_line: Generative harmonized copy-paste beats full-scene generation for instance segmentation at matched compute, because exact label fidelity outweighs global scene coherence
problem: The field is moving from copy-paste augmentation toward full-scene generation, assuming scene coherence is worth the label-fidelity risk, without a clean matched-compute comparison.
core_hypothesis: For instance segmentation, per-instance label exactness is the binding constraint; copy-paste with generative harmonization (relighting/boundary blending of pasted real instances) retains exact masks while buying enough local realism, so it dominates full-scene generation at equal GPU budget until generators reach near-perfect mask obedience.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched total compute (generation + training), harmonized copy-paste will yield higher instance AP than full-scene generation across two datasets, with the advantage concentrated in mask-quality metrics (boundary AP) rather than classification components.
why_important: Prevents premature abandonment of a cheap, label-exact technique and defines the obedience threshold generators must cross before full generation becomes the right choice.
why_possibly_novel: Both techniques are known; the matched-compute head-to-head with a stated crossover criterion (generator obedience level) appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix a compute budget; build corpora via (a) harmonized copy-paste and (b) full-scene mask-conditioned generation; train identical instance segmenters; compare AP and boundary AP on real validation.
main_risk: Harmonization quality varies by implementation; a weak harmonizer would unfairly handicap arm (a).
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Full-scene generation is strictly more powerful and will subsume copy-paste as generators improve.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Scene-level coherence (shadows, contact points) may matter more for instance AP than assumed, favoring full generation even with imperfect labels.
fastest_falsification: Small-budget version of the head-to-head on one dataset; boundary-AP comparison delivers the verdict.

one_line: Generated training data improves segmentation calibration even when it does not improve accuracy, because soft generator-label disagreement near boundaries acts as structured label smoothing
problem: Generated data is judged solely by accuracy deltas; its effect on confidence calibration, which matters for deployment under shift, is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: Imperfect mask obedience concentrated near boundaries exposes the downstream model to systematically noisy boundary supervision, which functions as spatially structured label smoothing, improving calibration (especially near boundaries and under domain shift) independent of accuracy effects.
falsifiable_prediction: Models trained with generated-pair admixture will have lower calibration error than accuracy-matched controls, with the improvement concentrated in boundary bands and growing under evaluation shift; explicitly denoising the generated labels will remove the calibration gain.
why_important: If generated data is a free calibration regularizer, its value accounting changes: pipelines currently discarding noisy pairs may be discarding the calibration benefit.
why_possibly_novel: Label smoothing and boundary label softening are known regularizers; identifying generator disobedience as an implicit, spatially structured instance of them, with a shift-dependent calibration benefit, appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train (a) real-only, (b) real+generated, (c) real+generated-with-corrected-labels; match accuracy via early stopping; compare boundary-band expected calibration error in-domain and under one corruption shift.
main_risk: Calibration differences may be small and sensitive to the calibration metric binning choices.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Label noise in generated pairs is purely harmful; the goal is to eliminate it.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The noise may be too structured (systematically biased rather than symmetric) to act like smoothing, harming calibration instead.
fastest_falsification: Compare boundary-band calibration of arms (b) and (c) on one dataset; if correcting labels helps calibration too, the mechanism claim dies.

one_line: Iterative self-generation loops (model labels real images, generator trains on them, model retrains on generated pairs) collapse at a rate predictable from boundary-entropy loss per cycle
problem: Self-improving data loops are being built for segmentation without a quantitative early-warning signal for the known risk of iterative degeneration.
