core_hypothesis: Each cycle removes high-frequency boundary detail (both generator smoothing and pseudo-label smoothing), so the entropy of boundary-shape statistics decays geometrically with cycle count, and the decay rate measured in the first two cycles predicts the cycle at which downstream real-domain accuracy begins declining.
falsifiable_prediction: Running the loop for 5+ cycles will show monotone boundary-entropy decay; the fitted geometric rate from cycles 1-2 will predict the accuracy-decline onset cycle within one cycle of the observed onset, across two datasets.
why_important: Provides an actionable stopping criterion and monitoring metric for self-generating segmentation pipelines before quality visibly collapses.
why_possibly_novel: Model-collapse studies focus on generative-model quality in image or text space; a dense-prediction-specific collapse metric tied to boundary geometry with predictive (not just descriptive) use appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement a minimal loop on one dataset, run 6 cycles, log boundary-shape entropy and real-domain mIoU per cycle, test the prediction rule; repeat once on a second dataset.
main_risk: Collapse dynamics may be dominated by class-distribution drift rather than boundary smoothing, in which case the metric watches the wrong variable.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Collapse in self-training loops is a known qualitative risk managed by adding fresh real data, not something with a predictable quantitative onset.
why_it_might_be_wrong: With strong real-data anchoring each cycle, entropy may plateau rather than decay geometrically, making the predictive rule inapplicable exactly where practice operates.
fastest_falsification: Two cycles on a small dataset, check whether boundary entropy even decreases; if flat, the driving assumption fails immediately.

one_line: Segmentation models trained on synthetic data learn renderer fingerprints (anti-aliasing and mipmap signatures), and the degree of fingerprint reliance predicts the model's sim-to-real gap
problem: Synthetic-trained models may key on renderer-specific micro-artifacts invisible to humans, but there is no standard audit for artifact reliance nor evidence linking it to transfer failure.
core_hypothesis: Renderers imprint consistent low-level signatures (anti-aliasing kernels, mipmap trilinear blending, texture filtering); models exploit them as easy features, and a fingerprint-reliance score (performance drop when signatures are ablated by resampling) predicts the sim-to-real gap across models and training recipes.
falsifiable_prediction: Across models trained with different recipes on the same synthetic data, the fingerprint-reliance score will rank their real-domain performance inversely, and interventions that reduce reliance (artifact randomization) will improve transfer proportionally to the reliance reduction.
why_important: Provides both a diagnostic (audit any synthetic-trained model for artifact dependence) and a mechanism-level explanation for why some recipes transfer better than others.
why_possibly_novel: Renderer forensics exist in image-forensics literature; importing them as a training-time reliance audit predictive of segmentation transfer appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train 5 models with varied augmentation recipes on one synthetic set; compute fingerprint-reliance via signature-ablated re-evaluation; rank-correlate with real-domain mIoU.
main_risk: Signature ablation (resampling/re-antialiasing) also alters legitimate image content, inflating measured reliance.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Sim-to-real gaps are attributed to content and appearance mismatch; renderer micro-artifacts are not part of the standard explanation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Strong photometric augmentation may already destroy fingerprints during training, leaving reliance near zero for all practical recipes.
fastest_falsification: Evaluate one synthetic-trained model on signature-ablated synthetic validation data; a negligible drop means reliance is not there to begin with.

one_line: Deliberately corrupting synthetic boundary pixels (simulating motion blur and edge bleed) improves real transfer because perfectly sharp synthetic edges teach an unrealistic edge model
problem: Synthetic data's perfectly crisp object boundaries are treated as an asset (clean supervision), but real boundaries are optically degraded, and the mismatch in edge appearance statistics is unaddressed.
core_hypothesis: Models trained on optically perfect edges learn edge detectors tuned to step discontinuities that real cameras never produce; injecting physically motivated edge degradation (motion blur streaks, chromatic aberration, edge bleed) into synthetic images, while keeping labels sharp, aligns the edge-appearance distribution and improves boundary transfer more than global blur augmentation.
falsifiable_prediction: Edge-localized degradation will beat global-blur augmentation on real-domain boundary F-score at matched augmentation budgets, and the gain will concentrate on moving objects and high-contrast boundaries where real optical degradation is strongest.
why_important: A renderer-post-processing recipe that is nearly free and targets the exact pixels where segmentation value concentrates, boundaries.
why_possibly_novel: Blur augmentation is standard but global; edge-localized, physically structured degradation with sharp-label retention as a targeted sim-to-real fix appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three arms on one synthetic set: {no degradation, global blur augmentation, edge-localized degradation}; train and compare real-domain boundary F-score, stratified by object-motion proxies.
main_risk: Edge-localized degradation requires labels to localize edges, risking a leakage of label information into the augmentation that complicates interpretation.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Sharper synthetic imagery is better imagery; degradation should be applied globally if at all, as generic augmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Real datasets' annotation conventions may align better with sharp synthetic edges than with degraded ones, reversing the expected benefit.
fastest_falsification: Single comparison run of edge-localized vs global blur arms on one dataset pair, boundary metrics only.

one_line: Unnaturally low noise in synthetic homogeneous regions (skies, walls) teaches a 'clean means uniform' prior that misfires on real textured surfaces, driving a specific class of transfer errors
problem: Renderers output near-noiseless uniform regions, unlike real sensors; the downstream consequence of learning from statistically impossible uniformity is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: Models trained on synthetic data internalize that low-variance regions belong to specific classes (sky, wall, road), so on real images they over-assign those classes to any smooth region and, conversely, fragment genuinely uniform real regions that carry sensor noise, producing a signature error pattern absent in real-trained models.
falsifiable_prediction: Error analysis stratified by local variance will show synthetic-trained models disproportionately misclassifying real low-variance patches toward 'uniform classes' relative to real-trained controls, and adding calibrated sensor noise only to synthetic uniform regions will preferentially remove this error mode.
why_important: Identifies a cheap, targeted fix (region-selective noise injection) and a diagnostic error signature for synthetic-data pipelines, more actionable than global realism scores.
why_possibly_novel: Sensor-noise augmentation is common globally; the region-statistics mechanism and its class-directional error signature appear undescribed.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train on synthetic data with {no noise, global noise, uniform-region-selective noise}; evaluate real-domain confusion stratified by local patch variance; test for the predicted directional error and its selective removal.
main_risk: Local variance stratification conflates uniformity with distance and scale effects, requiring careful covariate control.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Global noise augmentation suffices; where noise is added spatially is irrelevant.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Normalization layers may standardize local variance early enough that the model never sees the uniformity cue.
fastest_falsification: Variance-stratified confusion analysis on existing synthetic-trained vs real-trained checkpoints; no training needed.

one_line: Path-traced and rasterized synthetic data with matched visual quality transfer differently, because light-transport correctness affects learned shading cues beyond what appearance metrics capture
problem: Synthetic datasets are produced by renderers with different light-transport fidelity, and the choice is made on cost and looks, without evidence on whether light-transport correctness itself matters downstream.
core_hypothesis: Segmentation models exploit shading-derived cues (contact shadows, interreflections, ambient occlusion) as depth and support-relation evidence; rasterization approximates these incorrectly, so path-traced data trains models whose shading cues transfer to reality better, even when human raters and FID cannot distinguish the two datasets.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched appearance-metric scores, path-traced-trained models will beat rasterized-trained ones on real targets specifically in error categories involving support and contact relations (object-ground boundaries, under-object shadows), rather than uniformly.
why_important: Would justify (or dismiss) the significant compute premium of physically correct rendering for training data with a mechanism-level, category-resolved answer.
why_possibly_novel: Renderer comparisons exist at the aggregate-mIoU level; a cue-level analysis testing where light-transport fidelity manifests downstream appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render one scene corpus with both pipelines, verify appearance-metric parity, train two segmenters, compare real-domain errors stratified by boundary type (object-ground vs object-object vs object-sky).
main_risk: Achieving genuine appearance-metric parity between pipelines is hard; residual global quality differences confound the cue-level story.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: If two datasets look equally realistic by standard metrics, they will train equally good models; light-transport correctness is aesthetics.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Shading cues may be dominated by texture cues in modern models, making light-transport fidelity genuinely irrelevant.
fastest_falsification: Object-ground boundary error comparison between existing models trained on a rasterized and a path-traced public synthetic set (accepting dataset confounds as a first pass).

one_line: Synthetic data teaches models to expect label-aligned image gradients, and part of the sim-to-real drop is the model meeting real datasets' sloppy polygon annotations, not real images
problem: Sim-to-real evaluation confounds two shifts: image-appearance shift and label-convention shift (pixel-perfect synthetic labels vs polygonal, rounded human annotations).
core_hypothesis: A measurable fraction of the reported sim-to-real gap is annotation-convention mismatch: synthetic-trained models localize boundaries at true image gradients, while real ground truth places boundaries at simplified polygon edges, penalizing the model precisely where it is most correct.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-annotating a small real evaluation set with pixel-accurate labels will shrink the measured sim-to-real gap for synthetic-trained models substantially more than for real-trained models, and the shrinkage will concentrate in boundary-band metrics.
why_important: If part of the gap is an evaluation artifact, method rankings and the perceived difficulty of sim-to-real transfer are distorted; fair evaluation needs convention-controlled labels.
why_possibly_novel: Annotation quality is discussed for training; its asymmetric interaction with the training-data source at evaluation time, as a component of the sim-to-real gap, appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pixel-accurately re-annotate 150 images of a real benchmark; evaluate one synthetic-trained and one real-trained model on both label versions; compare gap changes in boundary-band and interior metrics.
main_risk: Careful re-annotation is expensive and itself convention-laden; needs an explicit written boundary protocol.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: The sim-to-real gap measures image-domain difference; evaluation labels are treated as neutral ground truth.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Boundary-band pixels may be too small a fraction of the metric for convention mismatch to move aggregate numbers meaningfully.
fastest_falsification: Evaluate both models with a boundary-tolerant metric (ignore a 3-5px band); if the gap ordering is unchanged, convention mismatch is minor.

one_line: Texture-tiling periodicity in synthetic scenes is absorbed as a spatial prior by segmentation models, detectable as periodic structure in feature-map spectra and removable by tile randomization
problem: Game-engine scenes reuse tiled textures with fixed spatial periods; whether models internalize this periodicity and what it costs at transfer time is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Models trained on tiled-texture synthetic data develop feature detectors tuned to the tiling frequencies, visible as spectral peaks in feature-map statistics; on real images lacking those periods, these detectors contribute noise, and randomizing tile scale/phase during rendering removes the peaks and improves transfer on texture-heavy classes.
falsifiable_prediction: Feature-map spectra of synthetic-trained models will show peaks at renderer tiling frequencies absent in real-trained models; tile-randomized training will eliminate the peaks and yield measurable transfer gains concentrated in ground/vegetation/wall classes.
why_important: A concrete, checkable instance of shortcut learning from procedural content, with a renderer-side fix and a model-side audit that pipelines can adopt.
why_possibly_novel: Texture bias is studied via style experiments; explicit spectral detection of tiling absorption and its causal removal appears novel.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train on default-tiled vs tile-randomized renders; compute feature-map power spectra on held-out images; verify peak presence/absence; compare per-class real-domain IoU.
main_risk: Spectral peaks may be too weak to detect above natural texture regularities (brick, fence patterns) present in both domains.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Tiled textures are a cosmetic shortcut of game engines with no specific learned consequence beyond generic 'low realism'.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Downsampling in early layers may alias away tiling periods before features can lock onto them.
fastest_falsification: Spectral analysis of feature maps from one existing synthetic-trained checkpoint; peaks either exist or they do not.

one_line: Synthetic-vs-real discriminability persists at tiny patch sizes, implying the artifact channel is local and can be washed out by cheap local perturbation instead of global adaptation
problem: Domain discrepancy is treated as a global image property demanding global adaptation machinery, but if discriminability lives in tiny patches, far cheaper local remedies would suffice.
core_hypothesis: A classifier can distinguish synthetic from real using patches as small as a few pixels (via noise, demosaicing, and rendering micro-statistics); the patch-size profile of discriminability identifies the artifact scale, and matching perturbations at exactly that scale removes most of the model-relevant domain signal at negligible cost.
falsifiable_prediction: Discriminator accuracy will remain far above chance at very small patch sizes; applying scale-matched local perturbations to synthetic training data will reduce both patch discriminability and the downstream sim-to-real gap, with gap reduction proportional to discriminability reduction across perturbation strengths.
why_important: Replaces heavyweight adversarial feature alignment with a measurement-driven, training-free data operation whose target (artifact scale) is empirically identified.
why_possibly_novel: Patch-based domain discrimination has been used as an analysis tool; closing the loop from the discriminability-vs-scale profile to a scale-matched intervention with predicted downstream effect appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train synthetic-vs-real patch discriminators at 5 patch sizes; identify the smallest high-accuracy scale; construct scale-matched perturbations; train segmenters on perturbed vs vanilla synthetic data and compare real-domain performance.
main_risk: Local artifact removal may not touch the semantically relevant part of the gap, decoupling discriminability from downstream transfer.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Domain gap is semantic and global; low-level artifact matching is regarded as insufficient by construction.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The correlation between patch discriminability and segmentation transfer may be weak, since segmenters can ignore cues discriminators exploit.
fastest_falsification: Patch-discriminator accuracy at 5px on one synthetic-real pair; chance-level accuracy kills the local-artifact premise instantly.

one_line: The renderer's tone-mapping operator is recoverable from a downstream segmenter's weights by probing, proving pipeline leakage into task models and quantifying it as a transferable-risk score
problem: It is unknown how much renderer-pipeline information persists inside models trained on synthetic data, and there is no quantitative leakage measure to compare training recipes.
core_hypothesis: Global nonlinear transforms like tone mapping shape learned feature statistics enough that a probe on frozen features can identify which of several tone-mapping operators produced the training data; probe accuracy is a leakage score that decreases with augmentation strength and predicts transfer gap across recipes.
falsifiable_prediction: Probes will identify the training tone-mapper well above chance from frozen features of synthetic-trained segmenters; leakage score will correlate inversely with real-domain performance across models trained with graded augmentation.
why_important: Establishes an information-theoretic style audit for 'how much renderer is inside your model', useful for certifying synthetic-data pipelines and comparing augmentation recipes without target-domain labels.
why_possibly_novel: Property-inference attacks exist in ML security; repurposing them as a sim-to-real pipeline-leakage meter with predictive validity for transfer appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render one corpus under 4 tone-mappers; train segmenters; train linear probes on frozen features to classify the tone-mapper from held-out synthetic images; compute leakage scores under 3 augmentation recipes and correlate with real-domain mIoU.
main_risk: Probes may detect residual image-level differences rather than model-internalized ones if evaluation images are not carefully controlled.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Models learn task-relevant content; global photometric pipeline choices wash out during training and are not recoverable from weights.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Tone-mapping differences may be erased by the first normalization layer, making probe accuracy chance-level regardless of leakage elsewhere.
fastest_falsification: Single probe experiment with 2 tone-mappers and one segmenter; above-chance probe accuracy is a quick existence proof, chance accuracy a quick refutation.

one_line: There is a critical period for artifact lock-in: artifact-randomized synthetic data early in training prevents renderer-shortcut reliance that later randomization cannot undo
problem: Artifact randomization is applied uniformly across training; if shortcut reliance forms early and resists later correction, the schedule matters more than the total amount.
core_hypothesis: Renderer-artifact shortcuts are acquired in early training when easy features dominate learning; once early layers commit to artifact features, later randomization fails to displace them, so front-loading randomization prevents lock-in while back-loading is nearly useless at matched budget.
falsifiable_prediction: Models trained with randomization only in the first quarter of training will match full-randomization transfer performance, while randomization only in the last quarter will barely improve over no randomization, measured by both fingerprint-reliance scores and real-domain mIoU.
why_important: Cuts augmentation compute significantly and connects sim-to-real practice to critical-period learning phenomena, giving schedules a principled design rule.
why_possibly_novel: Critical periods are documented for other deficits (blur, label noise); their existence for renderer-artifact shortcut formation in synthetic-data training appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Four arms (no/early-only/late-only/full randomization) at matched budgets on one synthetic-real pair; compare transfer and reliance scores.
main_risk: Learning-rate schedule interactions could mimic or mask phase effects; requires an LR-controlled design.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Augmentation benefit scales with the amount applied, roughly independent of when it is applied.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense-prediction fine-tuning dynamics may keep features plastic throughout, letting late randomization work just as well.
fastest_falsification: Early-only vs late-only arms alone (two runs) give the ordering that the claim stands or falls on.

one_line: Generator ensembles from the same decoder family fail to add effective diversity: shared VAE/decoder artifacts make 'multi-generator' synthetic corpora behave like single-generator ones downstream
problem: Pipelines diversify synthetic data by sampling from multiple generators, assuming generator count increases effective data diversity, but many generators share decoder lineages and artifact signatures.
core_hypothesis: Downstream diversity benefits track the number of distinct artifact families (decoder lineages), not the number of generator checkpoints; corpora pooled from same-family generators will train models statistically indistinguishable from single-generator corpora, while cross-family pooling yields real gains.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched corpus size, pooling k same-family generators will produce downstream transfer within noise of one generator, while pooling generators across distinct decoder families will produce significant gains, and an artifact-space clustering of the corpora will predict which poolings help.
why_important: Prevents wasted engineering on pseudo-diversity and gives a concrete criterion (artifact-family distinctness) for composing generator ensembles.
why_possibly_novel: Ensembling generators is common practice; the lineage-based null result and the artifact-clustering predictor appear unstated and untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build corpora from {1 generator, 3 same-family, 3 cross-family} at matched size; train segmenters; compare transfer; cluster corpora in a forensic-artifact feature space and check the predicted correspondence.
main_risk: Cross-family generators also differ in content quality, confounding the family effect with quality effects.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: More generators means more diversity means better synthetic corpora.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Content-level diversity between same-family checkpoints (different fine-tunes) may dominate artifact-level similarity, making same-family pooling genuinely useful.
fastest_falsification: Same-family pooling vs single-generator arms (two runs); a clear pooling gain falsifies the null-result core.

one_line: Speckle-aware augmentation must be multiplicative to transfer: additive-noise-trained invariances provably fail to cover SAR speckle statistics, explaining poor optical-to-SAR transfer
problem: Optical-pretrained segmentation models are adapted to SAR with generic noise augmentation, but SAR speckle is multiplicative and signal-dependent, unlike the additive noise models augmentations simulate.
core_hypothesis: Invariances learned from additive noise do not span multiplicative noise (the induced feature perturbation scales with local intensity), so augmentation with correctly parameterized multiplicative speckle (gamma-distributed, look-number matched) yields disproportionately better SAR transfer than intensity-matched additive noise augmentation.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched noise energy, multiplicative-speckle-augmented models will outperform additive-noise-augmented models on SAR segmentation, with the advantage growing in high-backscatter regions where the two noise models diverge most.
why_important: SAR labels are scarce and optical-to-SAR transfer is a standard need; getting the noise family right is a zero-cost correction to a widespread practice.
why_possibly_novel: Speckle filtering is a mature field, but the invariance-mismatch framing (additive-trained invariances failing on multiplicative perturbations) as a transfer explanation with an intensity-stratified test appears unarticulated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train on optical data with additive vs multiplicative augmentation at matched SNR; evaluate on a labeled SAR set; stratify performance gaps by local backscatter intensity.
main_risk: The optical-to-SAR gap may be dominated by geometry (layover, shadowing) rather than noise statistics, capping any augmentation effect.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Noise augmentation is noise augmentation; the specific noise family matters little once magnitude is tuned.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Log-transforming SAR inputs (common preprocessing) converts multiplicative to additive noise, potentially making the distinction moot in practice.
fastest_falsification: Run both augmentation arms on log-scaled inputs; if the multiplicative advantage disappears under log transform, the practical claim collapses.

one_line: SAR incidence-angle shift is a low-dimensional, physically parameterized domain shift: explicit angle conditioning beats generic domain adaptation at matched data
problem: SAR segmentation models degrade across acquisition geometries, and the community applies generic unsupervised DA, ignoring that the shift-generating variable (incidence angle) is known, continuous, and recorded in metadata.
core_hypothesis: Backscatter changes with incidence angle follow class-specific, smooth, physically constrained curves, so conditioning the model on the angle (or normalizing inputs along fitted per-class angular responses) exploits the shift's one-dimensional structure and outperforms adversarial or self-training DA that treats domains as unstructured.
falsifiable_prediction: Angle-conditioned models trained on angles A and tested on unseen angle B will beat angle-blind DA baselines given identical data, and their error will grow smoothly (not abruptly) with angular extrapolation distance.
why_important: Demonstrates a general principle, that metadata-parameterized shifts should be modeled, not adapted away, on a domain where the physics is clean and the metadata is free.
why_possibly_novel: Angle normalization exists in SAR radiometry; treating angle as a conditioning variable for segmentation and benchmarking it against modern DA appears rare to absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble multi-angle SAR scenes of the same areas; train angle-conditioned vs angle-blind vs DA-adapted models; evaluate cross-angle generalization curves.
main_risk: Multi-angle datasets with consistent labels over the same terrain are scarce; label misregistration could dominate results.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Cross-geometry degradation is another unstructured domain gap for generic adaptation machinery.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Angle interacts with terrain slope per pixel (local incidence angle), so the shift may be high-dimensional in practice, not one-dimensional.
fastest_falsification: Plot per-class backscatter statistics vs angle on existing data; if curves are erratic rather than smooth, the low-dimensional premise dies.

one_line: Optical-to-SAR translation networks teach translator artifacts, not SAR physics: DEM-based physical simulation beats learned translation as SAR training data at matched volume
problem: A popular recipe generates SAR training data by translating optical images with image-to-image networks, assuming learned translation captures what matters about SAR formation.
core_hypothesis: Learned translators reproduce SAR texture superficially but miss geometry-dependent effects (layover, foreshortening, shadowing) that define SAR appearance; segmenters trained on translated data learn translator regularities, while physically simulated SAR from elevation models, despite cruder texture, teaches the geometry and transfers better to real SAR.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched training volume, physical-simulation-trained models will beat translation-trained models on real SAR segmentation, with the advantage concentrated in high-relief terrain where geometric effects dominate, and reversed or absent in flat terrain.
why_important: Arbitrates between two synthetic-data philosophies (learned appearance vs physical structure) on a domain where they diverge sharply, guiding investment for SAR and other physics-heavy sensors.
why_possibly_novel: Both data sources exist separately; the terrain-stratified head-to-head designed to separate texture fidelity from geometric fidelity appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate both corpora for the same regions (translation from optical; simulation from DEMs); train identical segmenters; evaluate on labeled real SAR stratified by terrain relief.
main_risk: Simulation quality depends heavily on DEM resolution; a poor DEM handicaps the physics arm unfairly.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Learned image translation is the modern, superior route to cross-modal training data; physical simulation is outdated.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For land-cover classes defined mostly by texture (crops, water), translator texture fidelity may matter more than geometry, flipping the result outside mountains.
fastest_falsification: Evaluate both corpora's models on a small high-relief labeled SAR subset only; the geometry-dominated stratum is where the claim is sharpest.

one_line: Seasonal shift in agricultural remote sensing is a low-dimensional phenology trajectory per class, so shift correction should interpolate along trajectories rather than adapt distributions
problem: Crop segmentation models degrade across acquisition dates, and date-to-date shift is handled as generic domain adaptation, ignoring that vegetation changes follow smooth, class-specific phenological curves.
core_hypothesis: Per-class spectral evolution over the season traces smooth low-dimensional trajectories; modeling shift as position along a fitted trajectory (with day-of-year and growing-degree-day covariates) enables zero-shot correction to unseen dates that beats distribution-matching DA trained on the same data.
falsifiable_prediction: A trajectory-interpolation approach will outperform adversarial/statistic-matching DA for unseen mid-season dates, and both will fail comparably for out-of-trajectory events (drought, pest damage), confirming the mechanism boundary.
why_important: Agricultural monitoring needs date-robust models; exploiting phenological structure converts an adaptation problem into a regression problem with much better sample efficiency.
why_possibly_novel: Phenology modeling is established in remote sensing science; wiring it into segmentation-model domain correction and benchmarking against generic DA appears underexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Multi-date labeled crop dataset: fit per-class trajectories on dates {t1,t3,t5}; test correction quality on held-out {t2,t4}; compare against DA baselines given identical dates.
main_risk: Inter-annual and inter-field variability may widen trajectories into bands too broad for useful interpolation.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Date shift is one more domain gap; temporal structure is not explicitly exploited by adaptation methods.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern multi-temporal transformers may implicitly learn trajectories already, leaving explicit modeling no headroom.
fastest_falsification: PCA of per-class spectral statistics across dates; if trajectories are not low-dimensional and smooth, the premise fails before any model is built.

one_line: Cross-sensor optical satellite shift is dominated by point-spread-function differences, not spectral band differences: PSF matching recovers most cross-sensor transfer
problem: Models trained on one optical satellite degrade on another, and the loss is attributed to spectral band mismatch, driving band-translation research, while PSF/effective-resolution differences go unmodeled.
core_hypothesis: Segmentation features are more sensitive to spatial texture statistics (set by the sensor PSF and resampling chain) than to moderate spectral response differences, so convolving source imagery with the target's relative PSF (or deconvolution in the other direction) recovers the majority of cross-sensor performance loss without touching bands.
falsifiable_prediction: PSF matching alone will close more of the cross-sensor gap than band translation alone across sensor pairs with similar band sets, and the residual after PSF matching will correlate with spectral-response divergence, cleanly ordering the two factors.
why_important: PSF matching is a deterministic, label-free preprocessing step; establishing its primacy would simplify cross-sensor pipelines that currently rely on learned translation.
why_possibly_novel: PSF harmonization exists in radiometric processing communities; its quantified role in deep segmentation transfer relative to spectral factors appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For two same-region sensor pairs, apply {nothing, PSF match, band translation, both} to training data; train four models per pair; decompose gap closure by factor.
main_risk: PSFs are imperfectly published and vary across the field of view, limiting matching fidelity.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Spectral band differences are the salient cross-sensor obstacle; resolution differences are handled by resampling to common GSD.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Naive resampling to common ground-sample distance may already implicitly match texture statistics well enough that explicit PSF work adds little.
fastest_falsification: One sensor pair, PSF-match arm vs plain-resample arm; if equal, the claim's practical content is gone.

one_line: Geographic generalization failure in building segmentation is mostly a roof-material prior problem, and material-randomized procedural cities close geography gaps better than geography-matched real data augmentation
problem: Building extraction models trained in one region fail in others, attributed vaguely to 'geographic domain shift' spanning architecture, layout, and sensors, with no decomposition of what actually transfers badly.
core_hypothesis: The dominant failure component is the learned association between roof appearance (material, color) and the building class; procedural synthetic cities with aggressive roof-material randomization break this association and transfer to unseen geographies better than adding real data from a second geography, because randomization covers material space rather than sampling two points in it.
falsifiable_prediction: Material-randomized synthetic training will outperform two-region real training on held-out third-region evaluation, and error analysis will show its advantage concentrated on buildings with locally atypical roof materials.
why_important: Global mapping applications need geography-robust extraction; identifying the binding cue would replace expensive multi-region labeling with cheap procedural randomization.
why_possibly_novel: Procedural city data exists; the specific claim that roof-material association is the dominant geographic-transfer failure mode, with a third-region test design, appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train {region-A real, regions-A+B real, material-randomized synthetic + region-A real} and evaluate all on region C; stratify errors by roof-material typicality estimated from color statistics.
main_risk: Sensor and GSD differences between regional datasets may masquerade as geography effects.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Geographic shift is holistic (architecture, density, vegetation, sensors); no single cue dominates, so more diverse real data is the remedy.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Building shape and context conventions (row houses vs compounds) may dominate over materials in many region pairs.
fastest_falsification: Stratify an existing model's cross-region errors by roof-color typicality; if errors are not concentrated on atypical roofs, the premise is wrong.

one_line: Models trained on single-time-of-day aerial imagery learn solar-geometry shortcuts (shadow direction as a feature), failing predictably when sun azimuth changes
problem: Aerial datasets are collected in narrow acquisition windows with consistent sun position, and whether models exploit shadow direction as a spurious cue is unknown because test sets share the same window.
core_hypothesis: Consistent shadow azimuth acts as a hidden supervisory signal (e.g., building shadows always north-west implies a fixed appearance template); models keyed to it will degrade on imagery with different solar geometry in a way predictable from the azimuth difference, and shadow-direction randomization (via synthetic relighting) removes the dependence.
falsifiable_prediction: Cross-azimuth evaluation will show degradation monotone in azimuth difference for standard-trained models but flat for relight-randomized models, with errors concentrated on shadow-adjacent pixels of elevated objects.
why_important: Reveals a systematic, dataset-construction-induced fragility in aerial mapping models, along with a measurable fix, relevant to any program consuming imagery across seasons and hours.
why_possibly_novel: Shadow robustness is studied as detection nuisance; the framing of solar geometry as a learned shortcut with a monotone azimuth-difference degradation law appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use multi-time-of-day imagery of the same areas (or synthetic relighting of one set); train on one azimuth; evaluate across azimuth deltas; fit degradation vs delta; repeat with relight-randomized training.
main_risk: Same-area multi-azimuth imagery with consistent labels is scarce; synthetic relighting fidelity becomes load-bearing.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Shadows are noise to be robust against, not a shortcut being actively exploited; acquisition-window consistency is a data-cleanliness virtue.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Nadir imagery with small elevated-object fractions may offer too weak a shadow signal for models to bother exploiting.
fastest_falsification: Evaluate an existing aerial model on horizontally flipped imagery (which reverses shadow azimuth but preserves content statistics); a significant drop is quick evidence of shadow-direction reliance.

one_line: Flat-terrain synthetic SAR data actively hurts mountainous segmentation: without layover and foreshortening in training, models misread relief-induced artifacts as objects
problem: Synthetic SAR generators often assume flat ground for simplicity; whether flat-world synthetic data is merely suboptimal or actively harmful for relief terrain is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Layover and foreshortening produce bright, structured artifacts that flat-world-trained models have never seen and will systematically misclassify as man-made classes; adding flat-world synthetic data to training therefore decreases mountainous-area performance below the no-synthetic baseline (negative transfer), while DEM-aware synthetic data increases it.
falsifiable_prediction: On high-relief test areas, the flat-synthetic-augmented model will underperform the real-only baseline with false positives spatially coinciding with predicted layover zones (computable from DEM and orbit geometry), while the DEM-aware arm will outperform both.
why_important: Documents a concrete case where synthetic data's harm is geometrically predictable pixel-by-pixel, a rare opportunity to verify a negative-transfer mechanism rather than just observe aggregate decline.
why_possibly_novel: SAR simulation with terrain exists; the negative-transfer claim with layover-zone-localized error prediction appears unstated and untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train {real-only, +flat synthetic, +DEM-aware synthetic}; evaluate on labeled high-relief SAR; overlay false positives with computed layover masks and test spatial coincidence.
main_risk: Labeled high-relief SAR segmentation data is scarce; may need to hand-label a small evaluation set.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Any reasonable synthetic SAR data helps when real labels are scarce; simplifications degrade gracefully.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Models may treat layover artifacts as generic unknowns rather than confidently misclassifying them, making flat synthetic data neutral rather than harmful.
fastest_falsification: Evaluate a flat-synthetic-trained model on one mountainous scene and check false-positive coincidence with computed layover zones; a single-scene analysis suffices for a first verdict.

one_line: Simulated-cloud augmentation in change detection creates false invariance that hides genuine surface change: models learn 'ignore big appearance deltas', suppressing true-change recall
problem: Cloud-robustness training injects synthetic clouds so models ignore them, but change detection requires the opposite sensitivity to genuine large appearance changes, and the interference between these objectives is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: Synthetic-cloud augmentation teaches an invariance to large, spatially coherent appearance deltas; this invariance generalizes beyond clouds and suppresses detection of true abrupt surface changes (construction, flooding) whose appearance signature is statistically similar at the feature level, creating a measurable recall deficit on abrupt-change classes.
falsifiable_prediction: Cloud-augmented change-detection models will show lower recall on abrupt large-area changes than non-augmented controls at matched precision, and the deficit will scale with cloud-augmentation strength, while gradual-change recall stays unaffected.
why_important: Warns that a routine robustness augmentation can silently erode the core capability of a monitoring system, exactly on the high-consequence events it exists to catch.
why_possibly_novel: Augmentation-objective interference is discussed abstractly; this concrete invariance-collision in change detection with a strength-dependent prediction appears undocumented.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train change detectors at 4 cloud-augmentation strengths; evaluate on a test set with annotated abrupt and gradual changes plus real clouds; plot recall by change type against augmentation strength.
main_risk: Benefits of cloud robustness may outweigh the recall deficit in aggregate metrics, hiding the trade-off unless change types are separated.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Robustness augmentations are additive goods; making models ignore clouds does not affect their sensitivity to real changes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Clouds may be spectrally distinctive enough that the learned invariance stays cloud-specific and never touches surface-change sensitivity.
fastest_falsification: Compare abrupt-change recall of one cloud-augmented vs one control model on an existing benchmark with change-type labels.

one_line: Pan-sharpening is a domain: models trained on pan-sharpened imagery fail on native multispectral data beyond what resolution accounts for, because sharpening artifacts became features
problem: Much training imagery is pan-sharpened for visual quality, and deployment often runs on native-resolution data, with the sharpening process treated as a benign resolution enhancement rather than a distribution choice.
core_hypothesis: Pan-sharpening injects characteristic spatial-spectral correlations (spectral distortion at edges, injected high-frequency luminance) that models learn as class evidence; performance on native data degrades more than a resolution-matched control predicts, and the residual is attributable to sharpening-artifact reliance.
falsifiable_prediction: Models trained on pan-sharpened data and tested on native data upsampled to the same GSD will underperform models trained on native data throughout, with the gap exceeding the reverse-direction gap, and artifact-reliance probes (evaluating on artifact-suppressed sharpened data) will predict the per-model deficit.
why_important: Pipelines silently mix sharpened and native imagery; quantifying sharpening as a domain would set data-hygiene standards for remote-sensing ML.
why_possibly_novel: Pan-sharpening quality is studied for reconstruction fidelity; its role as a learned domain for downstream segmentation appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Same scenes in native and pan-sharpened form; train both ways; evaluate both ways with resolution matched by resampling; decompose the asymmetric gap.
main_risk: True high-resolution ground truth for fair labeling across both versions may be tricky to align.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Pan-sharpening adds information and is at worst neutral for downstream models; resolution is the only variable worth matching.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern consistency-based sharpening methods may inject artifacts too weak to function as learnable shortcuts.
fastest_falsification: Cross-evaluate two existing models (one trained per version) on both versions; the asymmetry check needs no new data collection.

one_line: Off-nadir view-angle mismatch dominates aerial building-segmentation transfer, and 3D-aware view resampling of training data beats appearance-level adaptation at matched cost
problem: Aerial building datasets mix nadir and off-nadir imagery inconsistently, and cross-dataset transfer failures are treated as appearance gaps, ignoring that facade visibility and rooftop displacement change geometrically with view angle.
core_hypothesis: The dominant cross-dataset factor for building segmentation is view-angle distribution mismatch (facades visible or not, roof offset from footprint); resampling training views with true 3D city models to match the target's angle distribution closes more gap than style-based adaptation of the original views.
falsifiable_prediction: View-resampled training will beat style-adapted training on off-nadir targets, with gains concentrated in tall-building areas where geometric displacement is largest, and no gain on nadir-only targets.
why_important: Clarifies whether aerial-domain transfer budgets should buy 3D geometry (city models, mesh reconstruction) or appearance adaptation, with a class of applications (dense urban mapping) hanging on the answer.
why_possibly_novel: Off-nadir difficulty is acknowledged in dataset papers; a controlled comparison of geometric view resampling versus appearance adaptation as competing transfer mechanisms appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use a photogrammetric city mesh to re-render training imagery at target-matched view angles; train {original, style-adapted, view-resampled} models; evaluate on an off-nadir target stratified by building height.
main_risk: Mesh rendering quality may introduce its own domain gap that eats the geometric benefit.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Cross-dataset aerial transfer is an appearance/style problem; geometry differences are absorbed by data diversity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern datasets may already span enough view angles that the mismatch is small compared to sensor and label-convention differences.
fastest_falsification: Stratify an existing model's cross-dataset errors by building height and view angle metadata; absence of the predicted geometric error pattern kills the premise.

one_line: Sensor radiometric-calibration drift over a satellite's lifetime is a slow, monotone distribution shift correctable at the input layer, and models silently degrade along it at a measurable rate
problem: Long-lived Earth-observation models are trained on archive imagery and deployed for years, while the sensor itself drifts radiometrically; ML evaluations never stratify performance by acquisition epoch relative to training data.
core_hypothesis: Detector aging produces slow monotone radiometric drift; segmentation accuracy declines correspondingly with time-distance from the training epoch, and a per-band affine input correction fitted from pseudo-invariant calibration sites recovers most of the decline without model retraining.
falsifiable_prediction: Evaluating a fixed model over acquisition years will show monotone performance decline with epoch distance; applying published calibration-drift corrections (or corrections fitted on invariant sites) will flatten the decline curve substantially.
why_important: Establishes model aging as a maintenance problem with a cheap input-side fix, relevant to every operational EO pipeline whose retraining cadence is slower than sensor drift.
why_possibly_novel: Radiometric drift is well known to calibration teams; its propagation into deep-model performance decline and the sufficiency of input-side correction appear unquantified in the ML literature.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fixed model, test sets sampled from 5+ acquisition years of one sensor over stable regions, performance-vs-epoch curve with and without drift correction.
main_risk: Land-cover change over years confounds sensor drift; requires stable-site selection or change masking.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Distribution shift in EO is about geography and season; the sensor itself is assumed stationary within a mission.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Agency-side reprocessing may already normalize drift in distributed products, leaving nothing for the input correction to fix.
fastest_falsification: Evaluate one public model on early-mission vs late-mission imagery of stable desert calibration sites; a flat curve ends the claim quickly.

one_line: The LiDAR sim-to-real gap is dominated by ray-drop and intensity statistics, not geometry: matching per-material dropout and intensity response beats appearance-style adaptation of point clouds
problem: Simulated LiDAR gets geometry nearly right (ray casting is exact), yet sim-trained segmentation models transfer poorly, and the community adapts feature distributions without isolating which channel carries the gap.
core_hypothesis: Real LiDAR returns exhibit material- and range-dependent dropout and intensity responses that simulators model crudely; a decomposition experiment will show that injecting realistic drop/intensity statistics into simulation closes most of the gap, while geometric perturbations close little, inverting the usual realism priorities.
falsifiable_prediction: In matched arms {vanilla sim, +realistic ray-drop, +realistic intensity, +both}, the both-arm will recover the majority of the sim-to-real segmentation gap, with per-class gains largest for materials with distinctive reflectivity (vegetation, retroreflective signs, dark vehicles).
why_important: Points LiDAR simulation investment at the sensor-response channel, which is learnable from unlabeled real sweeps, rather than at expensive world-modeling.
why_possibly_novel: Ray-drop modeling exists in isolated simulator papers; a controlled gap decomposition establishing dominance of the sensor-response channel over geometry for segmentation appears unavailable.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit dropout/intensity models per material class from unlabeled real sweeps; retrain segmenters on the four arms; evaluate on labeled real LiDAR; decompose gap closure.
main_risk: Simulator geometry may be less perfect than assumed (asset shapes, scene composition), leaving a geometry residual misattributed to sensor response.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: LiDAR sim-to-real requires learned domain adaptation of features; the gap is diffuse and not attributable to a single sensor channel.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Scene-content differences (traffic density, object mix) may dominate everything sensor-related, making all sensor modeling secondary.
fastest_falsification: Ablate intensity input entirely from a sim-trained and a real-trained model; if gap persists identically without intensity, the intensity half of the claim collapses.

one_line: Beam-pattern shift (channel count and spacing) is a resampling problem, not a domain-adaptation problem: geometric resampling to the target pattern beats feature-space alignment across LiDAR models
problem: Models trained on one LiDAR (e.g., 64-beam) degrade on another (e.g., 32-beam or solid-state patterns), and the fix of record is unsupervised DA, though the shift-generating process (scan-pattern geometry) is exactly known.
core_hypothesis: Cross-device degradation is mostly explained by point-density and elevation-angle distribution mismatch, which is deterministically simulable; resampling source point clouds to the target scan pattern (dropping/interpolating beams) recovers most cross-device performance, outperforming adversarial feature alignment given no target labels.
falsifiable_prediction: Pattern-resampled training will beat feature-alignment DA on cross-device benchmarks for segmentation, and the residual gap after resampling will correlate with intensity-response differences, not density differences, showing the geometric component is solved.
why_important: Fleet operators mix LiDAR models constantly; a deterministic, training-free-at-deployment solution would displace fragile adaptation machinery.
why_possibly_novel: Beam subsampling is a known augmentation; the strong claim that pattern resampling essentially solves the geometric component, with a residual analysis pinning what remains, appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Two-device dataset pair; train {vanilla, resampled-to-target, DA-adapted}; evaluate cross-device; decompose residual by density-vs-intensity ablations.
main_risk: Solid-state scan patterns with motion distortion may not be reachable by resampling spinning-LiDAR data.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Cross-sensor LiDAR transfer is a hard domain-adaptation problem requiring learned alignment.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Networks may key on subtle inter-beam correlations that resampling cannot reproduce, keeping the learned-adaptation advantage.
fastest_falsification: Resample-only arm vs vanilla on one public cross-device benchmark; if resampling does not beat vanilla clearly, the premise is in trouble.

one_line: Adding physically motivated beam divergence (footprint widening with range) to LiDAR simulation closes more sim-to-real gap per engineering hour than any appearance-level randomization
problem: Simulated LiDAR treats beams as ideal rays, producing edge-perfect returns on distant thin structures, unlike real sensors whose diverging beams produce mixed returns and edge artifacts at range.
core_hypothesis: Ray-ideal simulation teaches models that distant thin objects (poles, riders, wires) have crisp point support, so they over-segment or hallucinate structure at range; simulating beam divergence (multi-ray footprint integration with mixed-return logic) fixes a range-dependent error family that appearance randomization cannot touch.
falsifiable_prediction: Divergence-aware simulation will improve real-domain segmentation specifically for thin classes at long range, with a gain profile increasing in range bins, while randomization-based arms show flat range profiles.
why_important: Long-range thin-structure perception is safety-relevant for driving; a physics-correct simulation detail targeting it is more valuable than aggregate mIoU moves.
why_possibly_novel: Beam divergence is documented in sensor literature; its downstream effect on segmentation transfer and range-stratified error structure appears unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render matched sim corpora {ideal-ray, divergence-aware}; train segmenters; evaluate on real LiDAR with errors stratified by class thinness and range bin.
main_risk: Multi-ray simulation cost may force approximations that reintroduce edge artifacts of a different kind.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: LiDAR simulation realism is about world content and generic noise; beam optics are negligible at driving ranges.
why_it_might_be_wrong: At typical urban ranges, footprints may stay small enough that divergence effects are lost in other noise sources.
fastest_falsification: Compare range-binned thin-class errors of an existing sim-trained model against a real-trained control; absence of a range-growing deficit removes the target the fix is aimed at.

one_line: Adverse-weather LiDAR shift is governed by the spatial clustering of particle returns, not their rate: simulations matching only drop/return rates fail, matching cluster statistics transfers
problem: Rain/snow/spray simulation for LiDAR is tuned to match aggregate return rates and attenuation, yet weather-sim-trained models still fail on real weather, suggesting the matched statistics are the wrong ones.
core_hypothesis: Real precipitation and spray returns are spatially and temporally clustered (plumes behind vehicles, gust bands), while simulators scatter them independently; models can reject independent clutter easily but fail on structured clutter that mimics objects, so matching second-order spatial statistics of weather returns is the necessary condition for transfer.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched return rates, cluster-statistics-matched weather simulation will yield markedly better real-weather segmentation than independent-scatter simulation, with the gap concentrated in false-object errors near vehicles and in gusts.
why_important: Adverse weather is a leading operational-domain failure for autonomous driving; identifying which statistic must be matched converts weather simulation from art to specification.
why_possibly_novel: Weather augmentation for LiDAR exists; the second-order-statistics sufficiency/necessity framing with a matched-rate controlled comparison appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit cluster statistics from real weather sweeps (unlabeled); build matched-rate independent vs clustered simulations; train and evaluate on labeled real-weather data; stratify by proximity to moving vehicles.
main_risk: Labeled real-weather LiDAR segmentation data is scarce and weather metadata is coarse.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Matching return rates and attenuation curves is the accepted definition of realistic weather simulation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Point-level networks may not exploit spatial correlations of clutter at the scales where clustering lives, making both simulations equivalent downstream.
fastest_falsification: Visual/statistical comparison of real vs simulated weather-return spatial autocorrelation, then a single pair of training runs at matched rates.

one_line: Missing rolling-shutter motion distortion in LiDAR simulation causes a specific real-world failure on fast crossing objects, and adding per-point timestamp skew to sim data fixes exactly that failure
problem: Spinning LiDAR accumulates points over a rotation while objects move, producing skewed object geometry that most simulators omit; the downstream consequence for segmentation is unquantified.
core_hypothesis: Models trained on distortion-free sim data learn rigid object-shape priors; on real fast crossing objects (skewed by ego-relative motion during the sweep), they fragment or misclassify instances, an error family absent for longitudinal traffic; simulating per-point acquisition time and applying motion skew eliminates this family.
falsifiable_prediction: Real-domain error analysis will show sim-trained models failing disproportionately on high-lateral-velocity objects relative to real-trained controls, and the skew-simulated training arm will close that specific stratum's gap while leaving static-object performance unchanged.
why_important: Crossing objects (pedestrians, cyclists at intersections) are among the highest-consequence perception targets; a simulation detail that specifically fixes them is safety-relevant.
why_possibly_novel: Motion compensation is standard in mapping pipelines; the training-data-side effect of distortion absence on segmentation of dynamic objects appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train {distortion-free, skew-simulated} on matched sim; evaluate on real data with object-velocity annotations; compare error rates binned by lateral velocity.
main_risk: Velocity annotations or track-derived velocity estimates are needed on the real evaluation set.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Rolling-shutter skew is a mapping/odometry concern that segmentation networks absorb without special treatment.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Real training sets already contain skewed objects, so real-trained models handle them; but sim-trained deficits may still be dominated by other factors, burying the skew effect.
fastest_falsification: Velocity-binned error comparison of one existing sim-trained model vs one real-trained model on a dataset with tracks; no new training needed for the deficit check.

one_line: Cross-city and cross-country driving shifts are hierarchically different: cross-city is texture-level (adapting input statistics suffices), cross-country adds layout-grammar shift (requiring context relearning)
problem: Driving domain adaptation treats all geographic transfer as one problem class, though moving between cities within a country and moving between countries plausibly shift different levels of scene structure.
core_hypothesis: Within-country transfer is dominated by low/mid-level appearance (road surface, vegetation, signage style) fixable by input-statistics adaptation, while cross-country transfer additionally shifts scene grammar (lane conventions, sidewalk presence, intersection topology) that input-level methods cannot touch; therefore method rankings will invert between the two transfer types.
falsifiable_prediction: Input/statistics-level adaptation methods will close most of the cross-city gap but a minority of the cross-country gap, while context-relearning approaches (partial decoder retraining on pseudo-labels) will dominate cross-country transfer, producing a reproducible ranking inversion.
why_important: Method selection for geographic expansion is currently benchmark-lottery; a two-regime taxonomy with a diagnostic (layout-statistics divergence) would make it principled.
why_possibly_novel: Geographic DA benchmarks exist, but the explicit two-level decomposition with predicted method-ranking inversion appears unformulated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three-dataset design (two cities same country, one city another country); run one input-level and one context-level adaptation method on both transfer types; test for ranking inversion; measure layout-statistics divergence as the mediating variable.
main_risk: Dataset triplets confound sensor and labeling differences with geography; needs sensor-matched sources.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Geographic domain gap is a single continuum where stronger shift just needs stronger adaptation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Layout grammar may transfer through the backbone more easily than assumed, keeping input-level methods competitive everywhere.
fastest_falsification: Measure whether input-statistics adaptation gains differ systematically between one cross-city and one cross-country pair; a uniform gain profile contradicts the two-regime claim.

one_line: Camera-extrinsics randomization in simulation transfers better than photometric randomization for driving segmentation, because rig geometry is the axis real deployments actually vary
problem: Domain randomization budgets are spent overwhelmingly on photometric axes (textures, lighting, weather), while deployment fleets vary mostly in camera mounting geometry, an axis usually fixed in sim.
core_hypothesis: For fleet-scale deployment, the operative test-time variation is rig geometry (height, pitch, lens); training with extrinsics randomization builds viewpoint-equivariant features that transfer across rigs, delivering more real-world robustness per sample than equivalent photometric randomization, which addresses variation reality does not present as strongly.
falsifiable_prediction: On multi-rig real evaluations, extrinsics-randomized sim training will beat photometric-randomized sim training at matched sample budgets, while on single-rig evaluations the ordering reverses or ties, localizing the benefit to rig variation.
why_important: Aligns randomization budgets with the actual variance structure of deployment, a resource-allocation principle extensible to other robotic domains.
why_possibly_novel: Both randomization types exist; the claim that their ranking flips with the rig-diversity of the evaluation, and the deployment-variance-matching principle behind it, appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sim corpora with {photometric-only, extrinsics-only, both} randomization; evaluate on real data pooled across rigs vs single-rig subsets; compare ordering across evaluation types.
main_risk: Multi-rig real segmentation data with rig metadata is limited; may need to composite from several datasets with label harmonization.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Photometric randomization is the core of sim-to-real robustness; camera geometry is handled by calibration, not learning.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Simple geometric augmentation (crop, scale, perspective jitter) may already span rig variation, making explicit extrinsics randomization redundant.
fastest_falsification: Compare extrinsics-randomized sim training against a strong geometric-augmentation baseline on one multi-rig evaluation; a tie kills the practical claim.

one_line: Dropping the intensity channel from simulated LiDAR training data improves real-world transfer: geometry-only sim supervision avoids learning the simulator's wrong reflectance model
problem: Simulated LiDAR intensity is known to be physically crude, yet sim-training pipelines feed it to models anyway on the assumption that any extra channel helps.
core_hypothesis: Simulator intensity is wrong in structured, learnable ways; models allocate capacity to these fictitious reflectance cues and lose it at test time, so ablating intensity during sim training (or replacing it with noise) produces better real-domain segmentation despite less input information, an instance of harmful-channel pruning under domain shift.
falsifiable_prediction: Geometry-only sim-trained models will beat geometry+sim-intensity models on real evaluations where intensity is available to neither or both, with the deficit of the intensity arm concentrated in classes whose simulated reflectance diverges most from reality (vegetation, wet roads).
why_important: A counterintuitive, immediately actionable recipe change; more broadly, establishes that under sim-to-real shift, less (wrong) input can beat more input, informing multimodal sim design.
why_possibly_novel: Channel ablation studies exist in-domain; the cross-domain claim that a systematically wrong simulated channel is net harmful, with a class-level divergence prediction, appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train {geometry-only, geometry+sim-intensity} on matched sim; fine-tune neither; evaluate both on real LiDAR with intensity masked at test time for parity; compare per-class deltas against a measured sim-real intensity divergence per class.
main_risk: Test-time parity design is contestable; reviewers may argue real intensity should be used when available, changing the question.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: More sensor channels in training are better; imperfect simulated intensity still carries useful signal.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Even crude intensity may correlate with real reflectance ordinally, providing net-positive signal that outweighs the learned artifacts.
fastest_falsification: Two training runs with/without sim intensity, one real evaluation; a clear win for the intensity arm settles it against the claim.

one_line: Traffic-agent behavior models in simulators leave layout signatures that segmentation models absorb: sim-trained models fail on real-but-implausible-in-sim configurations at predictable locations
problem: Simulation realism audits cover appearance and sensor models but never the behavior model that places dynamic agents, though it determines the joint spatial distribution of objects that context-using segmenters learn.
core_hypothesis: Rule-based traffic models produce over-regular agent configurations (lane-centered, minimum-gap, norm-compliant); segmentation models internalize these as context priors and misparse real scenes containing configurations the behavior model never generates (jaywalkers mid-block, vehicles at odd angles, crowding violations), and such failures are minable by ranking real scenes by their likelihood under the sim behavior model.
falsifiable_prediction: Real scenes with low likelihood under the simulator's behavior model will show disproportionately higher segmentation error for sim-trained models than for real-trained controls, and enriching sim training with behavior-noise (rule-violating agents) will preferentially fix low-likelihood scenes.
why_important: Extends the sim-to-real realism checklist to behavioral realism with a concrete mining tool, targeting exactly the anomalous scenes that matter most for safety.
why_possibly_novel: Behavior realism is studied for planning; its effect on perception training data and a likelihood-based failure-mining method appear new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Score real scenes by sim-behavior-model likelihood; compare error-vs-likelihood slopes for sim-trained and real-trained models; retrain with rule-violating agents and re-measure the slope.
main_risk: Behavior-model likelihood scoring on real scenes requires tracking and map alignment, adding pipeline complexity.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Perception training is insensitive to the traffic model; behavior realism matters only for planning and prediction stacks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Per-pixel appearance evidence may dominate context so thoroughly that layout priors contribute negligible error even in anomalous scenes.
fastest_falsification: Error-vs-likelihood slope comparison using an existing sim-trained checkpoint and any real dataset with tracks; one analysis, no training.

one_line: Map-conditioned synthetic scene generation transfers better than free generation because layout comes from reality: the transferable component of driving scenes is the map, not the pixels
problem: Driving-scene generators are trained to synthesize everything jointly; whether anchoring generation on real HD-map layouts changes downstream transfer value is untested as a controlled question.
core_hypothesis: Scene layout (road topology, lane geometry, static infrastructure placement) is both the hardest component for generators to get statistically right and the most consequential for segmentation context priors; conditioning generation on real map layouts while synthesizing appearance yields training data whose downstream transfer approaches real data much closer than fully generated scenes at matched generator quality.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched corpus size and generator, map-conditioned corpora will beat unconditioned corpora on real-domain segmentation by a margin exceeding the gap between unconditioned corpora and no-synthetic baselines, and the advantage will concentrate in layout-dependent classes (lane markings, sidewalks, crossings).
why_important: Identifies which scene component must be real for synthetic data to work, guiding the architecture of driving data engines toward map-anchored generation.
why_possibly_novel: Map-conditioned generation exists as a capability; the controlled transfer-value comparison isolating layout provenance for segmentation appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One scene generator run in {map-conditioned, free} modes at matched size; train two segmenters plus a real-only baseline; evaluate on real data with class-stratified analysis.
main_risk: Map-conditioned generation may also improve image quality per se, confounding layout provenance with sample fidelity.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Better generators will eventually synthesize everything; conditioning on real maps is an engineering convenience, not a transfer principle.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Layout statistics of strong free generators may already match maps closely, shrinking the conditioning advantage to nothing.
fastest_falsification: Compare lane-topology statistics of free-generated scenes to real map statistics; a close match removes the mechanism before any training.

one_line: Night-driving domain shift is a mixture of two sub-domains (artificially lit vs unlit), and adapting to their mixture fails where per-sub-domain adaptation succeeds
problem: Day-to-night adaptation treats night as one domain, though urban lit scenes and rural unlit scenes have almost opposite photometric structure (high local contrast vs global underexposure).
core_hypothesis: The night domain is bimodal; adaptation methods matching the pooled night distribution converge to a compromise appearance model that fits neither mode, so splitting night data by an illumination-source statistic and adapting per mode yields consistent gains over pooled adaptation at identical data and compute.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-mode adaptation will beat pooled adaptation on both lit and unlit test subsets simultaneously, and the pooled model's errors will concentrate at mode boundaries (transitions between lit and unlit regions within scenes).
why_important: A case study in domain definition as a first-class variable: adaptation performance may hinge less on the method and more on how the target 'domain' is carved, with night driving as a high-value instance.
why_possibly_novel: Day-night adaptation is heavily studied as a single transfer; the explicit bimodality claim with within-scene mode-boundary error prediction appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Cluster night images by illumination statistics into lit/unlit; run one adaptation method pooled vs per-cluster; evaluate on both subsets and on annotated transition regions.
main_risk: The lit/unlit split may be a continuum rather than a bimodal structure, weakening the mode-specific framing.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Night is a coherent target domain; more night data and stronger methods are the path, not domain redefinition.
why_it_might_be_wrong: High-capacity adaptation methods may fit multimodal targets without difficulty, making the split unnecessary.
fastest_falsification: Histogram illumination statistics of night datasets for bimodality; absence of bimodality undercuts the premise immediately.

one_line: Underwater domain shift is parameterized by physical water type and range: attenuation-model-based augmentation (Jerlov-style parameter sweeps) beats learned style transfer for cross-water segmentation transfer
problem: Underwater segmentation models fail across sites (coastal vs open ocean vs turbid harbor), and the remedy of record is learned style adaptation per site, ignoring that underwater image formation is a well-parameterized physical process.
