core_hypothesis: Cross-site underwater shift is dominated by wavelength-dependent attenuation and backscatter governed by a few physical parameters; augmenting training data by sweeping a physical underwater image-formation model across water types covers the cross-site variation space more faithfully than style transfer fitted to specific target sites, and generalizes to unseen sites where style transfer cannot.
falsifiable_prediction: Physics-swept augmentation will beat target-fitted style transfer on held-out third-site evaluations while losing narrowly on the fitted site, demonstrating a coverage-vs-fit trade favoring physics for site generalization.
why_important: Marine robotics and reef monitoring need site-robust segmentation without per-site adaptation data; a physics-parameterized augmentation is deployable with zero target data.
why_possibly_novel: Underwater image-formation models are used for restoration; using them as a shift-coverage augmentation for segmentation with a third-site generalization test appears rare.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three underwater datasets from distinct water types; train {vanilla, physics-swept, style-fitted-to-site-B} on site A; evaluate all on sites B and C.
main_risk: Physical model parameters (veiling light, scattering phase) may be too coarse to capture real site differences like particulate texture.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Underwater appearance is too complex for parametric models; learned adaptation per deployment site is the practical route.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Biological content shift (different species, substrates) between sites may dominate optical shift, capping any optics-side intervention.
fastest_falsification: Fit the physical model's parameters per site and check how much inter-site image-statistics variance they explain; low explained variance kills the premise pre-training.

one_line: Turbidity acts as a range-dependent low-pass filter, so underwater augmentation must couple blur strength to scene depth; uniform-blur augmentation teaches physically impossible images and transfers worse
problem: Turbidity augmentation for underwater segmentation applies uniform degradation over the image, though real turbidity degrades far scene content much more than near content.
core_hypothesis: Models can exploit the depth-degradation coupling as a distance cue, and training on uniformly degraded images breaks this cue while presenting statistically impossible inputs; depth-aware degradation (using estimated or stereo depth to modulate blur/contrast per pixel) produces models that transfer better to real turbid water at matched augmentation strength.
falsifiable_prediction: Depth-coupled augmentation will beat uniform augmentation on real turbid evaluations, with the advantage concentrated on scenes with large depth ranges and absent on near-planar scenes, confirming the coupling mechanism.
why_important: A physically consistent augmentation upgrade costing only a depth estimate, relevant to all range-dependent degradation media (fog, haze, smoke) beyond underwater.
why_possibly_novel: Depth-aware fog synthesis exists for driving; the general claim that physically inconsistent (depth-decoupled) degradation actively hurts transfer, with the planar-scene control, appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Augment a clear-water dataset with {uniform, depth-coupled} turbidity at matched strength; train two models; evaluate on real turbid footage stratified by scene depth range.
main_risk: Monocular depth estimates underwater are poor, injecting noise into the coupled augmentation.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Degradation augmentation is about matching global severity statistics; spatial structure of the degradation is a refinement without measurable payoff.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Networks may be locally invariant enough that the spatial structure of degradation is irrelevant, leaving only severity to matter.
fastest_falsification: Compare the two augmentation arms on one dataset with a large-depth-range test subset; a tie there ends the coupling claim.

one_line: Generative models cannot synthesize useful industrial defect training data because defects are tail events: procedural physics-based defect models beat learned generators at matched effort, and the gap grows with defect rarity
problem: Industrial defect segmentation suffers extreme data scarcity, and teams increasingly train generators on the few available defect examples, assuming generative interpolation can expand the defect distribution.
core_hypothesis: Learned generators trained on scarce defect examples mode-average toward typical defects and cannot extrapolate the physical tail (rare crack morphologies, unusual contaminations); procedural models built from defect-formation physics (fracture mechanics, corrosion growth) sample the tail by construction, so procedurally-augmented training will beat generatively-augmented training on rare-defect recall, with the advantage increasing as evaluation defects get rarer.
falsifiable_prediction: On a defect benchmark stratified by training-set-similarity, generative augmentation will win on common defect types while procedural augmentation will win on rare types, with a crossover reproducible across two inspection domains.
why_important: Defect segmentation is valuable precisely on rare defects; establishing where generative augmentation fails and procedural modeling wins would redirect industrial ML practice.
why_possibly_novel: Both augmentation routes exist in industrial vision; the rarity-stratified head-to-head with a stated crossover claim appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One defect dataset; hold out rare morphologies entirely from training; augment via {generator trained on common defects, procedural defect model}; compare recall on held-out rare morphologies.
main_risk: Building credible procedural defect models requires domain expertise that varies wildly by defect type, threatening generality.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Generative augmentation is the modern answer to industrial data scarcity; procedural modeling is legacy engineering.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Foundation generative models may carry enough general crack/damage priors from web-scale pretraining to extrapolate defect tails after all.
fastest_falsification: Sample heavily from a generator trained on common defects and measure whether any samples land near held-out rare morphologies (feature-space coverage test); no downstream training needed.

one_line: Farm-to-farm shift in weed/crop segmentation is dominated by soil-background statistics, not plant appearance: background-swap synthetic data closes cross-farm gaps at near-zero generation cost
problem: Weed segmentation models fail when moved between farms, and the failure is attributed to plant variety differences, motivating expensive multi-farm labeling, while soil appearance (color, moisture, texture, residue) varies at least as strongly and is never isolated.
core_hypothesis: Models key on background-foreground contrast statistics; soil shift alone explains most cross-farm degradation, so compositing existing labeled plants onto diverse soil backgrounds (real soil textures, no generative model needed) recovers most cross-farm transfer without any new plant data.
falsifiable_prediction: Background-swap-augmented training will close a majority of the cross-farm gap on farms with similar crops but different soils, and error analysis will show the baseline's failures concentrated in soil-appearance outlier regions (wet patches, residue cover) rather than on unusual plants.
why_important: Agricultural robotics needs cheap cross-farm robustness; if the answer is soil diversity rather than plant diversity, data-collection budgets are being spent on the wrong axis.
why_possibly_novel: Background augmentation is generic practice; the domain-specific dominance claim (soil over plant appearance) with residue/moisture-stratified error analysis appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Two farms with same crop, different soils: train on farm A {vanilla, background-swapped}; evaluate on farm B; stratify errors by a soil-anomaly score.
main_risk: Cross-farm datasets confound growth stage and lighting with soil, requiring collection-matched pairs.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Plant appearance variation (cultivar, growth stage) is the primary cross-farm obstacle for weed segmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Growth-stage differences may dominate in practice, making soil augmentation a minor lever.
fastest_falsification: Evaluate an existing model on same-farm imagery re-composited onto foreign soil textures; a small drop means soil is not the binding factor.

one_line: Greenhouse-to-field transfer is primarily an illumination-spectrum shift correctable by per-channel input renormalization, not a structural domain gap requiring retraining
problem: Plant segmentation models trained in greenhouses (diffuse, spectrum-shifted artificial light) degrade outdoors, and the degradation is treated as a full domain gap requiring adaptation pipelines.
core_hypothesis: The dominant shift component is global and spectral (light source spectrum and diffuseness changing color ratios and shadow statistics), which lives in the first-order image statistics; a fitted per-channel affine correction (estimated from a handful of unlabeled field images) recovers most greenhouse-to-field performance, leaving only a small residual for structural adaptation.
falsifiable_prediction: Input renormalization will recover the majority of the greenhouse-to-field drop across two crops, while the same correction applied to a genuinely structural shift (different crop) will recover almost nothing, validating the diagnosis.
why_important: If a spectral correction suffices, agricultural teams can skip adaptation infrastructure for this transfer, and the result calibrates expectations about which transfers are 'shallow'.
why_possibly_novel: Color-constancy corrections are standard image processing; using them as a designed falsification of the 'deep domain gap' framing for a specific agricultural transfer appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Greenhouse-trained model, field test set: evaluate {raw, affine-corrected, full fine-tuning} and compute the fraction of the gap closed by correction alone; include the different-crop control.
main_risk: Field imagery adds wind motion, occlusion, and density changes that may be larger than assumed, capping the spectral share.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Greenhouse-to-field is a canonical domain gap needing adaptation or field labels.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Shadow structure under direct sun is a spatial (not just spectral) change that affine channel correction cannot represent.
fastest_falsification: Apply gray-world or fitted affine correction to field images and evaluate an existing greenhouse model; hours of work, immediate answer on the recovered fraction.

one_line: Sim-to-real for fruit segmentation fails on occlusion statistics of foliage, not fruit appearance: procedural plant models with measured leaf-angle distributions beat photorealistic generative fruit imagery
problem: Synthetic orchard data emphasizes photoreal fruit rendering, yet real orchard segmentation errors concentrate on partially occluded fruit, whose visibility statistics depend on canopy architecture that synthetic scenes model casually.
core_hypothesis: The transfer-limiting statistic is the distribution of fruit-visibility fractions and occlusion boundary types induced by foliage geometry; procedural canopies fitted to measured leaf-angle and internode distributions reproduce these statistics, so cruder-looking but occlusion-faithful synthetic data beats prettier fruit renders with unrealistic canopies.
falsifiable_prediction: Occlusion-faithful procedural data will beat appearance-optimized generative data on real orchard evaluation, with the advantage concentrated in the low-visibility-fraction strata, and the visibility-fraction histogram divergence between synthetic and real will predict per-arm transfer.
why_important: Yield estimation hinges on detecting mostly-hidden fruit; getting the occlusion statistics right is the actionable lever, and the visibility-histogram metric gives generators a concrete target.
why_possibly_novel: Synthetic agriculture datasets exist; the occlusion-statistics-first design principle with a predictive divergence metric appears unarticulated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build both corpora for one crop; measure visibility-fraction histograms against a hand-annotated real sample; train both arms; evaluate stratified by visibility fraction.
main_risk: Annotating true visibility fractions on real data is labor-intensive and partly subjective.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Photorealistic fruit appearance is the quality axis for synthetic orchard data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern amodal-segmentation heads may handle occlusion robustly enough that appearance fidelity returns as the binding constraint.
fastest_falsification: Compare visibility-fraction histograms of an existing synthetic orchard set against real annotations; a close match refutes the premise that current synthetic canopies are occlusion-unfaithful.

one_line: Specular highlights on wet and polished industrial surfaces are the dominant unmodeled shift axis in factory deployments, and highlight-structure randomization beats global photometric randomization
problem: Factory segmentation models degrade when surface finish or wetness changes (coolant, oil, polishing stage), and pipelines respond with global photometric augmentation that does not resemble the actual specular structure of such changes.
core_hypothesis: Specularities are spatially structured (elongated along curvature, source-linked, saturating) and models treat them as object evidence; randomizing highlight structure specifically (rendering or compositing physically plausible specular lobes varying in position, extent, saturation) builds the right invariance, while global brightness/contrast jitter does not overlap the specular manifold at all.
falsifiable_prediction: Highlight-randomized training will outperform global-photometric training on wet/polished test conditions at matched augmentation budget, with errors of the baseline concentrated exactly on saturated specular pixels and their halos.
why_important: Surface-condition variation is ubiquitous in manufacturing and food processing; a targeted augmentation family addressing it would transfer across many factory tasks.
why_possibly_novel: Specularity removal is studied in graphics/vision; specular-structure augmentation as a domain-shift inoculation for industrial segmentation appears under-explored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect dry/wet paired imagery of one production line (or wet a subset deliberately); train with {global photometric, highlight-randomized} augmentation on dry data; evaluate on wet data with specular-pixel-stratified errors.
main_risk: Compositing physically plausible speculars without 3D surface models may look wrong enough to add a new artifact axis.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Photometric jitter covers illumination-related variation; wetness is a minor condition change within augmentation reach.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Saturated speculars destroy information no invariance can recover, so the fix may cap out at the information-theoretic limit regardless of augmentation.
fastest_falsification: Error analysis of an existing model on wet frames: if errors are not concentrated at specular pixels, the axis is not dominant and the idea dies.

one_line: Biofouling on fixed underwater cameras is a canonical slow distribution shift: performance decays along a measurable fouling trajectory and is recoverable by input-side compensation without retraining
problem: Fixed underwater monitoring cameras foul progressively (algae, biofilm), degrading segmentation over weeks, but ML pipelines treat performance decay as unexplained drift and schedule blind retraining.
core_hypothesis: Fouling imposes a smooth, monotone, optically characterizable transformation (contrast loss, green-shift, localized occlusion) whose trajectory can be tracked from image statistics alone; a compensation function fitted along the trajectory restores model inputs toward the clean-lens distribution, recovering most accuracy without labels or retraining until physical occlusion dominates.
falsifiable_prediction: On longitudinal fixed-camera data, segmentation accuracy will decay monotonically with a fouling index computed from image statistics; input compensation fitted from the index will recover the majority of the decay in the early-to-mid trajectory and fail sharply past an occlusion threshold, giving a predictable maintenance trigger.
why_important: Provides a maintenance-scheduling primitive (compensate until threshold, then clean) for long-deployed environmental sensors, replacing guesswork retraining with a measurable control loop.
why_possibly_novel: Slow sensor-side drift as a first-class, physically tracked domain shift with an explicit compensation-then-maintain policy appears absent from segmentation literature, which focuses on scene-side shift.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One longitudinal fixed-camera dataset spanning a fouling cycle with periodic sparse labels; compute the fouling index, fit compensation, plot accuracy over time for raw vs compensated inputs.
main_risk: Fouling is spatially patchy and organism-dependent, potentially breaking the smooth-trajectory assumption.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Model performance decay in deployment is met with periodic retraining or recalibration on fresh labels; sensor-surface optics are an operations issue, not an ML variable.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Beyond mild fouling, information loss may be unrecoverable so early that the compensation window is too short to be useful.
fastest_falsification: Correlate a simple fouling index with segmentation confidence/accuracy over one deployment's archive; no correlation, no idea.

one_line: Conveyor-belt wear is a slow domain drift with a knowable direction: pre-aging belt textures in training data ('drift-direction augmentation') inoculates food-processing segmentation against months of future drift
problem: Segmentation systems on processing lines degrade over months as belts scratch, stain, and fade; retraining is reactive because drift is treated as unpredictable.
core_hypothesis: Belt wear follows a predictable visual trajectory (scratch density up, contrast down, stain accumulation) that can be simulated forward; augmenting training data with synthetically pre-aged backgrounds along this trajectory produces models whose performance stays flat over real aging, unlike models with generic augmentation of matched strength.
falsifiable_prediction: On longitudinal production data, drift-direction-augmented models will show significantly flatter accuracy-vs-time curves than generic-augmentation controls, and the advantage will disappear if the plant replaces the belt (resetting drift), confirming mechanism specificity.
why_important: Demonstrates a general template, forecast the drift direction and augment along it, applicable to any deployment with directional environmental aging (roads, tools, containers).
why_possibly_novel: Augmentation is normally isotropic around the training distribution; explicitly anisotropic augmentation along a forecast drift direction appears unformulated as a principle.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Archive data from one line across a belt lifecycle: train on early-period data with {generic, pre-aged} augmentation; evaluate monthly slices; compare slope of accuracy decay.
main_risk: Access to longitudinal industrial data is the practical bottleneck; simulated aging may miss unforeseen drift components (new stain chemistry).
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Drift is handled reactively by monitoring and retraining; augmentation is for generalization, not for forecasting.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Drift may be dominated by discrete events (maintenance, product changes) rather than smooth aging, making the forecast direction wrong.
fastest_falsification: Fit the aging trajectory on archive imagery and verify it is smooth and directional; a non-directional drift structure ends the idea.

one_line: Cross-farm livestock segmentation shift is dominated by coat-pattern distribution differences between herds, and breed-conditioned synthetic coat randomization predicts and closes cross-farm gaps
problem: Livestock monitoring models trained on one herd fail on others, and the failure is attributed to barn conditions and cameras, while herd-specific coat-pattern distributions (breed mix, marking statistics) are an unexamined shift axis.
core_hypothesis: Models overfit the training herd's coat-pattern statistics as class evidence; the cross-farm gap correlates with divergence between herd coat-pattern distributions (measurable from unlabeled images), and texture-randomizing or breed-balancing synthetic coats during training removes the dependence, closing the gap on pattern-divergent farms specifically.
falsifiable_prediction: Cross-farm performance drops will rank-correlate with unlabeled coat-statistics divergence across farm pairs, and coat-randomized training will preferentially close gaps on high-divergence pairs while leaving low-divergence pairs unchanged.
why_important: Gives livestock-vision deployments a pre-deployment transfer predictor from unlabeled footage plus a targeted augmentation fix, replacing per-farm labeling.
why_possibly_novel: Animal re-identification studies coat patterns as signal; treating herd-level coat statistics as a domain-shift axis for segmentation with a divergence-based transfer predictor appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Multi-farm cattle dataset: compute coat-statistic divergences between farm pairs from unlabeled data; measure cross-farm segmentation drops; test rank correlation; retrain with coat randomization and re-measure high-divergence pairs.
main_risk: Camera and barn-illumination differences may swamp coat effects, requiring careful covariate control.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Cross-farm variation is about facilities and cameras; the animals themselves are treated as the stable part of the scene.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Segmentation (unlike re-identification) may rely mostly on silhouette and context, making coat statistics irrelevant to the mask task.
fastest_falsification: Evaluate an existing model on coat-recolored copies of its own test set; insensitivity to recoloring means coat statistics are not load-bearing.

one_line: Construction-site segmentation violates the stationary-domain assumption by design (the scene's own evolution is the shift), and time-conditioned training beats domain-adaptation framings
problem: Construction monitoring treats each project phase as a new domain requiring adaptation, though phase progression is a structured, roughly ordered process shared across projects.
core_hypothesis: Scene evolution on construction sites follows a common coarse grammar (earthworks, structure, envelope, finishing) inducing predictable class-distribution and appearance trajectories; conditioning the model on estimated project phase (inferable from unlabeled imagery) outperforms both a phase-blind model and pairwise domain adaptation between phases, especially for classes whose appearance changes most across phases.
falsifiable_prediction: Phase-conditioned models will beat phase-blind models on held-out projects, with gains concentrated in phase-ambiguous classes (concrete surfaces, scaffolding), and the learned phase representation will transfer across projects (probing accuracy for phase on unseen sites).
why_important: Reframes a costly serial-adaptation problem as a single conditional model, and provides a template for other deliberately non-stationary environments (mines, refits, disaster response).
why_possibly_novel: Temporal domain adaptation exists for gradual natural drift; exploiting a shared structural grammar of scene evolution as the conditioning variable appears unexplored for segmentation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Multi-project time-lapse dataset: train phase-blind vs phase-conditioned (phase from a self-supervised temporal ordering); evaluate on held-out projects per phase.
main_risk: Project heterogeneity (residential vs infrastructure) may break the shared-grammar assumption.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Non-stationarity is handled by periodic retraining or continual learning; the environment's evolution is noise, not structure to condition on.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Phase may be too coarse a variable, with within-phase variation exceeding between-phase variation.
fastest_falsification: Cluster unlabeled multi-project imagery temporally and test whether cluster assignments transfer across projects; failure of transferable phase structure kills the conditioning premise.

one_line: FID between domains does not predict segmentation transfer; a divergence over joint boundary-appearance statistics does, and the two metrics can be made to disagree by construction
problem: Domain distance for dense prediction is measured with appearance-distribution metrics inherited from generative-model evaluation, without evidence that they track what segmentation transfer actually depends on.
core_hypothesis: Segmentation transfer depends on the joint distribution of local appearance and label-boundary geometry, which FID-style marginal appearance metrics ignore; a metric comparing boundary-conditioned appearance statistics (appearance distributions in boundary bands vs interiors) will predict transfer where FID fails, and adversarial dataset pairs can be constructed where the metrics disagree and transfer follows the boundary-conditioned metric.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a suite of synthetic-real and real-real dataset pairs, the boundary-conditioned divergence will rank transfer gaps with substantially higher correlation than FID, and constructed pairs (appearance-matched but boundary-statistics-mismatched, and vice versa) will show transfer tracking the new metric.
why_important: The field needs a validated domain-distance instrument for dense prediction; without one, dataset investments and adaptation choices are steered by a metric optimized for image realism, not task transfer.
why_possibly_novel: Critiques of FID exist for generation; a constructive replacement designed around label-boundary-conditioned statistics with adversarial validation pairs appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble 10 dataset pairs with measured transfer gaps; compute both metrics; compare rank correlations; then build the two constructed pairs and verify the predicted dissociation.
main_risk: The new metric needs labels on both domains for boundary conditioning, limiting its use to labeled-pair studies unless proxy boundaries suffice.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Lower FID to the target domain means better transfer; appearance distance is an adequate proxy for task-relevant domain distance.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For most natural dataset pairs the two metrics may correlate so strongly that the improvement is real but practically negligible.
fastest_falsification: Compute both metrics on 5 pairs with known transfer gaps; if FID already ranks them near-perfectly, the headroom claim collapses.

one_line: Aggregate domain-shift metrics mislead because segmentation transfer is bottlenecked by the worst-shifted frequent class: a max-over-classes metric predicts transfer better than any mean
problem: Domain distances are computed over pooled feature distributions, implicitly averaging per-class shifts, though a single badly shifted high-pixel-share class can dominate downstream mIoU loss.
core_hypothesis: Transfer degradation is closer to a weakest-link function than an average: per-class shift measured separately and aggregated by a pixel-frequency-weighted maximum will predict transfer gaps better than pooled or mean aggregations, and interventions targeted at the single worst-shifted frequent class will move aggregate transfer more than diffuse adaptation.
falsifiable_prediction: Across dataset pairs, frequency-weighted-max aggregation will outperform mean and pooled metrics in predicting mIoU drops, and per-pair, adapting only the identified bottleneck class (targeted synthetic data or augmentation) will recover a disproportionate share of the aggregate gap.
why_important: Changes both measurement and intervention practice: adaptation effort becomes class-targeted, and shift audits produce actionable bottleneck identifications rather than one abstract number.
why_possibly_novel: Per-class shift analysis appears descriptively in papers; elevating aggregation functional form (max vs mean) to a tested hypothesis with intervention validation appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 8 dataset pairs, compute per-class feature shifts, compare predictive power of aggregations; pick 2 pairs and run bottleneck-class-targeted training interventions.
main_risk: Per-class shift estimation needs target labels or reliable pseudo-labels, which are noisy exactly where shift is large.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Domain distance is a global property of dataset pairs, sensibly summarized by pooled or averaged statistics.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Class confusions under shift are cross-class phenomena (A absorbs B), which neither max nor mean over per-class marginals captures.
fastest_falsification: Regression comparison of aggregations on existing multi-pair transfer results from published benchmark tables plus recomputed features; largely analysis-only.

one_line: Shift metrics computed in task-trained feature spaces predict transfer better than metrics in general-purpose self-supervised spaces, and the difference grows with task specificity
problem: Domain distances are increasingly computed in off-the-shelf foundation-model feature spaces for convenience, assuming feature-space choice is second-order for shift measurement.
core_hypothesis: Shift that matters is shift in the features the task model actually uses; distances in general self-supervised spaces overweight task-irrelevant variation (backgrounds, styles the segmenter ignores) and underweight task-critical variation, so segmentation-trained feature spaces yield systematically better transfer prediction, with the advantage largest for specialized tasks (thin structures, texture-defined classes).
falsifiable_prediction: Across dataset pairs, transfer-gap prediction from distances in segmentation-trained features will beat distances in general features, and the prediction-quality gap will correlate with a task-specificity index (how much task features diverge from general features).
why_important: Standardizing on foundation-feature shift metrics may systematically misrank adaptation needs; establishing task-conditionality would change measurement protocols across the shift literature.
why_possibly_novel: Feature-space sensitivity of shift metrics is occasionally noted; a systematic task-conditionality study with a specificity index appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: 10 dataset pairs, distances computed in 3 feature spaces (general SSL, segmentation-trained, task-specific fine-tuned); compare rank correlations with measured transfer gaps.
main_risk: Circularity concern: task-trained features come from models related to those being evaluated; needs careful separation of measurement and evaluation models.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Strong general-purpose features are the best universal ruler for measuring distribution shift.
why_it_might_be_wrong: General spaces may contain task subspaces as directions, so a learned projection could equalize the comparison, dissolving the dichotomy.
fastest_falsification: Three-space comparison on 5 pairs with existing pre-trained encoders; days of compute, mostly evaluation.

one_line: Label-shift/covariate-shift decomposition is ill-posed at pixel level but well-posed at region level, and region-level decomposition predicts which adaptation method family will work
problem: The classic decomposition of shift into label shift and covariate shift underlies method selection in classification, but pixels are not exchangeable units, and no accepted analogue exists for segmentation.
core_hypothesis: At region level (connected components or superpixel groups), shift decomposes meaningfully into composition shift (which regions occur; analogous to label shift) and appearance shift (how regions look; analogous to covariate shift); the measured mix predicts method-family effectiveness, with resampling/reweighting methods winning under composition-dominant shift and feature-alignment methods winning under appearance-dominant shift.
falsifiable_prediction: Dataset pairs classified as composition-dominant vs appearance-dominant by the region-level decomposition will show the predicted method-family ranking flip, reproducibly across pairs within each category.
why_important: Gives segmentation DA the missing diagnostic layer that classification has had for years: measure first, then choose the method family, instead of benchmarking everything.
why_possibly_novel: Shift-type diagnostics for dense prediction with a validated link from measured shift type to method-family choice appear absent; papers assume covariate shift implicitly.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define the region-level decomposition; compute it on 8 pairs; run one representative method per family on each; test the predicted ranking flip.
main_risk: Region definitions (superpixels vs components) may change the decomposition materially, hurting robustness of the diagnostic.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Segmentation domain shift is treated monolithically as covariate shift; label-shift tooling is considered inapplicable to dense tasks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Composition and appearance shift may be so correlated in real pairs that the decomposition never dissociates, leaving no method-selection signal.
fastest_falsification: Compute the decomposition on known pairs and check whether pairs even spread across the two regimes; if all pairs are mixed, the diagnostic has no discriminative range.

one_line: Classification-derived transferability estimators fail for segmentation because spatial error correlation violates their independence assumptions, and their failure is predictable from error-cluster size
problem: Cheap transferability estimators (source-model-output-based scores) are being imported from classification to rank source models and datasets for segmentation transfer without checking their statistical assumptions against dense-prediction error structure.
core_hypothesis: These estimators assume roughly independent per-example errors; segmentation errors cluster spatially (a wrong region is thousands of correlated wrong pixels), inflating estimator confidence and breaking rankings precisely when transfer fails via large coherent regions, so estimator error will scale with the spatial autocorrelation length of the target-domain error field.
falsifiable_prediction: Across transfer pairs, transferability-estimator ranking quality will degrade monotonically with measured error-cluster size, and a corrected estimator operating on effective-sample-size-adjusted region units will restore ranking quality.
why_important: Prevents the community from adopting silently miscalibrated model-selection tools for dense prediction, and supplies the corrected estimator as a usable replacement.
why_possibly_novel: Transferability estimation is an active area centered on classification; the spatial-correlation failure mode analysis and region-unit correction for segmentation appear new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble 12 source-model/target pairs with known fine-tuned performance; compute standard estimators and ranking quality; measure error autocorrelation; test the predicted degradation relation and the corrected estimator.
main_risk: Fine-tuned 'ground truth' transfer performance is itself noisy across seeds, limiting achievable ranking-quality measurement.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Transferability scores validated on classification carry over to other tasks with minor recalibration.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Pixelwise scores aggregated over enough images may average out spatial correlation, leaving classification-derived estimators adequate in practice.
fastest_falsification: Compute one standard estimator's ranking quality on segmentation pairs split into low vs high error-autocorrelation groups; no difference between groups undercuts the mechanism.

one_line: Methods ranked on sim-to-real benchmarks do not rank the same on real-to-real shifts because the two shift families have structurally different statistics, making the standard benchmark a biased method selector
problem: Domain adaptation for segmentation is developed almost exclusively on synthetic-to-real benchmark pairs, and the community extrapolates method rankings to real-world (real-to-real) deployment shifts without evidence of rank stability.
core_hypothesis: Sim-to-real shift is dominated by low-level artifact and appearance mismatch (which artifact-normalizing methods exploit), while real-to-real shift is dominated by content and layout differences; therefore method rankings will show systematic inversions between the two families, with artifact-oriented methods overperforming on sim-to-real and underperforming on real-to-real relative to content-oriented methods.
falsifiable_prediction: Evaluating a fixed suite of adaptation methods on matched sim-to-real and real-to-real pairs will yield low rank correlation between families, with the predicted directional inversions, reproducible across two suites.
why_important: If the field's default benchmark family is a biased selector, years of method development may be optimized for the wrong shift structure; deployment decisions need family-matched benchmarks.
why_possibly_novel: Individual papers note benchmark limitations; a systematic rank-stability study across shift families with a mechanism-level prediction of which methods flip appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: 6 adaptation methods x {2 sim-to-real pairs, 2 real-to-real pairs} with matched training budgets; compute cross-family rank correlations and test predicted inversions.
main_risk: Method implementations are tuned to sim-to-real conventions; fair retuning per pair is laborious but necessary for a clean claim.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Good performance on the canonical synthetic-to-real benchmarks indicates general domain-adaptation quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern methods may be dominated by self-training components indifferent to shift structure, keeping rankings stable across families.
fastest_falsification: Cross-tabulate already published results of common methods on one sim-to-real and one real-to-real benchmark; strong rank agreement in the literature would deflate the claim cheaply.

one_line: An 'augmentation compass': measuring target-domain distance separately along each augmentation axis predicts which augmentations will help, replacing trial-and-error augmentation search
problem: Choosing augmentations for a shifted target is empirical guesswork; the shift is measured (if at all) as one scalar, though augmentations act along specific perturbation directions.
core_hypothesis: Domain shift is anisotropic in the space of augmentation-reachable transformations; projecting the source-target discrepancy onto each augmentation axis (estimating, per axis, how far target statistics are along that transformation family) yields a profile that predicts per-augmentation transfer gains, because augmentation helps only along axes where the target actually lies.
falsifiable_prediction: Across targets, per-axis projections will rank per-augmentation gains with high correlation, and composite augmentation policies built from top-profile axes will match or beat exhaustive augmentation search at a fraction of its cost.
why_important: Converts augmentation selection under shift from a search problem to a measurement problem, with immediate savings for every deployment-adaptation workflow.
why_possibly_novel: Augmentation-policy search exists (in-domain), and shift metrics exist (scalar); the axis-resolved shift decomposition used as an augmentation selector appears unformulated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define projections for 8 augmentation axes (blur, noise, color temperature, contrast, scale, perspective, occlusion, JPEG); compute profiles for 4 shifted targets; train per-axis-augmented models; test profile-to-gain correlation.
main_risk: Axes interact (color temperature and contrast are not orthogonal), muddying per-axis attribution.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Broad augmentation cocktails are the safe default; predicting individual augmentation utility from measurements is not considered feasible.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Augmentation benefits may come mostly from generic regularization rather than shift coverage, decoupling gains from any shift profile.
fastest_falsification: Two targets, four axes, the correlation check on per-axis gains; a near-zero correlation on this mini-grid ends it.

one_line: Fifty labeled target images rank adaptation methods as reliably as full test sets, implying label-free shift estimation is over-invested relative to micro-labeling
problem: A large research area builds label-free transfer/shift estimators, implicitly assuming target labels are unobtainable even in small quantity, an assumption rarely priced against the alternative.
core_hypothesis: Because method-ranking is a lower-information task than performance estimation, tiny labeled target samples (tens of images, chosen with simple diversity sampling) produce method rankings that agree with full-test-set rankings with very high probability, dominating every label-free estimator at trivial labeling cost for dense prediction, where each image contains thousands of labeled pixels.
falsifiable_prediction: Across benchmark pairs and method suites, rankings from 50-image labeled subsets will agree with full-set rankings (high rank correlation, correct top-1 with high frequency), while state-of-the-art label-free estimators agree substantially less, at every subset size above a small threshold.
why_important: Would redirect research and practice: the operational question becomes how to label 50 images well, not how to avoid labels entirely, changing evaluation protocols for the shift community.
why_possibly_novel: Small-validation-set studies exist for classification hyperparameters; the explicit dense-prediction argument (pixels-per-image makes micro-sets information-rich) and the head-to-head against label-free estimators appear unmade.
minimal_falsification_experiment: 3 benchmark pairs, 6 methods each: bootstrap 50-image subsets, compute ranking agreement distributions, compare against two published label-free estimators on the same suites.
main_risk: Conclusion may not extend to rare-class-dominated evaluations where 50 images miss critical classes entirely.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Target labels are the scarce resource to be engineered around; label-free estimation is the practical path for method selection under shift.
why_it_might_be_wrong: In genuinely label-prohibitive settings (medical, classified data), even 50 images may be unobtainable, preserving the label-free niche regardless of statistics.
fastest_falsification: Bootstrap analysis on one existing benchmark's published per-image results; pure analysis, no training.

one_line: Boundary F-score degrades before region IoU under gradually increasing shift, making boundary metrics an early-warning channel for deployment drift monitoring
problem: Deployment monitoring watches aggregate segmentation quality proxies that move only after substantial degradation, missing the early phase where intervention is cheap.
core_hypothesis: Boundary localization depends on high-frequency, shift-fragile features while region identity depends on robust low-frequency context, so as shift increases gradually, boundary precision decays measurably earlier than region overlap; the boundary-to-region degradation lag is a usable early-warning signal, and its length is predictable from the shift type's frequency profile.
falsifiable_prediction: Along graded shift sequences (increasing corruption severity, seasonal drift archives), boundary F-score will show statistically detectable decline at lower shift levels than mIoU in most sequences, with longer lags for high-frequency shifts (blur, noise) than for low-frequency shifts (lighting, season).
why_important: A no-extra-cost reordering of monitoring dashboards (watch boundary metrics first) grounded in a frequency-based mechanism, applicable to any deployed dense-prediction system.
why_possibly_novel: Metric sensitivity differences are known qualitatively; the systematic lag structure, its shift-type dependence, and its framing as a monitoring primitive appear unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate fixed models along graded corruption suites and one real temporal-drift archive; detect per-metric changepoints; compare detection thresholds and lags across shift types.
main_risk: Boundary metrics are noisier, so earlier mean decline may not translate into earlier reliable detection after accounting for variance.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: mIoU (or its proxies) is the canonical health metric; other metrics are reporting variants that move together with it.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For context-destroying shifts, region identity may collapse first, inverting the lag exactly where early warning matters most.
fastest_falsification: One model, one corruption suite, both metrics vs severity; the ordering of detectable-decline onsets is visible in a day of evaluation.

one_line: Ensemble disagreement predicts transfer gap only when members differ in data ordering and augmentation draws, not just initialization seeds: diversity type, not diversity amount, drives shift detection
problem: Ensemble disagreement is the standard label-free proxy for transfer gap, but ensembles are built with whatever diversity is convenient, and the dependence of the proxy's validity on diversity type is unexamined for segmentation.
core_hypothesis: Under domain shift, useful disagreement arises from members having consumed different data-order-and-augmentation trajectories (exploring different shortcut solutions), while seed-only ensembles converge to functionally similar solutions whose agreement stays high even when all members are wrong the same way; hence gap prediction quality is governed by trajectory diversity, measurable by weight-space or function-space member distances.
falsifiable_prediction: Seed-only ensembles will systematically underestimate transfer gaps compared to data-order/augmentation-diverse ensembles at matched size, and gap-prediction error will correlate with measured member function-space diversity across ensemble constructions.
why_important: Calibrates a widely used shift-monitoring tool: teams relying on cheap seed ensembles may be blind to exactly the correlated failure modes that matter under shift.
why_possibly_novel: Ensemble diversity is studied for accuracy and calibration; its type-dependence for shift-gap estimation in dense prediction appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build 4 ensemble types (seed-only, data-order, augmentation-draw, combined) on one source; evaluate disagreement-vs-true-gap correlation over 6 shifted targets.
main_risk: Effect may shrink for large models where seed differences already induce substantial functional diversity.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Any independently trained ensemble's disagreement is a valid uncertainty and gap proxy; how diversity was injected is immaterial.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Data-order effects may be negligible under long training with shuffling, making all diversity types equivalent asymptotically.
fastest_falsification: Two ensemble types, three shifted targets, correlation comparison; roughly a week of small-model compute.

one_line: Entropy-reducing shifts (fog, blur, smoke) degrade segmentation gracefully while entropy-adding shifts (clutter, novel textures) degrade catastrophically, and an input entropy-delta statistic separates the regimes in advance
problem: Shift severity is treated as one-dimensional ('how far is the target'), but identical distances by standard metrics produce wildly different damage, and no pre-deployment statistic explains which shifts will be catastrophic.
core_hypothesis: Shifts that remove information (lowering local input entropy) push models toward prior-driven, smooth predictions whose errors are moderate and structured, while shifts that add unfamiliar structure (raising entropy in unfamiliar directions) trigger confident structured hallucinations; the sign and magnitude of an input entropy delta (computable without labels) predicts the degradation regime and its slope.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a suite of corruptions and natural shifts matched for feature-space distance, entropy-reducing shifts will show systematically flatter accuracy-vs-distance slopes than entropy-adding shifts, and the entropy-delta statistic will classify regime membership with high accuracy.
why_important: A label-free pre-deployment triage: knowing whether an environment's shifts are of the graceful or catastrophic kind changes safety margins, monitoring cadence, and fallback design.
why_possibly_novel: Corruption benchmarks average over shift types; the information-theoretic regime split with a predictive statistic appears unproposed for dense prediction.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble matched-distance shift pairs (fog vs clutter overlay, blur vs texture swap); measure degradation slopes for fixed models; test regime separation by the entropy-delta statistic.
main_risk: Matching shifts for feature-space distance while varying entropy delta is delicate; poor matching invalidates slope comparisons.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Shift severity (distance) determines damage; the direction or information-theoretic character of the shift is not a modeled variable.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The taxonomy may collapse in practice because real shifts mix both characters within one scene, leaving the statistic uninformative.
fastest_falsification: Fog-vs-clutter slope comparison on one model and one dataset; two curves, immediate visual verdict.

one_line: Cross-domain miscalibration of a segmentation model is predictable from its source-domain augmentation sensitivity, requiring no target data at all
problem: Deployment under shift needs calibration guarantees, but calibration under shift is only measurable after collecting shifted data, too late for design-time decisions.
core_hypothesis: A model's confidence robustness under perturbation is a stable trait: the slope of calibration error growth under parametric source-domain augmentations (noise, blur, color shifts) predicts its calibration error on genuinely shifted targets, because both stem from the same reliance profile on shift-fragile features.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a zoo of segmentation models, source-measured augmentation-sensitivity slopes will rank target-domain calibration errors with high correlation across multiple real shifted targets, and the ranking will be stable across target choices.
why_important: Enables selecting deployment models for calibration robustness at design time from source data alone, a missing capability in safety cases for perception systems.
why_possibly_novel: Accuracy-on-the-line style relationships link in-distribution and shifted accuracy; the analogous relationship for dense-prediction calibration via augmentation sensitivity appears unestablished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: 15 checkpoints varying architecture/training; measure augmentation-sensitivity slopes on source; measure calibration on 3 shifted targets; test rank correlation and stability.
main_risk: The relationship may hold within a model family but break across families (CNNs vs transformers), limiting the tool's generality.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Calibration under shift is idiosyncratic to the target and must be measured there; source-side statistics cannot substitute.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Real shifts include content novelty that augmentations never simulate, so augmentation sensitivity may miss the dominant miscalibration driver.
fastest_falsification: Five checkpoints, one shifted target, slope-vs-calibration scatter; a structureless scatter kills it in days.

one_line: There is a critical period for domain diversity: synthetic-domain variety introduced late in training fails to confer robustness that the same variety introduced early provides
problem: Synthetic-domain diversity (multiple renderers, randomization axes) is budgeted as a dataset property, ignoring training-time scheduling; if diversity has a critical period, most pipelines apply it suboptimally.
core_hypothesis: Feature invariances form early during training and resist revision; exposing the model to diverse synthetic domains only after the early phase yields measurably less domain robustness than early exposure with identical total data, because late diversity cannot reshape consolidated early-layer features.
falsifiable_prediction: Early-diverse/late-uniform training will beat late-diverse/early-uniform training on shifted-target evaluation at matched data and compute, with the difference traceable to early-layer feature invariance measures (CKA stability, invariance probes).
why_important: Would establish that when data is presented matters as much as what data exists, changing how every mixed-domain training pipeline schedules its corpora.
why_possibly_novel: Critical periods are documented for image deficits and label noise in classification; domain-diversity scheduling for segmentation robustness appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Two-phase training with diversity concentrated in either phase, matched totals; evaluate on 3 shifted targets; probe early-layer invariances at phase boundary and end.
main_risk: Learning-rate schedules confound phase effects; requires constant-LR or carefully matched schedule controls.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Dataset composition determines outcomes; presentation order washes out over sufficient epochs.
why_it_might_be_wrong: With enough late-phase training at adequate LR, features may remain plastic, erasing any critical-period effect.
fastest_falsification: The two-arm phase-swap experiment at small scale; one clear reversal or equality answers it.

one_line: Real-data fine-tuning after synthetic pretraining erases synthetic boundary-precision gains within a few hundred steps (forgetting is boundary-first), and freezing shallow decoder layers prevents it
problem: The standard recipe (synthetic pretrain, real fine-tune) is assumed to retain synthetic benefits, but what exactly survives fine-tuning is unmeasured at the metric-component level.
core_hypothesis: Synthetic pretraining's most distinctive contribution is boundary-localization precision (from pixel-perfect labels); real fine-tuning with sloppier labels overwrites precisely this component fastest, so boundary F-score decays toward real-only levels early in fine-tuning while interior accuracy keeps improving, and selectively freezing boundary-relevant layers preserves the synthetic advantage.
falsifiable_prediction: Tracking boundary and interior metrics per fine-tuning step will show boundary-metric decay toward the real-only baseline within the early phase; layer-freezing interventions targeted by boundary-sensitivity analysis will retain most synthetic boundary advantage at equal final interior accuracy.
why_important: If the recipe silently discards synthetic data's main gift, cheap interventions (selective freezing, boundary-weighted fine-tuning loss) could recover substantial value already paid for.
why_possibly_novel: Catastrophic forgetting is studied at task level; component-resolved forgetting (boundary vs interior) during the standard synthetic-to-real recipe appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Synthetic-pretrained model, fine-tune on real data logging boundary/interior metrics every N steps; repeat with selective freezing; compare final Pareto points.
main_risk: Real evaluation labels are themselves imprecise at boundaries, muddying measurement of the decay.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Fine-tuning preserves pretraining benefits while adapting to the target; what is lost is assumed minor and diffuse.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Boundary precision may be encoded redundantly enough that fine-tuning refines rather than erases it, showing no early decay.
fastest_falsification: Metric-component logging during one standard fine-tune; the decay curve either appears in the first run or does not.

one_line: Batch composition (mixed synth-real batches vs alternating pure batches) changes normalization statistics enough to explain a chunk of reported adaptation gains, a confound in mixed-data experiments
problem: Mixed-domain training implementations differ arbitrarily in whether batches interleave domains or alternate purely, and this detail is unreported despite directly changing batch-norm statistics and gradient noise structure.
core_hypothesis: With batch normalization, mixed batches compute statistics over a domain mixture (blurring domain-specific activation distributions), while alternating pure batches let statistics swing between domains; these regimes yield systematically different transfer performance at identical data ratios, an effect large enough to rival some published method deltas and absent under group/layer normalization.
falsifiable_prediction: At fixed data ratio and schedule, mixed-batch and pure-batch arms will differ measurably in target-domain performance for BN models and be statistically indistinguishable for GN/LN models, isolating normalization as the mechanism.
why_important: Identifies an unreported implementation knob as a reproducibility hazard in the mixed-data literature, and provides a mechanism-verified default recommendation.
why_possibly_novel: BN's domain sensitivity is known in adaptation contexts; batch-composition policy as a quantified confound in synthetic-real mixing experiments appears undocumented.
minimal_falsification_experiment: 2 (batch policy) x 2 (BN vs GN) factorial at fixed ratio on one synthetic-real pair; measure target performance across 3 seeds.
main_risk: Effect size may vary with batch size and ratio, requiring a small grid rather than one point to be conclusive.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Batch composition at fixed data ratio is an inconsequential implementation detail not worth reporting.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern large-batch training with sync-BN may average enough samples that composition effects vanish.
fastest_falsification: The BN-only pair of arms (two runs, three seeds); a null difference at typical batch sizes deflates the claim.

one_line: Re-estimating only normalization statistics on the target domain recovers a large fraction of gains claimed by complex adaptation methods, and should be the mandatory null model for sim-to-real papers
problem: Sim-to-real adaptation methods claim gains over source-only baselines, but the cheapest possible adaptation (updating norm statistics on unlabeled target data, zero learned parameters) is rarely reported as a baseline, so the marginal value of complex machinery is unknown.
core_hypothesis: A substantial share of adaptation-method gains on standard benchmarks is reproduced by norm-statistic re-estimation alone, and the share is predictable: it is largest when the shift is global-photometric and smallest when the shift is layout/content, giving both a null model and a shift-type diagnostic.
falsifiable_prediction: Across published-method reimplementations on two benchmarks, norm-recalibration will recover a large fraction of each method's gain over source-only, with the recovered fraction correlating with a measured photometric-vs-structural shift index of the benchmark pair.
why_important: Recalibrates the field's sense of progress, forces honest accounting in future papers, and gives practitioners a zero-cost first move for any deployment shift.
why_possibly_novel: Norm-statistic adaptation is known as a technique; its systematic use as a null model with a quantified recovered-fraction analysis across methods and a shift-type predictor appears missing for segmentation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Reimplement 4 adaptation methods on 2 benchmark pairs; add the norm-recalibration arm; compute recovered fractions and correlate with the shift-type index.
main_risk: Transformer architectures without batch statistics limit the null model's applicability, requiring an analogue (e.g., LN affine recalibration).
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Adaptation-method gains over source-only baselines reflect the value of their specific mechanisms (alignment, self-training, style transfer).
why_it_might_be_wrong: Best current methods may already dominate norm recalibration by wide margins on all pairs, making the null model uninformative for state-of-the-art claims.
fastest_falsification: Norm-recalibration vs source-only on one benchmark: if the recovery is negligible there, the strong version dies immediately.

one_line: Self-training on target pseudo-labels works mainly by re-fitting class decision thresholds, not by feature learning: a logit-adjustment-only control reproduces most of its gain
problem: Self-training is the dominant ingredient in segmentation domain adaptation, credited with teaching target-domain features, but the mechanism has not been decomposed against much cheaper explanations.
core_hypothesis: Under shift, class priors and confidence scales move, so much of pseudo-label self-training's gain comes from re-fitting the output layer's effective thresholds to target statistics; a control that freezes all features and only adjusts per-class logit offsets/scales (fitted on the same pseudo-labels) will recover a majority of the self-training gain on standard benchmarks.
falsifiable_prediction: The logit-adjustment control will recover most of self-training's mIoU gain on at least one canonical benchmark pair, with the unexplained residual concentrated in classes with genuinely new target appearance (where feature learning is truly needed).
why_important: Mechanism clarity redirects effort: if thresholds explain most gains, cheap calibration replaces expensive iterative retraining in many deployments, and residual analysis identifies where feature adaptation genuinely matters.
why_possibly_novel: Threshold effects are acknowledged in pseudo-labeling design (class-balanced thresholds), but a feature-frozen decomposition quantifying their share of total gains appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One benchmark pair: run standard self-training; run feature-frozen logit adjustment on identical pseudo-labels; compare gains, per-class residual analysis.
main_risk: Iterative self-training's gains may compound through improved pseudo-labels in later rounds, which the one-shot control structurally cannot match.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Self-training adapts representations to the target domain; that is why it works.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For large sim-to-real gaps, features may be genuinely unusable without adaptation, capping the threshold-only recovery at a small fraction.
fastest_falsification: The feature-frozen control is a single cheap run on top of any existing self-training pipeline.

one_line: Domain-adversarial training's benefit is mostly generic regularization from gradient noise, not domain invariance: a matched-noise control without any domain discriminator reproduces the gains
problem: Domain-adversarial objectives are motivated by invariance theory, but their gains have never been separated from the generic regularization effect of injecting structured gradient noise into feature learning.
core_hypothesis: The adversarial gradient acts primarily as an anisotropic noise/regularizer improving generalization broadly rather than aligning domains specifically; a control that injects domain-label-free gradient perturbations matched in magnitude and layer profile will achieve statistically similar target-domain gains, and measured domain invariance (discriminator accuracy on features) will correlate poorly with target performance across runs.
falsifiable_prediction: Matched-noise controls will fall within the seed-level confidence interval of adversarial training's target performance on standard pairs, and across a grid of runs, feature-level domain-discriminability will not predict target mIoU.
why_important: If invariance is not the working mechanism, theoretical motivation and method design in a large literature need revision, and simpler noise-based regularizers could replace unstable adversarial training.
why_possibly_novel: Critiques of domain-invariance theory exist; the matched-noise causal control for segmentation adaptation appears unrun.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One benchmark pair, three arms (source-only, adversarial, matched-noise), 5 seeds each; plus invariance-vs-performance scatter across all runs.
main_risk: Constructing a fair matched-noise control (matching magnitude, layer distribution, and temporal profile) is technically delicate and contestable.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Domain-adversarial training works by making features domain-invariant, per its theoretical motivation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Invariance may matter precisely in the hardest classes where noise controls fail, visible only in class-stratified analysis.
fastest_falsification: The invariance-vs-performance scatter from existing published or reproduced runs; a strong correlation defends the standard account cheaply.

one_line: Synthetic-data pretraining selects flatter loss-basins: robustness gains attributed to synthetic content partly reflect optimization geometry, testable by sharpness-matched controls
problem: Synthetic pretraining often improves robustness to shifts unrelated to the synthetic content, an anomaly unexplained by coverage arguments.
core_hypothesis: Abundant, noise-free, easily-fit synthetic data changes early optimization trajectories toward flatter basins; flatness (not content coverage) then confers generic shift robustness, so sharpness metrics will differ systematically between synthetic-pretrained and real-only models, and sharpness-matched real-only controls (via SAM-style optimizers) will reproduce much of the robustness gain without any synthetic data.
falsifiable_prediction: Synthetic-pretrained models will occupy measurably flatter minima; flat-seeking optimization on real data alone will close a substantial share of the robustness gap to synthetic-pretrained models on shifts unrelated to synthetic content.
why_important: Separates two entangled explanations of synthetic data's value (information vs optimization), with direct consequences for whether teams should buy data or change optimizers.
why_possibly_novel: Flat-minima robustness links exist generally; attributing synthetic-pretraining robustness specifically to basin selection with a matched-control design appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train {real-only, synthetic-pretrained, real-only+flat-seeking-optimizer}; measure sharpness and robustness on content-unrelated shifts; compare gap closure.
main_risk: Sharpness metrics are reparameterization-sensitive; conclusions need multiple flatness measures to be credible.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Synthetic pretraining helps because of what the data contains (coverage, diversity, labels), not how it shapes optimization.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Flatness differences may be an epiphenomenon of dataset size rather than synthetic character, disappearing under size-matched controls.
fastest_falsification: Sharpness measurement on existing checkpoint pairs (synthetic-pretrained vs real-only); if flatness does not differ, the mechanism is absent.

one_line: Low-realism-first curricula work through shape-bias induction: the ordering benefit exists only when early data has exaggerated shape cues, testable by cue-conflict evaluation
problem: Realism-ordered curricula (train on cartoons/low-poly first, photoreal later) sometimes help transfer, but the mechanism is unexplained, so nobody knows when to expect the benefit.
core_hypothesis: Low-realism data helps not because of gradual difficulty but because texture-poor rendering forces shape reliance during the early bias-formation phase; the curriculum benefit therefore requires early-phase shape-cue dominance and will vanish if low-realism data is texture-rich (e.g., noisy but shapeless), and the benefit's size will track post-training shape-bias measured by cue-conflict tests.
falsifiable_prediction: Curricula starting with texture-poor low-realism data will beat both reverse ordering and texture-rich low-realism starts, and final shape-bias scores will mediate the transfer improvement (statistical mediation across arms).
why_important: Turns an anecdotal trick into a design rule (engineer early data for shape dominance) and connects synthetic-curriculum practice to the shape/texture-bias literature quantitatively.
why_possibly_novel: Shape bias and curricula are separately studied; the mediation claim that shape-bias induction is the active ingredient of realism curricula appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Four arms {shape-poor-first, shape-rich-low-realism-first, photoreal-first, mixed}; measure transfer to real targets and cue-conflict shape bias; run mediation analysis.
main_risk: Constructing texture-rich-but-low-realism early data that controls difficulty is fiddly; poor construction weakens the dissociation.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Curriculum orderings help via difficulty progression; realism is a proxy for difficulty.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The benefit may come from optimization warm-up dynamics indifferent to cue composition, breaking the mediation.
fastest_falsification: Two-arm comparison (shape-poor-first vs shape-rich-first at matched realism); if transfer is equal, shape mediation fails.

one_line: Interleaved sim-real cycling beats single-pass sim-then-real at equal compute: domain rehearsal prevents each domain's gains from overwriting the other's
problem: The universal recipe is one pass of synthetic pretraining followed by one pass of real fine-tuning; whether alternating between the domains dominates this schedule is untested as a controlled question.
core_hypothesis: Sequential training suffers bidirectional forgetting (synthetic boundary precision lost in real phase; real appearance statistics absent in sim phase); interleaving domains in repeated short cycles acts as rehearsal, retaining both components and yielding better real-domain performance and better shift robustness at matched total steps.
falsifiable_prediction: Cycled schedules will beat sequential schedules on real-domain evaluation and on held-out shifts at equal compute across two dataset pairs, with the advantage growing as the number of cycles increases up to a saturation point.
why_important: A recipe-level improvement requiring no new data or methods, immediately adoptable by any synthetic-plus-real pipeline.
why_possibly_novel: Rehearsal is standard in continual learning; treating the two-domain training recipe as a continual-learning problem with cycle-count as the control variable appears unexamined for segmentation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Matched-compute arms {sequential, 2-cycle, 4-cycle, 8-cycle} on one synthetic-real pair; evaluate real-domain and shifted-target performance.
main_risk: Interleaving complicates learning-rate scheduling; unfair schedules could produce artifactual orderings either way.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Pretrain-then-fine-tune is the correct order; revisiting synthetic data after real data would pull the model backward.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The final phase's domain dominates in practice; ending on real data may be all that matters, making cycling equivalent to sequential.
fastest_falsification: Sequential vs 4-cycle at small scale; a tie or sequential win in the first comparison ends the strong claim.

one_line: Forgetting under domain shift is layer-heterogeneous: weight-consolidation penalties help backbones but actively hurt decoder heads, so uniform continual-learning regularization is miscalibrated for segmentation
problem: Continual domain adaptation applies parameter-consolidation penalties uniformly across the network, assuming forgetting has uniform cost structure across layers.
core_hypothesis: Backbone features are domain-general (worth protecting) while decoder decision surfaces must track the current domain (protection is harmful); uniform penalties therefore sit on a bad trade-off, and layer-group-specific penalty schedules (strong on backbone, zero or negative on head) will dominate uniform ones across sequential-domain benchmarks.
falsifiable_prediction: In sequential adaptation over 3+ domains, layer-heterogeneous consolidation will beat the best uniform penalty on both average accuracy and backward transfer, and ablations will show uniform penalties' failures concentrated in head-layer rigidity (per-layer plasticity analysis).
why_important: Continual deployment (season cycles, site changes) is the realistic shift regime for fielded segmentation; a structural fix to a default method design choice has broad applicability.
why_possibly_novel: Layer-wise learning-rate practice exists; a principled forgetting-cost asymmetry claim for dense-prediction architectures with consolidation-schedule consequences appears unformulated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sequential three-domain benchmark; arms {no penalty, uniform grid, backbone-only, head-only}; compare average accuracy and backward transfer with per-layer plasticity logging.
main_risk: The backbone/head dichotomy may be too coarse; the true structure could be depth-continuous, requiring finer schedules.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Consolidation strength is one scalar hyperparameter; where it applies in the network is not a first-order design variable.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For small domain gaps, heads may barely need to move, making uniform penalties near-optimal and the refinement pointless.
fastest_falsification: Backbone-only vs uniform arms on one two-domain sequence; the ordering in this single comparison carries the core claim.

one_line: Test-time adaptation amplifies synthetic-training biases: entropy minimization on real streams pushes synthetic-pretrained models toward their generator's systematic errors, a compounding interaction
problem: Test-time adaptation (TTA) and synthetic pretraining are both becoming standard, but their interaction is unstudied: TTA trusts the model's own confident predictions, which synthetic training has systematically biased.
core_hypothesis: Synthetic-pretrained models are confidently wrong in generator-characteristic ways (boundary offsets, class priors); entropy-minimizing TTA reinforces confident predictions, so it amplifies exactly these biases over the adaptation stream, causing larger drift for synthetic-pretrained models than real-trained ones, with drift direction predictable from the pretraining corpus's known biases.
falsifiable_prediction: Under identical TTA on identical real streams, synthetic-pretrained models will degrade (or gain less) relative to real-pretrained models over stream length, with error growth concentrated in the bias directions measured before TTA (e.g., signed boundary offsets, class-prior gaps).
why_important: Flags a dangerous default-stack interaction for deployed systems combining two popular techniques, and provides a pre-deployment audit (measure biases first, predict TTA drift).
