why_possibly_novel: TTA failure modes are studied generically (collapse, noise); the specific compounding with synthetic-pretraining biases and its directional predictability appear unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Two pretrained models (synthetic-heavy vs real), same TTA method on the same long real stream; log per-class errors and boundary offsets over time; compare drift against pre-measured bias vectors.
main_risk: TTA methods vary widely; the interaction may be method-specific, requiring a small method suite for generality.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: TTA is a shift-mitigation layer that helps regardless of pretraining provenance; more adaptation is safer.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Synthetic-pretrained models may be better calibrated under shift (see boundary-noise regularization effects), making TTA safer for them, not riskier.
fastest_falsification: One TTA run per model on a shared stream with bias-direction logging; divergence patterns visible within a day of experiments.

one_line: Harmful synthetic training samples are identifiable before training by gradient conflict against a small real anchor set, and pruning them beats training on everything
problem: Synthetic corpora contain a mixture of helpful and harmful samples for real-domain performance, but current practice filters (if at all) by visual quality, which is uncorrelated with training harm.
core_hypothesis: A sample's harm is predicted by the alignment of its training gradient with the average gradient of a small real anchor set on a partially trained model; samples with persistently negative alignment damage real-domain performance, and pruning the most-conflicting fraction yields better final models than full-corpus training at reduced compute.
falsifiable_prediction: Removing the bottom slice of gradient-aligned synthetic samples will improve real-domain mIoU over full-data training, while removing random or lowest-visual-quality slices of equal size will not, across two corpora and two architectures.
why_important: Provides an operational, task-grounded definition of synthetic-sample harm and a cheap curation step that converts bigger-is-better generation into measured selection.
why_possibly_novel: Gradient-based data valuation exists in classification and instruction-tuning contexts; a validated harm-pruning pipeline for synthetic dense-prediction corpora with quality-filter controls appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Score one synthetic corpus by anchor-gradient alignment; train {full, harm-pruned, random-pruned, quality-pruned} at matched retained size; compare real-domain performance.
main_risk: Gradient alignment scores computed on early checkpoints may not predict late-training harm (scores are trajectory-dependent).
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Synthetic data curation means visual-quality filtering; below-par samples are aesthetic failures, and more data is otherwise better.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Harm may be emergent at the distribution level (over-representation effects) rather than attributable to individual samples, making per-sample scores meaningless.
fastest_falsification: Score-then-prune on a small corpus with one retrain; if harm-pruned does not beat random-pruned, per-sample harm attribution fails.

one_line: Synthetic data hurts exactly the classes it over-represents relative to the target label marginal: silent prior mismatch is a necessary-condition failure that class-frequency matching fixes for free
problem: Synthetic corpora are generated with class balances chosen for convenience (balanced, or generator-natural), shifting the effective label prior of training data away from the target's, a mismatch nobody audits.
core_hypothesis: Per-class harm from synthetic admixture is systematically related to the over-representation ratio (synthetic class share vs target class share); over-represented classes invade neighboring classes' pixels at decision boundaries, so re-weighting or re-sampling synthetic data to the target marginal removes most class-level harm without touching the images.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-class IoU changes from synthetic admixture will correlate negatively with over-representation ratio (invaded neighbors will show precision drops), and marginal-matched resampling of the same corpus will flip most harmed classes to neutral-or-positive, reproducibly across two datasets.
why_important: A zero-generation-cost fix (resampling weights) for a widespread silent failure, plus an audit statistic (over-representation ratio) that should appear in every synthetic-data paper's table.
why_possibly_novel: Label-shift correction is classic for classification; its application as a synthetic-corpus design audit for dense prediction, with the neighbor-invasion mechanism, appears unformalized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One corpus with deliberately skewed class balance; train {as-is, marginal-matched}; per-class IoU deltas vs over-representation ratio; confusion-flow analysis for neighbor invasion.
main_risk: Pixel-level marginals are context-dependent (class share varies by scene type), so a single global matching target may be too crude.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Class balance in synthetic data is a free design choice; balanced generation is considered a virtue that helps rare classes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Loss re-weighting and strong augmentation may already neutralize prior mismatch, leaving nothing for marginal matching to fix.
fastest_falsification: Plot per-class deltas vs over-representation from any existing with/without-synthetic experiment pair; the correlation either exists in archived results or does not.

one_line: High-realism synthetic data can hurt more than low-realism data: near-domain errors are absorbed as facts while far-domain errors are discounted as noise (an uncanny-valley effect for training data)
problem: The community assumes monotonicity, more realism is always safer, so generator improvements are shipped into data pipelines without re-auditing downstream harm.
core_hypothesis: Models implicitly weight training signal by domain proximity: physically wrong content in obviously synthetic images is partially isolated (features are domain-gated), while the same wrong content in near-photoreal images is integrated into real-domain features, so at fixed content-error rate, downstream harm is non-monotonic in realism with a maximum near (but below) full realism.
falsifiable_prediction: Injecting identical controlled content errors (wrong shadows, impossible object supports) into low-, mid-, and high-realism variants of the same scenes will produce the largest real-domain error inheritance in the high-realism arm, with the inherited-error signature matching the injected error type.
why_important: If realism amplifies the cost of content errors, generator upgrades must be coupled to content-fidelity audits, and 'better-looking data' is not automatically better data, a consequential correction to current pipeline economics.
why_possibly_novel: Realism-vs-transfer studies assume monotone benefit; the error-absorption-gated-by-domain-proximity mechanism with controlled error injection appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One scene corpus at 3 realism tiers with matched injected error rates; train per tier (plus error-free controls); measure error-signature inheritance on real evaluation data.
main_risk: Realism tiers differ in more than realism (frequency content, color statistics), requiring careful matching to isolate the proximity mechanism.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: More realistic synthetic data is monotonically better; any harm comes from insufficient realism, not from too much.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Feature learning may not be domain-gated at all, making harm proportional to error rate regardless of realism, i.e., flat rather than peaked.
fastest_falsification: Two tiers (low, high) with injected shadow errors and error-free controls; four small runs expose the interaction sign.

one_line: Synthetic corpora have a 'poison tail': a small fraction of physically inconsistent images (impossible shadows, floating objects) causes disproportionate generalization damage, and physics-lint filters recover it
problem: Quality control for generated corpora targets average visual quality; the damage distribution across samples may instead be extremely heavy-tailed, dominated by rare physically incoherent images that look fine at a glance.
core_hypothesis: Physically inconsistent samples teach the model that certain physical regularities (shadow-object attachment, support relations) are unreliable, degrading its use of those cues everywhere, so harm scales super-linearly with the inconsistent fraction and removing the small inconsistent tail recovers most synthetic-data harm at negligible data loss.
falsifiable_prediction: Dose-response experiments (0%, 1%, 5%, 20% inconsistent samples) will show super-linear degradation of real-domain performance on physics-cue-dependent evaluations (shadow-boundary accuracy, support-relation-adjacent classes), and automatic physics-consistency filtering will recover near-clean performance at under 5% data removal.
why_important: Shifts synthetic-data QC from average-quality metrics to tail detection, a cheaper and more effective target, and quantifies how forgiving training is (or is not) to physical incoherence.
why_possibly_novel: Label-noise dose-response studies exist; physics-inconsistency (image-content coherence, not label error) as the harm variable with a super-linearity claim appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct inconsistent variants of a clean synthetic corpus by compositing without shadow/support coherence; run the dose-response; test a simple consistency-filter's recovery.
main_risk: Detecting 'physical inconsistency' automatically is itself hard; the filter may be the weakest link of the demonstration.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: A few odd images in a large corpus are harmless noise; average quality is what matters.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Networks may treat rare inconsistent samples as outliers with tiny effective weight, making the dose-response sub-linear instead.
fastest_falsification: The 0% vs 5% arms alone on physics-cue evaluations; a null difference at 5% strongly undercuts super-linearity.

one_line: Synthetic-data harm is model-size-dependent with a sign flip: small models gain from the same corpus that hurts large models, because capacity determines whether generator quirks are fit
problem: Synthetic-data value is validated on one model size and assumed to transfer across scales, though larger models have the capacity to fit generator-specific regularities that smaller models must ignore.
core_hypothesis: For a fixed synthetic corpus with characteristic generator artifacts, small models extract mostly the transferable content signal (net gain), while large models additionally fit artifact regularities that misfire on real data (net harm at the margin), producing a monotone trend of synthetic marginal value in model scale, crossing zero at a corpus-dependent capacity.
falsifiable_prediction: Sweeping model scale with fixed synthetic-real data, the marginal effect of the synthetic admixture on real-domain performance will decrease monotonically with scale and change sign, and the crossover scale will shift upward when the corpus is artifact-randomized (causally tying the flip to artifacts, not content).
why_important: Synthetic-data decisions made on small proxies systematically mislead at deployment scale (and vice versa); a scale-dependent value curve with a causal mechanism changes how pipelines validate data.
why_possibly_novel: Data-quality-vs-scale interactions are discussed for web text; a controlled sign-flip demonstration with artifact-randomization causality for dense prediction appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: 4 model scales x {with, without synthetic} x {vanilla, artifact-randomized corpus}; plot marginal synthetic value vs scale under both corpus variants.
main_risk: Compute-heavy design; also scale confounds optimization hyperparameters that must be re-tuned per size for fairness.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Synthetic data's benefit is a corpus property, roughly stable across model sizes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Larger models also generalize better from imperfect data, which may cancel or reverse the artifact-fitting effect, keeping marginal value flat.
fastest_falsification: Two well-separated scales with/without synthetic (four runs); a sign difference or strong trend in the marginal value appears immediately or not at all.

one_line: Mask-conditioned generation shrinks shape diversity: segmenters trained on generated pairs predict systematically smoother, more prototypical shapes, measurable as shape-distribution contraction on real data
problem: Generators regularize toward typical shapes when rendering objects into conditioning masks, but whether this shape prior contaminates downstream segmenters' output geometry is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Generated training pairs under-represent shape extremes (irregular, fragmented, highly concave instances), so downstream models' predicted shape statistics on real data contract toward prototypes (lower shape-complexity variance) relative to real-trained controls, harming exactly the irregular instances that matter in medical, damage-assessment, and biological applications.
falsifiable_prediction: Shape-descriptor distributions (convexity, boundary complexity, fragmentation) of predictions from generated-pair-trained models will have measurably lower variance than real-trained controls on identical test images, and per-instance IoU deficits will concentrate in the shape-extreme quantiles.
why_important: Identifies a structural ceiling of generation-for-segmentation for irregular-shape domains and defines a monitoring statistic (shape-distribution contraction) that pipelines can track.
why_possibly_novel: Mode collapse is a generator-side concept; its transmission into a downstream segmenter's output-shape statistics with instance-level consequences appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train on {real pairs, generated pairs} at matched size; compare prediction shape-descriptor distributions and shape-quantile-stratified IoU on a shape-diverse real test set.
main_risk: Shape contraction may partly reflect the segmenter's own smoothing priors, requiring the real-trained control to difference it out carefully.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Generated pairs are unbiased if masks are diverse; conditioning masks control the shape distribution, so no shape bias can enter.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If conditioning masks come from real label statistics, the generator's shape prior may only affect texture, not learned shape boundaries, nullifying the contraction.
fastest_falsification: Compare shape-descriptor variance of the two models' predictions on 500 real images; a variance match falsifies contraction without further work.

one_line: Synthetic-trained models hallucinate structures resembling their generator's texture priors on real images, and the hallucinations are traceable by nearest-neighbor retrieval into the training corpus
problem: Confident false-positive regions produced by synthetic-trained segmenters on real images are treated as generic errors, though they may be specific, attributable imports from the generator's learned texture distribution.
core_hypothesis: A distinguishable subset of real-image false positives corresponds to the model matching local real texture to generator-characteristic texture-class associations; retrieving nearest training patches for false-positive regions will show significantly elevated similarity to synthetic training patches (vs correct regions' retrievals), making hallucinations forensically attributable to corpus content.
falsifiable_prediction: False-positive regions of synthetic-trained models will retrieve synthetic training patches at higher similarity and higher synthetic-fraction than matched correct regions, an effect absent in real-trained controls, and removing the implicated training-texture clusters will preferentially eliminate the corresponding hallucination family.
why_important: Creates an error-forensics loop for synthetic pipelines (trace hallucination to corpus cluster, fix corpus, retrain), converting mysterious deployment errors into actionable data edits.
why_possibly_novel: Training-data attribution is emerging for generative models; applying retrieval-based attribution to dense-prediction errors with a corpus-editing intervention appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect false positives of a synthetic-trained model on real data; run patch retrieval into the mixed training corpus; compare synthetic-fraction statistics vs matched controls; edit corpus and retrain for one hallucination family.
main_risk: Patch-similarity retrieval may be dominated by generic texture matches, diluting attribution specificity.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Deployment errors under shift are diffuse consequences of the domain gap, not traceable to specific training-corpus content.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Errors may arise from feature-level interactions invisible to patch retrieval, making attribution systematically incomplete rather than merely noisy.
fastest_falsification: Retrieval statistics on 200 false-positive regions vs controls; the synthetic-fraction elevation either shows up or the forensic premise fails.

one_line: Most synthetic-data harm is a late-layer phenomenon: dropping synthetic data for the last training epochs (real-only cool-down) retains the benefits and sheds the harms
problem: Synthetic data's benefits (feature coverage) and harms (biased decision surfaces) are entangled across training, and no cheap recipe separates them.
core_hypothesis: Benefits accrue in early/mid training when features form, while harms concentrate in late training when decision boundaries calibrate to the (biased) mixture distribution; therefore a real-only cool-down phase at the end recovers most of the harm at zero extra cost, and its effect size localizes to output-adjacent layers (verifiable by layer-swap analysis between cooled and uncooled models).
falsifiable_prediction: Real-only cool-down will beat both full-mixture training and equal-length real-only training across mixing ratios, and transplanting only the cooled model's late layers onto the uncooled model's backbone will capture most of the cool-down gain.
why_important: A recipe-level, zero-cost fix that also localizes where in the network synthetic harm lives, informing more surgical interventions.
why_possibly_novel: Data-mixture curricula exist; the harm-localization claim with layer-transplant verification and the cool-down as its consequence appear untested for dense prediction.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One synthetic-real pair, arms {mixture, mixture+cool-down, real-only}; then layer-swap analysis between cooled/uncooled checkpoints on real evaluation.
main_risk: Cool-down may erase boundary-precision benefits along with harms if those also live late in the network, netting to zero.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Data mixtures act uniformly across training; scheduling within a fixed mixture is not a recognized lever for harm control.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Harm may live in early features (artifact detectors) rather than late decision layers, making cool-down useless and the localization claim backwards.
fastest_falsification: Cool-down arm vs mixture arm (two runs); the layer-swap analysis needs no additional training.

one_line: Public 'real' benchmarks are drifting synthetic-ward as web-scraped generated imagery leaks in, silently flattering synthetic-trained models in evaluation
problem: Newer segmentation datasets scrape web imagery from years when generated content is prevalent, so evaluation sets may contain generated or generator-post-processed images, changing what 'real-domain performance' measures.
core_hypothesis: Recent web-sourced benchmarks contain a measurable and growing fraction of generated or AI-edited imagery; synthetic-trained models perform relatively better on this contaminated slice than on verified-camera imagery, inflating their measured transfer and biasing method comparisons that involve synthetic training.
falsifiable_prediction: Applying generated-content detectors to benchmark releases by collection year will show a rising flagged fraction; per-slice evaluation will show synthetic-trained models' gap to real-trained models shrinking on flagged slices versus verified-camera slices, across multiple benchmarks.
why_important: Benchmark validity underpins every claim in the field; if the real-vs-synthetic distinction is eroding inside test sets, sim-to-real progress numbers need re-auditing and future benchmarks need provenance controls.
why_possibly_novel: Benchmark contamination by generated content is discussed for image-generation evaluation and LLMs; its quantified effect on segmentation transfer comparisons appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run two independent generated-content detectors over 3 benchmarks of different vintages; construct flagged/verified slices; evaluate one synthetic-trained and one real-trained model per slice; compare gap structures.
main_risk: Generated-content detectors have their own biases (flagging stylized or edited photos), so slice construction needs manual verification of a sample.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Benchmark test sets are ground-truth real imagery; contamination concerns apply to training data, not evaluation data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Segmentation benchmarks may be curated from sources (dashcams, dedicated collections) structurally immune to generated-content leakage, making the flagged fraction negligible.
fastest_falsification: Detector pass over one recent web-scraped benchmark; a near-zero flagged fraction ends the concern for that class of datasets.

one_line: Distillation from synthetic-trained teachers transfers their domain biases to students trained on real data, so 'clean' student pipelines silently inherit synthetic artifacts one generation removed
problem: Knowledge distillation is used to compress models whose training involved synthetic data, and the student is presumed clean because it only ever saw real images.
core_hypothesis: Teacher soft labels encode synthetic-origin biases (boundary offsets, class-prior tilts, texture-class shortcuts); students distilled on real images with such teachers reproduce a measurable fraction of these biases, so bias audits performed only on training-data provenance miss inherited contamination in deployed students.
falsifiable_prediction: Students distilled from synthetic-heavy teachers will exhibit the teachers' signature biases (signed boundary offsets, specific confusion patterns) at a significant fraction of teacher magnitude, while students distilled from real-trained teachers of equal accuracy will not, with all students trained on identical real images.
why_important: Deployment governance increasingly asks about training-data provenance; showing bias flows through distillation regardless of student data would change how model lineage must be audited.
why_possibly_novel: Distillation transfers of robustness and calibration are studied; the transmission of domain-shift-specific biases from synthetic training through soft labels appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Two teachers (synthetic-heavy, real-only) matched on real-domain accuracy; distill both into identical students on identical real data; run bias-signature audits (boundary offsets, confusion patterns) on all four models.
main_risk: Matching teacher accuracy while varying provenance is hard; unmatched teachers confound bias inheritance with capability differences.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: A student's properties come from its own training data and the teacher's accuracy; provenance-specific biases dilute away through distillation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Soft labels on real images may only convey target-domain-consistent information, filtering out synthetic-specific biases automatically.
fastest_falsification: Boundary-offset audit of one distilled student vs its synthetic-heavy teacher and a real-trained reference; a single audit pass on existing models if available.

one_line: Domain randomization confers only a small subset of the invariances it nominally randomizes, and post-hoc invariance probing predicts its diminishing returns before scaling it up
problem: Domain randomization (DR) is scaled by adding axes and widening ranges on faith, without measuring which randomized nuisances the model actually became invariant to.
core_hypothesis: Models exposed to randomization learn invariance selectively (only for nuisances whose variation exceeds a task-interference threshold), so an invariance-probe panel (measuring feature sensitivity per randomized axis) will show large gaps between randomized and acquired invariances, and those gaps will predict which additional randomization investment is wasted.
falsifiable_prediction: Across DR-trained models, per-axis acquired invariance measured by probes will be highly non-uniform despite uniform randomization budgets, and axes with saturated invariance will show zero transfer gain from doubled randomization while unsaturated axes show continued gains.
why_important: Turns DR budgeting from blind scaling into probe-guided allocation, potentially cutting simulation costs substantially while improving transfer.
why_possibly_novel: DR ablations measure end-task transfer only; an intermediate invariance-audit layer with predictive use for budget allocation appears unformalized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train DR models with a fixed axis set; build per-axis probes (feature distance under controlled single-axis variation); double randomization on saturated vs unsaturated axes; compare transfer deltas against probe predictions.
main_risk: Invariance probes measure feature-level sensitivity, which may not map cleanly to task-level robustness.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Randomizing an axis produces invariance to that axis roughly in proportion to the randomization width.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Invariance may be acquired holistically rather than per-axis, making per-axis probes the wrong measurement basis.
fastest_falsification: Probe panel on one existing DR-trained checkpoint; strongly non-uniform acquired invariance is the entry condition for everything else.

one_line: DR axes are sub-additive because early layers absorb multiple randomizations with shared invariance machinery: texture and lighting randomization together yield less than the sum of their solo gains
problem: Randomization axes are added to pipelines assuming roughly additive benefits, inflating expected returns of each new axis.
core_hypothesis: Different photometric randomizations (texture, lighting, color) are absorbed by overlapping early-layer invariance mechanisms, so their transfer benefits overlap substantially; a factorial DR experiment will show consistent negative interaction terms among photometric axes but near-zero interactions between photometric and geometric axes, reflecting separate absorption pathways.
falsifiable_prediction: In a 2x2x2 factorial (texture, lighting, viewpoint randomization), photometric-photometric interactions will be significantly negative while photometric-geometric interactions will be near zero, reproducibly across two sim-to-real pairs.
why_important: Gives DR pipeline designers a composition rule (diversify across pathway families, not within) and corrects cost-benefit projections for new axes.
why_possibly_novel: DR ablations are one-factor-at-a-time; the pathway-based interaction-structure prediction appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render the 8 factorial cells at matched budgets, train 8 models, estimate interaction terms on real-domain transfer with seed replication.
main_risk: Interaction estimates need tight seed variance; underpowered cells would render signs unreliable.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Each randomization axis contributes its own robustness; more axes are additively better.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Interactions might be positive (curriculum-like synergy) if joint randomization forces more abstract features, inverting the prediction.
fastest_falsification: Three cells (texture-only, lighting-only, both) at small scale expose the pairwise interaction sign quickly.

one_line: Randomization ranges should match the target-domain variance, not maximize width: over-randomization measurably reduces feature specificity and caps transfer ('invariance overdraft')
problem: DR practice favors the widest feasible randomization ranges on the theory that more invariance is always safer, but invariance to variation the target never exhibits must cost representation capacity.
core_hypothesis: For each axis there is an optimal randomization width near the target-domain's actual variance on that axis; widths beyond it force invariance to unrealistic variation, discarding discriminative information (measurable as reduced feature specificity for target-relevant distinctions) and degrading transfer, producing an inverted-U in width.
falsifiable_prediction: Sweeping randomization width per axis will show inverted-U transfer curves whose optima align with independently measured target-domain variances on those axes, and feature-specificity probes will decline monotonically past the optimum.
why_important: Replaces the maximalist DR doctrine with a measurement-driven rule (measure target variance per axis, set widths accordingly), improving transfer while cutting rendering cost.
why_possibly_novel: Over-randomization harm is occasionally reported anecdotally; the variance-matching optimum rule with feature-specificity mechanism appears unformulated and untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pick 2 axes (color temperature, object scale); sweep 5 widths each; train models; verify inverted-U and optimum-variance alignment against measured target statistics.
main_risk: Target-domain variance is estimated from limited samples, and optima may be broad, making alignment hard to establish sharply.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Wider randomization is safer; any excess invariance is at worst neutral.
why_it_might_be_wrong: High-capacity models may retain discriminative features despite wide randomization, flattening the U's right side to neutrality.
fastest_falsification: One axis, three widths (narrow, matched, extreme); a monotone improvement with width kills the overdraft claim.

one_line: Physically co-varying randomization (parameters sampled with realistic correlations) beats independent-axis randomization at matched sample count, because independence generates off-manifold worlds
problem: DR samples each parameter independently (sun angle, fog, wetness, exposure), producing many jointly impossible worlds (blazing sun with dense fog and long exposure), whose training value is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: Real environmental parameters co-vary strongly; independent sampling wastes a large fraction of renders on off-manifold combinations that teach nothing about reality and dilute on-manifold coverage, so sampling from a fitted joint distribution (correlations estimated from weather/imaging metadata) yields better transfer at matched render budgets.
falsifiable_prediction: Correlation-aware sampling will beat independent sampling on real-domain transfer at equal sample counts, and the advantage will scale with the fraction of off-manifold samples that independent sampling produces (controllable via correlation strength in the fitted model).
why_important: A sampling-strategy change with zero rendering-cost increase, plus a quantified account of when independence is acceptable (weakly correlated parameter sets).
why_possibly_novel: Structured DR exists in specific robotics contexts; the general on-manifold sampling principle with an off-manifold-fraction dose-response for segmentation transfer appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit a joint parameter distribution from public weather/exposure statistics; render matched corpora under independent vs joint sampling; train and compare transfer; vary correlation strength for the dose-response.
main_risk: Off-manifold worlds might actually help as hard exploration (the DR philosophy), reversing the prediction.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Independent uniform randomization is the canonical DR recipe; unrealistic combinations are a feature (forcing invariance), not a bug.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The DR philosophy may be right: impossible worlds may force stronger abstraction than realistic ones, and correlation-aware sampling may underperform.
fastest_falsification: Two matched corpora (independent vs joint sampling) and two training runs on one sim-to-real pair.

one_line: DR's gains are largely predictable from gradient variance across randomized copies of the same scene, revealing it as a variance-reduction technique measurable before full training
problem: There is no cheap predictor of how much a given randomization configuration will help transfer; every configuration change requires full training runs to evaluate.
core_hypothesis: DR works by exposing the model to nuisance-varied copies of identical content, and its benefit is governed by how much the induced gradient variance across copies covers the sim-to-real perturbation directions; a pre-training statistic (gradient dispersion across randomized copies, projected against sim-real feature differences) predicts final transfer gains across DR configurations.
falsifiable_prediction: Across 8+ DR configurations, the copy-gradient-dispersion statistic computed on a probe network will rank final transfer performance with high correlation, and configurations matched on the statistic but differing in nominal axis count will transfer equivalently.
why_important: Reduces DR configuration search from many full trainings to cheap probe measurements, and provides mechanistic clarity on what DR actually optimizes.
why_possibly_novel: DR theory exists in expectation-over-domains formulations; an operational pre-training predictor based on copy-wise gradient geometry appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate randomized copy-sets under 8 configurations; compute the statistic on a small probe; train full models; test rank correlation and the matched-statistic equivalence.
main_risk: Probe-scale gradient geometry may diverge from full-model geometry, degrading the prediction exactly for the expensive configurations of interest.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: DR configurations must be evaluated by end-to-end training; no intermediate statistic is trusted as a surrogate.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Transfer may hinge on rare randomization events (tail draws) invisible to variance statistics computed over typical copies.
fastest_falsification: Compute the statistic for 3 configurations with known transfer results from prior sweeps; rank agreement in this retrospective check gates further investment.

one_line: Randomizing nuisances the target domain holds fixed (e.g., viewpoint for a mounted camera) actively costs accuracy: fixed-nuisance identification should precede any DR design
problem: DR pipelines randomize every available axis, including ones that are constant in the deployment (camera height for a fixed installation, lighting for an indoor line), a systematic mismatch nobody prices.
core_hypothesis: Invariance to a deployment-constant nuisance strictly discards usable information (the model could have exploited the constancy as context); for fixed-camera deployments, viewpoint-randomized training will measurably underperform viewpoint-fixed training with matched data volume, with the deficit concentrated in classes that benefit from the stable geometry prior.
falsifiable_prediction: On fixed-camera evaluation, viewpoint-fixed synthetic training will beat viewpoint-randomized training at matched budgets, and the gap will grow for classes whose recognition depends on position-in-frame priors, while on multi-camera evaluation the ordering reverses.
why_important: Establishes deployment-variance profiling as a mandatory first step of DR design, replacing the randomize-everything default with a matched-invariance principle.
why_possibly_novel: DR papers report what randomization helps; the deliberate demonstration of randomization harm on deployment-constant axes with the class-level mechanism appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One procedural scene set rendered {fixed viewpoint, randomized viewpoint}; evaluate on fixed-camera real data and on multi-view real data; compare orderings and class-level deltas.
main_risk: Fixed-camera real evaluation sets with sufficient class diversity may need to be assembled from surveillance-style datasets with licensing constraints.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Extra invariance is harmless insurance; randomizing an axis the target holds fixed costs nothing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Position priors may contribute negligibly once appearance features are strong, making the insurance genuinely free.
fastest_falsification: The two-arm viewpoint experiment on one fixed-camera dataset; a null gap refutes the harm claim for the most intuitive axis.

one_line: The correct unit of randomization is the scene, not the image: within-scene appearance randomization (same layout, many appearances) teaches layout-invariant features faster than across-scene randomization
problem: DR pipelines randomize parameters per rendered image, conflating two different training signals: appearance variation of identical content versus content variation, whose distinct effects are never separated.
core_hypothesis: Presenting the same scene under many appearances provides aligned contrastive structure (identical labels, varied nuisances) that teaches nuisance invariance more sample-efficiently than the same appearance diversity spread across different scenes, where nuisance and content variation are confounded; matched-budget comparisons will show within-scene randomization reaching target invariance and transfer levels with fewer total images.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched render budgets, corpora organized as (fewer scenes x more appearance variants) will yield higher measured nuisance invariance and better sim-to-real transfer than (more scenes x fewer variants) up to a scene-diversity floor, below which layout coverage collapses and the ordering reverses, yielding a predictable interior optimum.
why_important: Gives DR a two-knob design theory (scene coverage vs variant depth) with an optimum, directly actionable in every rendering pipeline's sampling loop.
why_possibly_novel: The scenes-vs-variants trade appears in passing in dataset papers; its framing as implicit contrastive alignment with an invariance-acquisition-rate mechanism appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fixed budget corpora at 5 scene/variant splits; train identical models; measure invariance probes and real-domain transfer; locate the optimum and test its stability across two targets.
main_risk: The optimum's location likely depends on layout complexity of the target, complicating a clean general statement.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Total image count and randomization width determine DR value; how variation is grouped across scenes is immaterial.
why_it_might_be_wrong: SGD may not exploit within-scene alignment without an explicit contrastive objective, making grouping genuinely immaterial.
fastest_falsification: Two extreme splits at small scale with invariance probes; no invariance-rate difference means the alignment mechanism is inert.

one_line: Curriculum DR (narrow-to-wide randomization ranges) avoids the early-training underfitting that wide-from-start DR causes, reaching better transfer at equal budget
problem: DR applies full-width randomization from step zero, though early training may be unable to extract signal from maximally varied data, wasting the early budget.
core_hypothesis: Wide randomization at initialization slows the formation of basic task features (the model sees mostly nuisance variance before it can represent content), so widening ranges progressively as competence grows preserves early learning speed while reaching the same final invariance, dominating fixed-width DR at matched total steps.
falsifiable_prediction: Progressive-widening schedules will reach higher real-domain transfer than fixed-wide schedules at matched budgets, with learning-curve analysis showing the fixed-wide arm's deficit accumulating specifically in the early phase, and no deficit when starting from a pretrained backbone (competence already present).
why_important: A schedule-only DR improvement with a clean mechanistic signature, plus the pretrained-backbone prediction gives a practical rule for when curricula matter at all.
why_possibly_novel: Curricula over difficulty exist broadly; range-scheduling for randomization width with the pretrained-backbone dissociation test appears specific and untested for segmentation DR.
minimal_falsification_experiment: From-scratch and pretrained backbones x {fixed-wide, progressive} schedules at matched budgets on one sim-to-real pair; compare final transfer and early learning curves.
main_risk: Schedule hyperparameters (widening rate) add a tuning dimension that could unfairly favor either arm if not searched symmetrically.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Randomization width is a static dataset property; scheduling it is an unnecessary complication.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern optimizers with warm-up may already absorb the early difficulty, leaving no deficit for the curriculum to fix.
fastest_falsification: The pretrained-backbone cell alone: if fixed-wide matches progressive there but loses from scratch, the mechanism is confirmed cheaply; if fixed-wide never loses, the idea dies.

one_line: A large share of DR's transfer benefit is reproducible by test-time augmentation ensembling on a non-randomized model, identifying which randomization axes truly need training-time exposure
problem: DR requires expensive re-rendering and retraining per configuration, but for some nuisance axes its effect may be equivalent to simply averaging predictions over input perturbations at inference.
core_hypothesis: For photometric axes, DR's benefit approximates marginalization over nuisances, achievable post hoc by test-time augmentation (TTA-ensembling) with matched perturbation families; for geometric/structural axes, training-time exposure changes representations in ways inference-time averaging cannot mimic, so an axis-by-axis equivalence audit will split axes into 'deferable to test time' and 'training-essential'.
falsifiable_prediction: TTA-ensembling over photometric perturbations on a non-DR model will recover a large fraction of photometric DR's transfer gain, while TTA over geometric perturbations will recover little of geometric DR's gain, producing a stable axis classification across two dataset pairs.
why_important: Axes deferable to test time need no rendering or retraining, collapsing DR's cost for a known subset of nuisances and clarifying what training-time DR uniquely contributes.
why_possibly_novel: TTA and DR are separately mature; the systematic equivalence audit framing (which randomization can be moved to inference) appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train {no-DR, photometric-DR, geometric-DR} models; evaluate no-DR under matched photometric/geometric TTA-ensembling; compute recovered fractions per axis type.
main_risk: TTA inference cost scales with ensemble size, so 'equivalence' must be qualified by compute budget to be fair.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: DR's benefits require training-time exposure by definition; inference-time tricks are a separate, weaker category.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Training-time randomization may improve features even for photometric axes (better minima), leaving TTA structurally short everywhere.
fastest_falsification: Photometric recovered-fraction measurement on one pair (one no-DR model, one DR model, one TTA evaluation); low recovery ends the deferability claim.

one_line: Adversarially chosen randomization parameters (worst-case rendering per scene, selected by current-model failure) matches uniform DR's transfer with an order of magnitude fewer rendered images
problem: Uniform randomization spends most of its render budget on parameter draws the model already handles, and active-selection alternatives are untested at the rendering-pipeline level for segmentation.
core_hypothesis: Model failures concentrate in small regions of randomization-parameter space; a closed-loop pipeline that searches, per scene, for parameter draws maximizing current-model loss and renders only those, will match uniform DR's final transfer using a small fraction of the renders, with the efficiency ratio growing as training progresses and failure regions shrink.
falsifiable_prediction: Matched-transfer comparisons will show the active pipeline requiring several-fold fewer rendered images than uniform sampling, and ablations replacing loss-guided search with random search under the same loop will lose most of the efficiency, confirming the selection mechanism.
why_important: Rendering is the cost center of synthetic pipelines; a validated active-rendering loop changes the economics of DR for every simulation-based team.
why_possibly_novel: Active DR exists conceptually in RL and robotics control; a rendering-in-the-loop implementation for dense-prediction transfer with quantified render savings appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement the loop on a procedural pipeline with cheap re-rendering; compare renders-to-target-transfer curves of active vs uniform vs random-search arms on one sim-to-real pair.
main_risk: Worst-case draws may be adversarial artifacts (renderer edge cases) that teach nothing about reality, poisoning the loop.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Uniform coverage of randomization space is the safe and standard sampling policy; per-sample selection is not worth the loop complexity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Loss-guided selection may repeatedly mine the same failure family, collapsing diversity and underperforming uniform sampling at scale.
fastest_falsification: Small-scale loop with an early stopping comparison: if active does not beat uniform in renders-to-fixed-transfer by at least 2x at small scale, the order-of-magnitude claim is implausible.

one_line: Segmentation domain shift factorizes into sensor, appearance, geometry, and layout tiers with a strict transfer-difficulty ordering, testable by constructing single-tier shifts
problem: Domain shift for segmentation lacks an agreed decomposition, so methods, benchmarks, and claims are incomparable: each paper's 'domain gap' mixes different shift kinds in unknown proportions.
core_hypothesis: Shifts can be organized into four tiers (sensor/ISP, surface appearance, object geometry, scene layout); holding all else fixed and shifting one tier at a time in a controlled synthetic environment will reveal a strict difficulty ordering (sensor easiest to adapt, layout hardest), stable across architectures, because each tier requires changes at increasing network depth.
falsifiable_prediction: Single-tier constructed shifts of calibrated magnitude will produce transfer drops with the predicted ordering across architectures, and each tier's drop will correlate with adaptation-required depth (measured by which layers must be fine-tuned to recover performance).
why_important: A validated shift taxonomy with difficulty ordering would give the field a coordinate system: benchmarks could report tier composition, methods could declare tier scope, and results would finally compose.
why_possibly_novel: Informal tier language is everywhere; a controlled single-tier construction with calibrated magnitudes and the depth-correspondence test appears never executed.
minimal_falsification_experiment: In a procedural world, construct four single-tier shift pairs matched by a common magnitude scale (feature-space distance); train, transfer, and measure recovery-depth profiles per tier.
main_risk: Calibrating 'equal magnitude' across qualitatively different tiers is the crux and could be contested whichever scale is chosen.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Domain gap is a scalar; decompositions are narrative devices rather than measurable structure with stable orderings.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The tiers may not be separable even in simulation (layout changes alter shading and occlusion), undermining single-tier construction.
fastest_falsification: Build just the sensor-tier and layout-tier pairs and check the predicted extreme ordering; a reversal ends the taxonomy's core claim.

one_line: Dense prediction breaks classification-derived domain-generalization theory because errors propagate spatially: one shifted region corrupts its neighborhood through receptive fields, violating i.i.d.-example bounds
problem: Theoretical guarantees and intuitions for learning under shift assume independent examples; segmentation's unit of failure is a spatially extended region whose influence spreads, and no empirical characterization of this propagation exists.
core_hypothesis: Under partial-image shift (a shifted patch or region within an otherwise in-domain image), errors extend beyond the shifted region by a distance governed by effective receptive field size, so total error grows super-linearly with shifted-region area, and architectures with larger context aggregation show more propagation despite better in-domain accuracy, a measurable robustness-accuracy structure classification theory does not predict.
falsifiable_prediction: Splicing controlled shifted regions into test images will show error halos around shifted regions with radius scaling with architecture receptive field, and per-architecture halo size will predict full-image shift degradation better than in-domain accuracy does.
why_important: Establishes the empirical law connecting spatial context use to shift fragility, informing both architecture selection for deployment under shift and the correct statistical unit for dense-prediction shift theory.
why_possibly_novel: Effective receptive fields and shift robustness are separately studied; the error-propagation law with halo measurement as a shift-robustness predictor appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct spliced-shift test sets; measure error-halo radii across 4 architectures (CNN small/large context, transformer variants); correlate halo size with full-shift degradation.
main_risk: Splicing borders introduce artifacts that create their own halos, requiring careful blending controls.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: More context is better: global context aggregation is treated as uniformly beneficial, including under shift.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Context aggregation may help reject shifted regions (using surrounding evidence) rather than spread their corruption, inverting the halo prediction.
fastest_falsification: Single-architecture spliced-region test with halo measurement; presence or absence of halos beyond the region boundary is immediately visible.

one_line: Part of the sim-to-real gap is a label-convention artifact: relabeling real evaluation data under the synthetic geometric convention shrinks the measured gap without changing any model
problem: Synthetic labels are geometric truth (exact projections), real labels are annotator conventions (simplified polygons, class-boundary customs); measured 'gaps' conflate model failure with convention mismatch, and the conflation has never been sized.
core_hypothesis: A quantifiable fraction of reported sim-to-real gaps comes from convention mismatch rather than model error; this fraction varies by class (large for amorphous boundaries like vegetation, small for rigid objects) and can be measured by dual-convention relabeling of a modest evaluation subset.
falsifiable_prediction: On a dual-labeled evaluation subset (annotator convention vs geometric convention), synthetic-trained models will score systematically higher under the geometric convention while real-trained models score higher under the annotator convention, with the interaction effect sizing the convention component of the gap per class.
why_important: Every sim-to-real paper's headline number contains this artifact in unknown proportion; sizing it would recalibrate progress claims and motivate convention-explicit benchmarks.
why_possibly_novel: Label-convention issues are acknowledged qualitatively; the dual-convention interaction design that isolates and sizes the artifact appears unexecuted.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Dual-label 200 real images under both conventions with written protocols; evaluate matched synthetic-trained and real-trained models under both; estimate the interaction per class.
main_risk: Producing a faithful 'geometric convention' for real images is expensive and partially ill-defined for fuzzy materials.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Ground-truth labels are convention-free; measured gaps reflect model and domain properties only.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The convention component may be a few tenths of a point, real but negligible against multi-point domain gaps.
fastest_falsification: Evaluate both model types with boundary-tolerance bands of increasing width as a convention-insensitivity proxy; convergence of gaps at small tolerances would suggest a small convention component without any relabeling.

one_line: Shift effects compose predictably: performance under combined shifts is a simple function (approximately multiplicative in survival terms) of single-shift performances, enabling a 'shift algebra' for deployment forecasting
problem: Deployments face combined shifts (night + rain + new city), but evaluation only ever covers single shifts; without a composition rule, coverage of the combinatorial shift space is impossible.
core_hypothesis: For shifts acting through different mechanisms (photometric, weather, geographic), degradation composes approximately multiplicatively in retained-performance terms (retained(A+B) = retained(A) x retained(B)), with systematic deviations only for same-mechanism pairs (interference) and information-destroying pairs (floor effects), so a small set of single-shift measurements forecasts most combined conditions.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a grid of shift pairs and triples on segmentation benchmarks, the multiplicative rule will predict combined retained-mIoU within a small tolerance for cross-mechanism combinations and fail in the predicted directions (over/under-prediction) for same-mechanism and floor cases.
why_important: Would collapse the combinatorial evaluation burden of deployment certification into linear cost (measure singles, compute combinations), a practical foundation for safety cases under compound shift.
why_possibly_novel: Corruption benchmarks report singles; composition laws for shift effects on dense prediction with a mechanism-based deviation taxonomy appear unproposed.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct 6 single shifts spanning 3 mechanisms; evaluate a fixed model zoo on all singles, 15 pairs, and selected triples; fit and test the multiplicative rule with deviation analysis.
main_risk: Composition may be model-dependent (robust models compose differently), fragmenting the law into families.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Combined shifts are unpredictable emergent conditions requiring direct evaluation; no composition law is expected to hold.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Nonlinear failure thresholds (mode collapse of predictions under compound stress) may make any smooth composition rule useless precisely in the dangerous regimes.
fastest_falsification: One model, two cross-mechanism shifts, three evaluations (A, B, A+B); a large multiplicative-rule violation in the benign case ends the strong version immediately.

one_line: Class-agnostic boundary representations transfer across domains far better than class representations: boundary-first pretraining is a domain-generalization strategy, not just an architectural choice
problem: Under strong shift, everything degrades together in standard evaluations, hiding whether some representational components are intrinsically more domain-stable and could anchor transfer.
core_hypothesis: Boundary-ownership structure (where region transitions are) is governed by domain-stable image physics (occlusion, contrast, continuity), while class identity depends on domain-specific appearance statistics; therefore boundary-detection components of segmenters will retain far more cross-domain performance than classification components, and pretraining boundary structure first (then attaching classification) will yield better shifted-domain performance than joint training at matched compute.
falsifiable_prediction: Decomposed evaluation (boundary quality vs region-classification quality) across shifts will show systematically smaller boundary degradation; boundary-first curricula will beat joint training on shifted targets while matching it in-domain, across two shift families.
why_important: Identifies which part of segmentation knowledge is portable across domains, informing pretraining design, adaptation targets (adapt the classifier, trust the boundaries), and modular architecture choices for deployment.
why_possibly_novel: Edge-based pretraining exists historically; the domain-stability asymmetry claim with decomposed shift evaluation and its curriculum consequence appears untested in the modern context.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate boundary-vs-classification degradation for existing models across 3 shift types; then run boundary-first vs joint training at matched compute on one sim-to-real pair.
main_risk: Boundary quality metrics depend on class-agnostic boundary ground truth, which must be derived carefully from semantic labels to avoid circularity.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Representation components degrade together under shift; there is no separable 'portable core' worth designing around.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Boundary detection may rely on the same texture statistics as classification in learned models, making its apparent stability illusory outside hand-crafted-feature intuitions.
fastest_falsification: Decomposed degradation measurement on existing checkpoints across one strong shift; the asymmetry either appears or the premise dies without new training.

one_line: Domain gap grows superlinearly with label-space granularity: fine-grained taxonomies amplify shift damage, making coarse-to-fine adaptation a principled (not just convenient) strategy
problem: Datasets differ in label granularity (road vs road/lane/shoulder), and shift studies never control for it, though granularity plausibly interacts with how much domain-specific appearance detail the task requires.
core_hypothesis: Coarse classes are separable by domain-stable cues while fine distinctions depend on domain-fragile appearance details, so the same physical shift produces disproportionately larger relative degradation at finer granularities; the degradation-vs-granularity curve is superlinear, and adapting coarse levels first then refining (hierarchical adaptation) beats flat adaptation at matched budget.
falsifiable_prediction: Evaluating fixed shifts across nested label hierarchies (2, 8, 20, 60 classes derived from one dataset) will show relative mIoU degradation increasing superlinearly with class count, and hierarchical adaptation will beat flat adaptation on the finest level across two shift types.
why_important: Explains benchmark incomparability (gaps measured at different granularities are not commensurable), and yields a practical adaptation schedule grounded in the granularity-fragility law.
why_possibly_novel: Granularity effects on accuracy are known in-domain; the interaction of granularity with domain shift as a lawful superlinear amplification appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One dataset with a label hierarchy; construct nested tasks; evaluate transfer under 2 shifts at each granularity; fit the degradation-vs-classes curve; run hierarchical-vs-flat adaptation on the finest task.
main_risk: Class count confounds class rarity (finer classes are rarer); needs frequency-controlled analysis to isolate granularity itself.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Domain gap is a property of the image domains; the label space is an orthogonal design choice that scales difficulty uniformly.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fine distinctions might rely on geometry (lane markings are shapes) that is domain-stable, flattening or inverting the curve for some hierarchies.
fastest_falsification: Two-granularity comparison (coarse vs fine) under one shift with frequency-matched classes; the relative-degradation ratio either exceeds unity clearly or the amplification claim fails.

one_line: The domain-pair abstraction is wrong for deployment: shift arrives as ordered trajectories, and method rankings from pairwise benchmarks invert under trajectory evaluation
problem: All standard shift benchmarks evaluate source-to-target pairs, while real deployments experience continuous ordered drift (seasons, sensor aging, gradual geographic rollout); whether pairwise rankings predict trajectory performance is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Methods differ in trajectory-relevant properties invisible to pairwise evaluation (error accumulation under sequential adaptation, recovery after transient shifts, hysteresis); constructing ordered-shift evaluations from existing data (temporal orderings, severity ramps) will show method rankings substantially different from pairwise rankings, with self-training-based methods specifically vulnerable to error accumulation on trajectories.
falsifiable_prediction: Rank correlation between pairwise and trajectory evaluations of the same method suite will be low, with predicted directional flips (accumulating methods fall, stateless methods rise), reproducible across two trajectory constructions.
why_important: If pairwise benchmarks mispredict deployment behavior, the field's evaluation standard needs a trajectory tier; the result would define it and expose which method families are deployment-safe.
why_possibly_novel: Continual test-time adaptation exists as a subfield; the explicit rank-instability claim against pairwise benchmarks with directional predictions for method families appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build 2 trajectory benchmarks (severity ramp on corruptions; temporal ordering of a multi-season dataset); evaluate 6 methods pairwise and on trajectories; compare rankings.
main_risk: Trajectory construction choices (speed of drift, transients) may themselves determine rankings, requiring sensitivity analysis for credibility.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Pairwise source-target evaluation is an adequate proxy for deployment shift; trajectory effects are second-order.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Trajectory performance may be dominated by average pairwise difficulty along the path, keeping rankings stable and the pairwise abstraction adequate.
fastest_falsification: Evaluate 3 methods on one severity-ramp trajectory vs endpoints-only; a strong ranking agreement in this minimal case deflates the instability claim.

one_line: Per-class texture-vs-shape cue reliance measured on the source domain predicts per-class sim-to-real transfer without any target labels: a cue-reliance audit as a transfer forecast
problem: Per-class transfer outcomes are unpredictable before target data exists, so synthetic-data teams cannot prioritize which classes need more assets, randomization, or real anchors.
core_hypothesis: Texture cues are domain-fragile and shape cues domain-stable; a per-class cue-reliance score (measured on source data via cue-conflict stimuli or texture-scrambling sensitivity) will predict per-class sim-to-real IoU drops with useful accuracy, because transfer failure is concentrated where reliance on fragile cues is highest.
falsifiable_prediction: Across two synthetic-to-real pairs, per-class cue-reliance scores will rank per-class transfer drops with strong correlation, and interventions that shift specific classes toward shape reliance (targeted texture randomization) will improve exactly those classes' transfer, confirming the causal direction.
why_important: Provides a pre-deployment, target-free forecasting tool at class granularity, directly actionable in synthetic-data budgeting, and links the shape/texture-bias literature to transfer prediction quantitatively.
why_possibly_novel: Shape/texture bias is studied at whole-model level; per-class reliance measurement used as a class-granular transfer predictor with intervention validation appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute per-class cue-reliance on source-trained models via texture-scrambled and style-swapped source images; measure per-class transfer drops on real targets; test rank correlation; run targeted-randomization intervention for the 3 most texture-reliant classes.
main_risk: Cue-conflict construction for dense prediction (per-region style swaps) is technically finicky and may inject artifacts that distort reliance scores.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Per-class transfer is empirically idiosyncratic; class-level forecasts without target data are not considered feasible.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Per-class drops may be driven by target-side factors (class frequency, context change) that no source-side measurement can see.
fastest_falsification: Reliance-vs-drop scatter for one dataset pair using existing checkpoints; a flat scatter ends the forecasting claim.

one_line: ImageNet-style pretraining helps domain adaptation mostly through texture-statistics coverage, not semantics: label-free texture-corpus pretraining matches it for segmentation transfer
problem: Supervised classification pretraining is the default initialization for segmentation transfer pipelines, and its benefit is attributed to semantic knowledge, steering pretraining investment toward more labels.
core_hypothesis: For transfer under domain shift, the operative contribution of large-scale pretraining is exposure to broad natural-image texture and color statistics (which stabilizes early-layer features across domains); pretraining on label-free corpora engineered for texture-statistics coverage (no object semantics, e.g., texture crops and natural patches) will match classification pretraining for downstream shifted segmentation, while both beat from-scratch, isolating statistics coverage as the mechanism.
falsifiable_prediction: Texture-coverage pretraining will land within a small margin of classification pretraining on shifted-target segmentation across two pairs, and the residual advantage of classification pretraining will concentrate in classes requiring semantic disambiguation (visually similar classes), quantifying the semantic component.
why_important: If statistics coverage is the active ingredient, cheap unlabeled texture corpora replace expensive labeled pretraining for shift-robust segmentation, and pretraining design should optimize coverage metrics rather than label count.
why_possibly_novel: Ablations of pretraining exist (SSL vs supervised); a deliberately semantics-free, coverage-engineered pretraining arm designed to isolate the statistics mechanism for shift robustness appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain matched backbones on {classification corpus, semantics-free texture corpus, nothing}; fine-tune identically for segmentation; evaluate on shifted targets with class-stratified analysis.
main_risk: Constructing a genuinely semantics-free corpus with matched scale and diversity is difficult; residual object content would contaminate the isolation.
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Pretraining transfers semantic knowledge; its benefit under shift reflects generalizable object understanding.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Semantic pretraining may specifically help under shift by providing category priors robust to appearance change, exactly what texture corpora cannot supply.
fastest_falsification: Small-scale pretraining comparison (texture-corpus vs classification at reduced scale) on one shifted pair; near-parity or a large gap appears at small scale already.

one_line: Sim-to-real transfer is bottlenecked by the decoder, not the encoder: frozen synthetic-trained encoders with real-data-tuned decoders recover most of the gap, localizing where domain knowledge lives
problem: Adaptation methods treat the whole network as domain-contaminated, but the actual locus of sim-to-real failure within the encoder-decoder division has never been established, leaving intervention design unguided.
core_hypothesis: Synthetic-trained encoders learn largely domain-transferable features (geometry, contours, coarse texture classes), while decoders overfit domain-specific decision rules (exact boundary placement conventions, class-appearance thresholds); therefore swapping or lightly tuning only the decoder on limited real data will recover a disproportionate share of the sim-to-real gap, while the reverse (tuning only the encoder) recovers little at matched parameter budget.
falsifiable_prediction: In matched-budget partial-tuning experiments, decoder-only tuning will recover most of the achievable gap closure while encoder-only tuning recovers a small fraction, and the asymmetry will persist across architectures and grow with the amount of synthetic pretraining data (better encoders, equally biased decoders).
why_important: Localizing the gap turns adaptation from whole-network retraining into a small-decoder problem, cutting real-data needs and compute, and gives theory a concrete structural claim about where domain specificity resides in dense-prediction networks.
why_possibly_novel: Partial fine-tuning is common practice, but a systematic locus-of-gap study with matched parameter budgets and the pretraining-scale interaction prediction appears missing for sim-to-real segmentation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Synthetic-pretrained models at 2 pretraining scales; real-data budgets {1%, 10%}; arms {decoder-only, encoder-only, full tuning} at matched trainable parameters; compare recovered fractions.
main_risk: The encoder-decoder division is architecture-dependent; results may not translate across families (CNN vs transformer decoders).
territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
default_community_belief: Domain shift contaminates features throughout the network; encoders trained on synthetic data are considered the primary carriers of domain bias.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Early-layer texture statistics are exactly where synthetic and real images differ most, which argues the encoder is the true bottleneck, reversing the prediction.
fastest_falsification: Decoder-only vs encoder-only tuning at 1% real data on one pair; the asymmetry direction is visible in two runs.
